title: CVE-2026-89077 for platform teams: what to instrument before and after the upgrade
summary: CVE-2026-89077 for platform teams: what to instrument before and after the upgrade Platform teams inherit vulnerabilities with a different mandate than security teams. Neither party can hand the other a clean decision, and the CVE becomes an instrumentation project that must be finished before the patch window opens. The two facts that drive instrumentation CVE-2026-89077 is an incorrect implementation of an authentication algorithm in the SFTP module of Progress MOVEit Transfer, classified CWE-303, with a CVSS v3.1 vector of AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H and a base score of 7.5. Two fields matter for instrumentation. Network attack vector means reachability determines who can attempt exploitation. Low privileges required means an attacker needs a valid identity, and identity usage is something a platform team can observe if the logging exists. Baseline the identity population Before the upgrade, produce a list of every SFTP identity on each affected host. Include the authentication method and the last observed authentication. Where the platform does not log authentication events with sufficient detail, that gap becomes the first project item. A flaw in validation produces a successful authentication as its observable outcome, and success events without identity and source detail are not analysable. The list has a second use. After the upgrade, the same list is the input to credential review, and any identity that has not authenticated in a year becomes a candidate for removal rather than a permanent resident. Instrument reachability Reachability from untrusted networks is a property of the deployment, not the CVE. Record for each host which network paths can reach the SFTP listener and which partner address ranges are admitted. This is the input that turns a global CVE into a local priority. An affected host with no inbound SFTP reachability is patched on the normal cycle. An affected host accepting connections from the public internet is patched in the next window. Instrument the patch state Track version per node, not per deployment. Clustered MOVEit installations can have members at different builds, and the load balancer hides the difference. A record that says "MOVEit, patched" without node-level detail cannot answer the question the next audit will ask. The target versions are 2025.1.6 for the 2025.1 branch and 2026.0.4 for the 2026.0 branch. Affected ranges are before 2025.1.6 and from 2026.0.0 before 2026.0.4. Instrument the verification, not just the change A change record with a build number and no behavioural confirmation is an assertion. Add two fields to the change template: the identity used for the known-good authentication test and its result, and the date the partner confirmed a successful transfer. Those two fields convert a claim into evidence, and they cost minutes per host when collected during the window rather than weeks later during an audit. After the upgrade Keep authentication logging enabled at the detail level used for the investigation. The flaw is fixed on the patched host, and the log data answers a different question: whether any authentication occurred during the exposure window that policy did not expect. Retaining that data for the exposure period plus a reasonable margin is the difference between reconstructing events and guessing at them. The handoff Security teams decide when a CVE matters. Platform teams produce the evidence that decision depends on: who holds identities, what reaches the listener, which nodes run which build, and what changed after the upgrade. CVE-2026-89077 is a 7.5 that becomes urgent or routine based on that evidence, and the evidence only exists if someone instruments for it.

title: Cannot Read Properties of Undefined (Reading 'bind'): The Fix
summary: Originally published on CoreMesh . Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'bind') means your code ran something.bind(...) and something was undefined at that moment. The word in quotes is the property the engine tried to read, and bind is a method that only exists on functions. So the real bug is one step to the left of .bind : the function you expected to be there isn't. Usually it's a typo in a method name, a method defined on the wrong object, or a handler that hasn't been assigned yet when the binding runs. The fix is to find out what that left-hand expression actually is, then either make sure it's defined (most common), guard it, or use optional chaining so the missing case is handled on purpose. The sections below walk through those in order, from the most direct fix to the defensive patterns for async code. What the error means Here's the full message as V8 (Chrome, Edge, Node.js) prints it. Firefox and Safari word it differently, as the MDN page on this TypeError lists: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'bind') (V8: Chrome, Edge, Node.js) TypeError: "x" is undefined (Firefox) TypeError: undefined is not an object (evaluating 'obj.x') (Safari) Read it as three parts: Cannot read properties of undefined tells you the object on the left of the dot was undefined . If it says null instead, same problem, different nullish value. (reading 'bind') tells you which property was being read. It does not mean bind is broken. It means the thing you called bind on doesn't exist. The stack trace underneath points to the file and line. That line contains the .bind( you need to look at. MDN sums up the cause in one sentence: there was an unexpected type, most often an undefined or null value. You can't invoke a method on either of those. The engine doesn't know what you meant to bind, so it stops. Find the undefined object behind 'bind' Go to the line from the stack trace and split the expression at the last dot before bind . Everything to the left is the suspect. this . handleClick . bind ( this ) // suspect: this.handleClick service . api . request . bind ( service ) // suspect: service.api.request handlers [ name ]. bind ( ctx ) // suspect: handlers[name] Then check what the suspect evaluates to at that point. Three quick ways: Log it before the bind. A console.log(this.handleClick) on the line above is crude, but it answers the question in one reload. Set a breakpoint on the line in your browser's DevTools or in Node's inspector and hover the expression. Search the file for the exact name. If handleClick is only mentioned once, the method was never defined and you've found your typo. While you're there, work out why it's undefined. The common reasons are: Cause What it looks like Misspelled method name this.handleClik.bind(this) when the method is handleClick Method defined on another class or module Binding this.submit in a component that never declares submit Method is an arrow property or static, not where you think static format() bound as this.format Wrong key in a lookup handlers[action] where action is "SAVE" but the key is "save" Object not loaded yet Binding a method from data that arrives later from fetch Destructuring that missed const { onSave } = props when the parent never passed onSave The last two are the async cases, and they get their own section below. Fix 1: define the function or correct the name If the suspect should always exist, the right fix is to make it exist. Don't paper over a typo with a guard. Here's the most common shape of this bug in a class, followed by its fix: class Button { constructor () { try { // Typo: the class has no method called handleClik this . onClick = this . handleClik . bind ( this ); } catch ( err ) { console . log ( " Caught: " , err . message ); } // Correct name, same line otherwise this . onClick = this . handleClick . bind ( this ); } handleClick () { return " clicked, this is a " + this . constructor . name ; } } const button = new Button (); console . log ( button . onClick ()); The first attempt throws because this.handleClik is undefined . The second works because the name matches the declared method. In a React class component the pattern is identical: every this.x.bind(this) in the constructor needs a matching x() {} in the class body. How to confirm it worked: the error disappears and the bound function actually runs. If you fixed a typo, search the codebase for the misspelled name once more, because the same typo often appears in two places. If you'd rather not bind at all, a class field written as an arrow function keeps this without a bind call: class Button { handleClick = () => { return this . label ; }; } That removes the .bind( line entirely, which removes the place the error could be thrown. Fix 2: guard before you bind When the function is genuinely optional, such as a plugin hook or a callback a caller may or may not pass, check it first. MDN recommends testing for undefined and null explicitly: if ( hooks . onSave !== undefined && hooks . onSave !== null ) { this . save = hooks . onSave . bind ( this ); } For functions I'd go one step further and check the type, because a non-function value with a bind property is rare but a string or number in the wrong slot is not: if ( typeof hooks . onSave === " function " ) { this . save = hooks . onSave . bind ( this ); } MDN also notes you can test plain truthiness with if (foo) when you're sure foo won't be another falsy value like "" or 0 . For a function slot that's usually safe, but typeof reads clearer and costs nothing. How to confirm it worked: the error is gone, and when the hook is missing your code takes the branch you intended rather than silently doing nothing. Add a log or a thrown error with a clear message in the else branch if a missing hook should be a bug. Fix 3: optional chaining and a default Optional chaining ( ?. ) short-circuits to undefined instead of throwing when the thing on its left is null or undefined . It works for property access, bracket access and function calls, per the MDN optional chaining reference . For a bind, you put it between the possibly-missing function and .bind : const config = { hooks : {}, }; // hooks exists but onSave doesn't: no throw, result is undefined const save = config . hooks . onSave ?. bind ( config ); console . log ( " save: " , save ); // plugins doesn't exist at all: chain both steps const plugin = config . plugins ?. onLoad ?. bind ( config ); console . log ( " plugin: " , plugin ); // Grouping breaks the short-circuit. This still throws. try { const broken = ( config . plugins ?. onLoad ). bind ( config ); console . log ( broken ); } catch ( err ) { console . log ( " grouped: " , err . message ); } // Pair with ?? to supply a fallback function const onLoad = config . plugins ?. onLoad ?. bind ( config ) ?? (() => " default loader " ); console . log ( onLoad ()); Two details from that example matter in practice: Every nullable step needs its own ?. . If config.plugins can be missing, config.plugins.onLoad?.bind() still throws on plugins . MDN is explicit about this: if the root object itself may be nullish, you have to put ?. at that position as well. Parentheses end the chain. (a?.b).c evaluates a?.b to undefined , then reads .c on it and throws. MDN gives exactly this case. Keep the chain unbroken from the nullable step through to .bind . The nullish coalescing operator ( ?? ) pairs naturally here. fn?.bind(ctx) ?? fallback gives you a bound function or a default without an if . How to confirm it worked: the line no longer throws, and you've decided what undefined means downstream. If callers of save would themselves crash on undefined , you've only moved the error. That's what the ?? fallback is for. Prevent it in async code The async version of this bug is the one that passes every test and then fails in production. The function you're binding comes from a response, a lazy import or a store that hasn't populated yet. The code binds it once, early, and that moment is before the data exists. The rule is simple: don't bind anything that depends on awaited data until after the await , and validate what came back before you touch it. async function loadHandler ( registry , name ) { // Stand-in for a fetch, dynamic import, or store lookup const entry = await Promise . resolve ( registry [ name ]); const fn = entry ?. handler ; if ( typeof fn !== " function " ) { throw new Error ( `No handler registered for " ${ name } "` ); } return fn . bind ( entry ); } const registry = { save : { label : " save-entry " , handler () { return " saved by " + this . label ; }, }, }; loadHandler ( registry , " save " ). then (( run ) => console . log ( run ())); loadHandler ( registry , " delete " ). catch (( err ) => console . log ( err . message )); The missing delete entry produces an error that names the problem instead of the generic reading 'bind' message. That's the goal in async code: turn an engine error at an unhelpful line into your own error at the point where the assumption failed. A few more habits that prevent the async flavour: Bind inside the function that uses the value, not at module load. Module-level const run = api.method.bind(api) executes before any data exists. In React, bind or wire handlers in render or in the handler itself , not in a constructor that runs before props have arrived. Data fetched in an effect is undefined on the first render, so a handler that binds data.callback has to tolerate that first pass. The same first-render gap causes server and client markup to differ, which is covered in the hydration mismatch fix guide . Check what fetch actually returned. A failed request that your code treated as success leaves response.handler undefined. If the failure is cross-origin, the browser console will say so, and the CORS error header checklist shows which header is missing. Give destructured callbacks a default. const { onSave = () => {} } = props means onSave.bind(this) never sees undefined . Same error, different property: 'map', 'length', 'id', '0' The word in quotes changes, the diagnosis doesn't. Whatever is left of that property was undefined . The table below maps the common variants to what's usually missing. Message ends with Left side was Typical cause (reading 'bind') a function Misspelled or undeclared method, callback not passed (reading 'map') an array API returned an object or nothing, state not initialized to [] (reading 'length') an array or string Same as map , or a split result on missing text (reading '0') an array Indexing rows[0] when rows was never set (reading 'id') an object Lookup by key missed, item not found, find() returned undefined (reading 'split') a string Field missing from a record, undefined passed where text was expected (reading 'text') an object Reading a nested field from an empty or error response The fixes are the same three: define the value, guard it, or chain it. For arrays, a default of [] is the cheapest prevention: const items = response ?. data ?. items ?? []; items . map (( item ) => item . id ); MDN's own example shows the bracket form for array indexes: arr?.[42] returns undefined instead of throwing Cannot read properties of undefined (reading '42') when arr is missing. Common mistakes and gotchas Fixing the symptom, not the cause. Wrapping a required method in ?. makes the error vanish and the feature silently stop working. Use optional chaining only where undefined is a legitimate state. Mixing up null and undefined in guards. if (fn !== undefined) lets null through, and null.bind throws the same way with null in the message. Use != null (loose), typeof fn === "function" , or ?. , which handles both. Expecting ?. to catch non-functions. obj.method?.() returns undefined if method is missing, but if method is a string, you get obj.method is not a function . Optional chaining checks for nullish, not for callability. Using ?. on an undeclared variable. undeclaredVar?.prop throws a ReferenceError , not undefined . Optional chaining only helps once the variable exists. Assigning through a chain. obj?.prop = 1 is a SyntaxError . Chains are for reading and calling, not writing. Breaking the chain with parentheses. (a?.b).c throws when a is nullish. Covered above, but it's the one that surprises people who think they already added the operator. Binding in a constructor before the data exists. The React and async case. The constructor runs once; props and fetched data arrive later. Blaming the error on a product you're using. If you're a user seeing this in a web app or a desktop client rather than a developer writing it, the bug is in that app's JavaScript. Reloading, clearing the cache or updating the app sometimes clears a stale state, but the real fix has to come from the app's developers. Reporting the exact message, including the word in quotes, helps them find it. Quick checklist Open the stack trace line and find the .bind( . Everything left of that dot is the suspect. Log it or hover it in a breakpoint. Typo or missing method? Fix the name or declare it. Done. Legitimately optional? Guard with typeof fn === "function" , or use fn?.bind(ctx) . Nullable at more than one level? Put ?. at every nullable step and don't wrap any part in parentheses. Need a fallback? Append ?? defaultFn . Comes from awaited data? Move the bind after the await and validate the result before binding. Same message with 'map' , 'length' , '0' , 'id' ? Same steps, default arrays to [] and objects to {} . Rerun and confirm the bound function actually executes, not just that the error is gone. FAQ What does cannot read properties of undefined mean? The value on the left of the dot was undefined, so JavaScript couldn't read the property named in quotes from it. The property name tells you what you tried to read; the fix is to find out why the object before it doesn't exist. How do I fix cannot read properties of null? The same way as the undefined version. Null is the other nullish value, and optional chaining (?.) and a typeof check both handle it. If you guard with !== undefined only, null still gets through. Why does this happen in React? Most often a class constructor binds this.someMethod before that method is declared, or a handler reads props or fetched data on the first render when it's still undefined. Fix the method name, or move the bind after the data arrives and give destructured callbacks a default. What's the difference between reading 'bind' and reading 'map'? Only the property that was being read. With 'bind' a function was missing; with 'map' an array was missing. Both mean the thing before the dot was undefined, and both are fixed by defining, guarding or chaining it. I see this error in an app I use, not in code I wrote. What can I do? The bug is in that app's JavaScript, so you can't fix it directly. Reloading, clearing the cache or updating to the latest version sometimes clears a stale state; otherwise report the exact message, including the quoted property name, to the app's support. The original, with any later corrections, is on CoreMesh . This article was drafted by an AI system, fact-checked against the official sources linked above, and reviewed by a human before publishing.

title: Give your coding agent a storyboard before asking for a product video
summary: A coding agent can write animation code, but a useful product video starts with a small specification you can actually review. Disclosure: I work on Claude Motion , an independent toolkit for your own Claude Code or Codex. This article was generated with AI assistance and checked against our published workflow. The brief below is illustrative, not a customer result or a benchmark. We are not affiliated with Anthropic. Start with one claim per scene For a 15-second release explainer, give each scene a job before asking for animation: Time Job Material to supply 0–5s State the problem One sentence your audience recognizes 5–10s Show the change A real screenshot, diagram or verified data 10–15s Give the next step One action and a readable destination This is a suggested structure, not a rule that every scene needs five seconds. If the viewer cannot read the copy, simplify it or change the timing. Here is a brief you can paste into an agent without installing any particular toolkit: Plan a 15-second, 16:9 product explainer. Audience: developers deciding whether to try a new workflow. Message: a local project stays editable after the MP4 export. Scene 1: show the problem of revising a finished video. Scene 2: show source → preview → export using a simple diagram. Scene 3: show one next step. Use only the assets I supply. Do not invent UI, testimonials, performance numbers or customer logos. Label diagrams as illustrative. Before writing animation code, return: - one claim and exact on-screen copy per scene; - timing, asset paths and any missing material; - which elements should remain still for reading. Wait for my storyboard review. Keep approval separate from rendering Review the storyboard as you would review a small code change. Is the claim true? Does the supplied screenshot actually show it? Is the destination useful to someone who has never seen the product? Then ask the agent to build a local preview and keep the source files. Request specific revisions such as “hold the second scene longer” or “replace that diagram label,” rather than repeatedly regenerating the entire video. For data animation, supply the values and units explicitly. A rising line should represent the data, not merely decorate a claim about growth. Inspect the exported file, too A working browser preview does not prove the exported MP4 is correct. Check the beginning, scene changes, and end of the actual file. Look for missing fonts, clipped text, blank frames and labels that disappear too quickly. If FFmpeg is installed, this command reports media properties; it does not judge visual quality: ffprobe -v error \ -show_entries format = duration:stream = codec_type,codec_name,width,height,r_frame_rate \ -of json output.mp4 If you intended narration, confirm an audio stream exists and listen to the export. An audio stream alone does not establish intelligibility or synchronization. Where our toolkit fits Claude Motion packages a storyboard-to-preview-to-export workflow and original starting styles for Claude Code and Codex. The setup and usage guide explains the connection process and prerequisites. You bring your own working agent access; model usage is billed separately. Free includes three Skills and the Editorial style. You can use the same review process with another renderer. The useful deliverable is the editable project, the rendered file, and enough checks to know what you are publishing.

title: Playwright recorded my 25 fps animation at about 9. The fix was to stop recording.
summary: I needed a short video of my portfolio for LinkedIn: the opening animation, a swordsman who cuts the screen in two, then a fast scroll through every section. Playwright records video in one option, so I started there. The first video looked fine in stills recordVideo on a browser context gave me a 25 fps WebM. Every frame I pulled out of it looked right. I had only checked stills. Played back, it stuttered, and the first person who watched it saw it at once. Measuring it frame by frame told the real story: the opening: 65% of frames identical to the one before the swordsman: 63% the scroll: 79 of 200 transitions were a freeze followed by a jump That is about 9 real frames per second inside a 25 fps file. The recorder is fed by the browser's screencast, which hands over a frame only when the compositor has one ready. On a heavy page it has fewer, and the gaps are filled with repeats. Nothing fails. The video is just wrong. Stop recording, start stepping If the browser cannot keep up in real time, take real time out of the equation. Every CSS animation and transition on a page is a Web Animation, reachable through document.getAnimations() , and a paused animation can be placed at any instant by setting its currentTime . So the capture becomes a loop: advance every animation by exactly 40 ms, take a screenshot, repeat. 25 frames per second by construction, however long each screenshot takes. // injected with context.addInitScript, before the page loads const seen = new WeakMap (); let t = 0 ; window . __step = ( dt ) => { t += dt ; for ( const a of document . getAnimations ()) { if ( a . timeline && a . timeline !== document . timeline ) continue ; let s = seen . get ( a ); if ( ! s ) { s = { start : t - dt , offset : a . currentTime || 0 }; seen . set ( a , s ); a . pause (); } a . currentTime = s . offset + ( t - s . start ); } }; Animations that start later, like the swordsman when his IntersectionObserver fires, are picked up on the next step and join the same clock. Scrolling gets the same treatment: one scrollTo per frame along an eased curve, instead of a smooth scroll that the recorder samples whenever it can. for ( let i = 1 ; i <= frames ; i ++ ) { const y = Math . round ( target * easeInOut ( i / frames )); await page . evaluate (( y ) => { window . scrollTo ({ top : y , behavior : ' instant ' }); window . __step ( 40 ); }, y ); await page . screenshot ({ path : `frames/ ${ String ( n ++ ). padStart ( 5 , ' 0 ' )} .jpg` , type : ' jpeg ' , quality : 95 }); } The frames go to ffmpeg as an image sequence. The new video has zero frozen frames in the opening, the descent and the scroll. The traps A timer that ignores your clock. The opening has a 7-second safety timeout that removes it if its end event never arrives. Each captured frame costs far more than 40 ms of real time, so that timer would have fired long before the virtual clock got there. I neutralised that one timeout in the capture script. Anything driven by setTimeout or requestAnimationFrame runs on wall time, not on yours: the text-scramble effect on my headings plays faster in the video than on the site, and I left it that way. Scroll-driven animations already have a clock. Animations bound to animation-timeline: view() follow the scroll position, so setting their currentTime makes no sense. The loop skips anything whose timeline is not document.timeline . Driving the scroll drives them. One frame can lie. A section flashed white for a single frame. In real time nobody would see it. In a 25 fps video it reads as a glitch. A frame-difference pass over the whole video found it, and I cut it. The upload has opinions too. LinkedIn's composer previewed my WebM, then dropped it as soon as I clicked Next. The same frames encoded as H.264 MP4, in yuv420p with standard colour range, stayed. What I take from it A screen recorder answers "what did the screen show?", and on a busy page the honest answer is "less than you asked for". For a demo, the better question is "what should the screen show at 40 ms, at 80, at 120?". The Web Animations API lets you ask it directly. And watch the playback, not the stills. Every still I checked was perfect. The 19-second result is in my LinkedIn post , and the site itself is at ayoubhammoudi.com . I am Ayoub Hammoudi, a full-stack engineer in Paris working on data and AI platforms. More of my work is at github.com/Ayoubhm07 .

title: How to give Claude Code (or any AI coding agent) a persistent memory in 5 minutes
summary: Every new session with my coding agent used to start the same way: me typing some version of "this is what the project does, the API lives here, we decided against that library in March," while the agent nodded politely and forgot all of it by the next morning. In my last post I compared eight memory layers for AI coding agents and confessed that I ended up building a ninth ( the comparison post is here ). This one is the practical follow-up: how to give your agent a persistent memory in about five minutes, using MaxGraph, the memory server I maintain. It works with Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, and anything else that speaks MCP. Quick disclosure, since this is dev.to and not my landing page: I sell this thing. There is a 7-day trial that needs no card, so you can verify everything below before paying anything. What you are installing MaxGraph is a local MCP server that gives your agent a knowledge graph. The graph stores entities (projects, files, services, people), observations (atomic facts attached to those entities), and relations between them. On top of that storage you get semantic search, a context digest at the start of every session, tasks and bugs with their own statuses, and a live dashboard that renders the whole graph as a physics simulation you can drag around with a mouse. Everything lives in plain text files on your machine, inside the data/ folder of the install. It works offline. If you ever want to leave, there is an NDJSON export. Install it in 5 minutes Three ways, in decreasing order of elegance. Path one: make the agent install it. My favorite, because it needs no terminal work from you at all. Paste this into your coding agent: Install MaxGraph: https://github.com/RuMemory/maxgraph. Follow AGENTS.md and do it all yourself. The repo ships an AGENTS.md written for exactly this situation. The agent reads it, picks the right installer for your OS, wires up the MCP config, and reports back. Watching an agent install its own memory is also a decent preview of the relationship you are about to have with it. Path two: the Claude Code plugin. Two commands: claude plugin marketplace add RuMemory/maxgraph claude plugin install maxgraph@maxgraph Path three: manual. Clone the repo and run the installer for your platform. On Windows: git clone https://github.com/RuMemory/maxgraph cd maxgraph powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File . \install.ps1 -Yes On Linux or macOS: git clone https://github.com/RuMemory/maxgraph cd maxgraph bash install.sh --yes If you are on Cursor or VS Code, the README in the repo has one-click deeplinks that register the MCP server for you, and docs/PAIRING.md walks through the pairing flow. I am not pasting those links here because they are long base64 blobs. Open the README and click. What happens after The installer drops an icon into your system tray, registers itself for autostart, and turns on auto-updates. From that point on, the server is just there, the way a database is just there. The first session after install feels ordinary. You work as usual. The difference is that the agent now writes things down as it goes: a decision you made together, a bug you hit, a summary when the session ends. You do not have to ask for this; the write instructions ship with the server. You can still say "remember this" when you want something specific captured, and I do that more often than I expected. The second session is where you feel it. At session start the agent asks for its context digest and gets a budgeted block: the key facts about your project, the decisions on record, the open bugs, the open tasks, and a recap of recent sessions. The "we decided against that library in March" conversation stops happening, because the agent read the March decision before you finished your coffee. The dashboard is the part I built partly for my own pleasure. It renders the whole memory graph as a live physics map: entities float, cluster by project, and you can drag nodes around to see what connects to what. It turned out useful beyond the aesthetics. An over-connected entity is visible at a glance, and an over-connected entity usually means it is polluting retrieval. One number, clearly labeled as my own measurement: across my projects I see roughly 43% savings on context tokens, because the session digest replaces the "paste the whole context doc again" habit. I measured this on my own sessions, by myself, for myself. Treat it accordingly. What this is not Three honest limits, so nobody buys the wrong thing. There is no hosted version. The server runs on your machine and the memory never leaves it, which is the entire point, but it also means there is no API key to paste and no cloud console to log into. It is not magic. The agent has to actually write things down for memory to exist, and it writes what it judges durable. That judgment is good but imperfect, and the safety net is that you stay in control: the storage is plain text files you can read, edit, or delete with any editor, and the export is NDJSON. Your agent's memory is yours in the most literal sense. And it will not organize the project for you. It remembers what happened. Deciding what should happen next is still your job. Try it The repo is at github.com/RuMemory/maxgraph . The trial is 7 days, no card required, which should cover at least a dozen "wait, how did you know that" moments from your agent. More details live on rezon-ai.ru , English version included. If it turns out useful, star the repo. If you hit a sharp edge, open an issue. The project is young, and every report lands in the same graph my own agent reads the next morning, which is the most literal dogfooding loop I have ever run.

title: I compared 8 memory layers for AI coding agents, then built a ninth anyway
summary: Every new chat with my coding agent started the same way. Ten minutes of me typing some version of "this is a Next.js app, the API lives here, we decided against Redis in March, please stop suggesting it." The agent would nod politely, help me for an hour, and forget everything by the next session. I tried rules files. I tried pasting a hand-written context doc into each conversation. I got tired of being my own retrieval system. So in early October I sat down and did what any reasonable person does instead of finishing actual work: I audited the memory layer market. GitHub API for stars, official pricing pages for money, READMEs for claims. Eight serious options. All numbers below are as of October 2026. I should mention my conflict of interest up front. The comparison annoyed me enough that I ended up building my own server, MaxGraph, and it is one of the eight rows in the table. I will try to be fair to the other seven anyway. You can judge whether I managed. The field, on one screen Tool GitHub stars UI Self-hosted Entry price Writes memory on its own mem0 66,894 Yes, dashboard in the OSS server and in Cloud Yes (Docker) $0, then $19/mo Yes (LLM extraction, Dream consolidation) Zep / Graphiti 4,953 / 31,591 Zep console has graph viz; Graphiti has none Graphiti only (needs Neo4j or FalkorDB); Zep server is closed Free 10k credits/mo, Flex $125/mo Yes (extraction from episodes) Letta (MemGPT) 25,091 Yes, web app and CLI Yes (OSS server) $0, Pro $20/mo Yes (sleep-time agents rewrite memory in the background) Basic Memory 4,123 Your editor or Obsidian; no own graph UI Yes, local-first $0, Cloud $15/seat/mo Partially (LLM writes notes during the chat) supermemory 31,172 Yes, console plus a consumer app Yes (OSS); paid self-host on the $399/mo Scale plan $0, Pro $19/mo Yes ("agents learn from it in real time") Official MCP memory server 91,088 for the whole monorepo No Yes (npx, one JSONL file) Free No (the agent calls tools if the system prompt tells it to) mcp-memory-service 2,006 Yes, 8-tab dashboard plus interactive D3 and 3D graphs Yes (SQLite, Hybrid, Milvus) Free, donations Yes (autonomous consolidation, insight cards) MaxGraph (mine) 2 Yes, live physics map of the whole graph Yes, that is the only mode 7-day trial, then a few dollars a month Yes A few honest notes on reading this table. The official MCP server's 91k stars belong to the entire modelcontextprotocol/servers monorepo, not to the memory package alone. Zep's 4,953-star repo holds examples and integrations now; the actual server went closed, and the open source path is Graphiti. And yes, the last row really says 2 stars. The repo is one week old. More on that later. What turned out to be a commodity I expected the comparison to reveal clear winners. Instead it revealed that the core of the idea got standardized while I was not looking. The knowledge graph data model, entities with observations and relations, is literally the schema of the official MCP reference server. mem0, Graphiti, cognee, Hindsight, and mcp-memory-service all store some flavor of the same triple. When I designed MaxGraph's storage I thought I was making a choice. I was following a convention that had already hardened. The observer pattern is also everywhere. Almost every serious tool now has an LLM pass that reads your conversation and writes structured memory without being asked: mem0 calls it single-pass extraction plus Dream consolidation, Letta runs sleep-time agents that rewrite core memory while the main agent idles, Zep has Observations on its Flex Plus tier, and even the free mcp-memory-service does autonomous consolidation with insight cards. The romantic idea of an agent that "remembers on its own" shipped in at least seven products before mine. Semantic search and MCP support come with literally every tool on the list, and Docker self-host too, except for the Zep server itself. A dashboard of some kind: mem0, Zep, Letta, supermemory, cognee, Hindsight, mcp-memory-service. I kept a tally while researching, and by the end my list of "things that make MaxGraph special" had lost most of its rows to the commodity column. That was the useful part of the exercise. It killed my lazy differentiation story and forced me to ask what is actually left. What I could not find anywhere Three gaps survived the audit. (This is the part where I am obviously biased, so I will describe them as facts about the market and let you weigh them.) First, tasks and bugs as first-class citizens of the memory graph. Every tool I checked stores facts about the world: user preferences, entities, episodes, decisions. None of the eighteen repos I looked at models work state. In MaxGraph a task is a node in the same graph as everything else, with an open or done status, and a bug is a node with open or fixed. The agent can ask "what is still open on this project" at session start and get an answer from the same store that holds the architecture decisions. I wanted this because my worst agent failure mode is forgotten TODOs that rot in a chat log, worse than any forgotten fact. Nobody sells that. If you know a counterexample, I genuinely want the link. Second, a live map. Several tools visualize the graph: Zep's console, mcp-memory-service with its D3 and 3D views, cognee's graph rendering. Those are static or lightly interactive pictures. MaxGraph's dashboard is a physics simulation where the memory graph floats, clusters, and can be dragged around. I will admit this is partly for the founder's own pleasure. Watching yesterday's session collapse into the project cluster is the closest thing I have to a save file for my own thinking. But it also changed how I debug the memory itself; I can see when an entity is over-connected and polluting retrieval. Third, the business model. Self-hosted memory is free almost everywhere (mem0, Graphiti, Letta, cognee, Hindsight, mcp-memory-service, supermemory's OSS app) or locked behind enterprise contracts (Zep BYOC, mem0 on-prem, cognee BYOC). The one public self-serve plan that includes self-hosting is supermemory's Scale at $399 a month. Nobody I found sells a self-hosted memory server to an individual developer for the price of a coffee. MaxGraph is that experiment: a 7-day trial, then a micro-subscription of a few dollars a month, for software that runs on your machine, stores plain local text files, and works offline. Whether anyone will pay for self-hosted software in 2026 is an open question I am funding personally. There is also a licensing choice worth one sentence: MaxGraph is BSL-1.1, source available, and every version converts to MIT four years after release. If I abandon the project or get hit by a bus, the code becomes fully open on a timer. Where MaxGraph is honestly weaker I promised fairness, so here is the part my marketing brain wanted to skip. There are no benchmarks for MaxGraph. mem0 publishes LoCoMo 92.5 and LongMemEval 94.4 (April 2026 numbers, measured on their managed platform, with the caveat that OSS is "directionally similar"). Hindsight has a public benchmarks site and a paper. MaxGraph has a claim of roughly 43% context-token savings from my own session-start measurements, taken on my own projects, by me. Treat it accordingly. There is no hosted cloud. If you want to paste an API key and never run a Docker container, MaxGraph is the wrong tool and mem0, Zep, or supermemory will serve you better today. My bet is that developers who care about memory care about where the memory lives, but it is a bet, not a fact. I have no enterprise paperwork either. Zep has SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA, Vectorize (behind Hindsight) has SOC 2, supermemory puts SOC 2 on its Scale tier. MaxGraph has a founder and a GitHub repo. The project has two stars and is one week old. The README is better than the documentation, the documentation is thinner than the vision, and there are sharp edges I have not found yet because only a handful of people have run it. mcp-memory-service, at 2,006 stars with a very active solo maintainer, is the mature version of the "local MCP memory with a dashboard" idea, and if my feature list speaks to you, you should try it too. Seriously. Competition here is good for everyone, including me, because it means the category is real. Why I am publishing the audit anyway The comparison was supposed to save me from building something redundant. It did the opposite: it showed me that the commodity layer (graph, observer, MCP, dashboard) is table stakes now, and that the interesting fights are happening at the edges. Work state in the graph. Memory you can see move. Pricing aimed at one developer's wallet instead of a procurement department. If you want to check my work, everything above traces back to public repos and pricing pages. If you want to check the product, MaxGraph is at github.com/RuMemory/maxgraph , with a 7-day trial and more details on rezon-ai.ru (there is an English version of the site). Star the repo if it turns out useful; at my current count of 2, you would be moving the chart. And if you have already solved the "agent forgets the project between sessions" problem with one of the seven other tools, tell me which one and why. I have a graph to update.

title: Why I built a lightweight, ad-free QR Scanner using Web Technologies
summary: As a developer, I’ve always been fascinated by how we can solve daily problems with simple web tools. One such problem I encountered was the "QR Scanner Struggle." Most of the QR scanner apps available today are bloated. They take too much space, require unnecessary permissions, and are often riddled with intrusive ads. I thought, "Why can't we just use the browser?" So, I built Fast QR Scanner. My main goal was to keep it minimal and privacy-focused. title: RFC 1918 Gateway Collisions: Why Downstream Routers Auto-Shift Subnets (and How to Diagnose via CLI)
summary: When cascading a secondary wireless router or homelab firewall behind an ISP-supplied Optical Network Terminal (ONT) or combo gateway, network administrators frequently run into silent routing failures or unexpected subnet shifts. Because consumer and prosumer hardware vendors overwhelmingly default to 192.168.1.1/24 or 192.168.0.1/24 , connecting the LAN port of an upstream modem to the WAN port of a downstream router triggers an immediate RFC 1918 WAN/LAN subnet collision . Vendor Auto-Shift Logic Matrix Rather than dropping the interface completely, modern router firmware executes an automatic DHCP pool migration during boot if it detects its default gateway subnet already exists on the WAN interface: Hardware Vendor Factory Default IP Auto-Shift Fallback Subnet Local DNS / mDNS Host ASUS (ASUSWRT) 192.168.50.1 / 192.168.1.1 192.168.2.1/24 router.asus.com Netgear 192.168.1.1 10.0.0.1/24 routerlogin.net TP-Link 192.168.0.1 192.168.1.1/24 tplinkwifi.net Linksys 192.168.1.1 10.0.1.1/24 myrouter.local Ubiquiti (UniFi) 192.168.1.1 192.168.2.1/24 unifi.ui.com For the complete 35+ vendor lookup table, default administrative ports, and factory credential specs, see the live reference at RouterIPGuide.com . Rapid CLI Gateway & Double NAT Verification Instead of guessing which fallback IP a router negotiated, query the routing table directly from your terminal: Linux ( iproute2 ) & macOS bash # Extract active default gateway IPv4 ip route show default | awk '{print $3}' # Verify if Double NAT is present (check hops 1 and 2) traceroute -n -m 4 1.1.1.1 Windows PowerShell PowerShell # Query next-hop default gateway (Get-NetRoute -DestinationPrefix '0.0.0.0/0').NextHop # Check first 4 hops for consecutive private RFC 1918 addresses tracert -d -h 4 1.1.1.1 If both Hop 1 and Hop 2 return private IPv4 ranges (192.168.x.x, 10.x.x.x, or 172.16.x.x – 172.31.x.x), your traffic is traversing two separate NAT tables. Resolution Architecture Upstream Bridge Mode: Place the ISP gateway into transparent bridge mode (disabling its NAT and DHCP server) so the downstream router receives the public WAN IP directly. Downstream AP Mode: If the ISP gateway cannot be bridged, configure the secondary router into Access Point (AP) mode and connect the ethernet backhaul strictly via LAN-to-LAN (or designated AP WAN bridge port). Open-Source Reference Datasets We maintain this dataset openly for network automation scripts and diagnostic tools: Interactive Subnet & Conflict Diagnostic Hub: RouterIPGuide Troubleshooting GitHub Repository: routeripguide/default-router-ip-reference Kaggle Dataset Mirror: Default Router Gateway IP Matrix Hugging Face Dataset: routeripguide/default-router-gateway-ip-matrix Open-Source Reference Datasets We maintain this dataset openly for network automation scripts and diagnostic tools: Interactive Subnet & Conflict Diagnostic Hub: RouterIPGuide Troubleshooting GitHub Repository: routeripguide/default-router-ip-reference Kaggle Dataset Mirror: Default Router Gateway IP Matrix Hugging Face Dataset: routeripguide/default-router-gateway-ip-matrix

title: How we built Renova's AI room redesigns
summary: Renova takes one photo of a room, a house exterior, a garden or a pool and turns it into the same space redesigned in a chosen style, seconds after you tap. Here's roughly how that pipeline came together. Keep the photo's geometry, change everything else. Renova is prompts on an image-edit model, plus a watermark. The prompts are written to keep the room's architecture and camera angle, so a "Scandinavian" redesign still has your window in the same wall, at the same size. One pipeline, many tools. Style redesign, virtual staging (furnishing an empty room), new walls and floors, furniture rearrangement, style transfer from a reference photo, floor-plan-to-3D-rendering, and occasion decorating all share the same core step, just with different inputs and constraints. That made it possible to add a new "tool" without building a new pipeline from scratch each time. One codebase, three platforms. Renova ships on iPhone, Android and the web from the same codebase, with the same account and the same design history following you between them. If you work on anything that edits or regenerates real photos rather than generating from scratch, the "keep structure, change material" problem is probably familiar — happy to compare notes in the comments. https://renovaroom.com

title: LangChain vs. LangGraph: How to Choose the Right Framework
summary: This post is an AI-assisted written adaptation of a video by IBM Technology . All ideas belong to the original creator. Watch the original on YouTube . LangChain and LangGraph are both open source frameworks designed to help developers build applications with large language models. That shared foundation is exactly why the choice can feel confusing at first — they look like competitors, and the internet treats them like a horse race. The useful question isn't which framework is "better." It's why you'd reach for one over the other — and that answer depends on the shape of the application you're building. This guide starts by defining what each framework actually is, using a concrete example for each, then compares them head-to-head on primary focus, structure, components, state management, and use cases. By the end you should know which one fits your next project, and when the honest answer is both. TL;DR LangChain is the abstraction layer. It wires LLM operations together by executing a sequence of functions in a chain — reusable components (document loaders, text splitters, prompts, LLMs, memory) combined to build a workflow. LangGraph is the workflow engine. A specialized library inside the LangChain ecosystem, purpose-built for stateful multi-agent systems, modeled as nodes (actions), edges (transitions), and state. Structure is where they split. LangChain's chain acts as a DAG — tasks run in a specific order and always move forward. LangGraph's graph allows loops and lets states move backwards and forwards. State management is the sharpest dividing line. LangChain can pass information back and forth through the chain but doesn't easily maintain persistent state across multiple runs; LangGraph makes state a core component every node can access and modify. They're complementary, not mutually exclusive. LangGraph lives inside the LangChain ecosystem, so the real choice is often about layering: use LangChain for the chaining and components, add LangGraph when the workflow needs loops, persistent state, and multiple agents. Two Frameworks, One Big Question LangChain and LangGraph are both open source frameworks designed to help developers build applications with large language models. That shared foundation is exactly why the choice can feel confusing at first. The useful question isn't which framework is "better." It's why you'd reach for one over the other — and that answer depends on the shape of the application you're building. A good place to start is to define what these two things actually are, beginning with LangChain. ▶ Watch this part of the video (00:00:00) LangChain: The Abstraction Layer for Chaining LLM Calls LangChain is the broader, more established of the two ecosystems. At its core, it's a way to build LLM-powered applications by executing a sequence of functions in a chain. Its job is to provide an abstraction layer that wires LLM operations together, rather than to act as a workflow engine. It's best thought of as the foundation layer. A Concrete Example Consider an application that needs to do three things in order: retrieve data from a website, summarize that data, and then use the summary to answer user questions. The workflow is retrieve → summarize → answer . LangChain breaks that workflow into components: Retrieve. A document loader fetches and loads content from various data sources. If some documents are large, a text splitter breaks text into smaller, semantically meaningful chunks. Summarize. A chain orchestrates the summarization process. It can include a prompt component that instructs an LLM to perform the summarization, plus an LLM component that passes the request to the large language model of your choosing. Answer. A second chain generates the answer. It might include a memory component to store conversation history and context, along with another prompt component and another LLM component to produce the answer based on the summary and the recorded context. Modularity Is the Point One thing worth noting: the LLM used in the answer component can be a completely different large language model from the one used in the summarize component. Nothing in the design forces you to commit to a single model across the entire workflow. That's the value of LangChain's modular architecture — you build complex workflows by combining high-level, reusable components rather than hand-rolling each step. ▶ Watch this part of the video (00:00:19) LangGraph: Stateful Multi-Agent Workflows LangGraph is a specialized library within the LangChain ecosystem. It is purpose-built for building stateful multi-agent systems that can handle complex, nonlinear workflows. A task management assistant agent is a good illustration of the kind of problem LangGraph is designed for. The workflow starts by processing user input, then branches into actions such as adding tasks, completing tasks, and summarizing tasks. LangGraph models this as a graph structure: Nodes represent actions. Add tasks, complete tasks, and summarize are all nodes. Edges represent the transitions between those actions. The process input node is the central node. User input arrives here, and it uses an LLM component to understand user intent and route to the appropriate action node. A second central component is state . The state component maintains the task list across all interactions. Each action node interacts with it in a specific way: The add task node adds new tasks to the state. The complete task node marks tasks as finished. The summarize node uses an LLM to generate an overview of current tasks. Because all nodes can access and modify the state, the assistant supports context-aware, stateful interactions. The graph structure lets the assistant handle various user requests in any order, always returning to the process input node after an action completes. The result is a flexible, stateful agent that can maintain context over extended interactions. ▶ Watch this part of the video (00:03:17) Head-to-Head: How They Actually Differ The two frameworks are best compared across several dimensions rather than a single feature checklist. The difference in primary focus is what drives every other trade-off between them. Primary focus. LangGraph exists to create and manage multi-agent systems and workflows. LangChain exists to provide an abstraction layer for chaining LLM operations into large language model applications. That is the core distinction. Structure. LangChain adopts a chain structure that acts as a DAG — a directed acyclic graph — meaning tasks execute in a specific order and always move forward. You might start with task one, branch into tasks two and three, then come back to a central task four. This works well when you know the exact sequence of steps required. LangGraph's graph structure is different because it allows for loops and revisiting previous states. State A can move backwards and forwards with states B and C. That is beneficial for interactive systems where the next step depends on evolving conditions or user input. Components. LangChain uses memory, a prompt component, an LLM component for passing things to the large language model, and an agent component that forms chains between all of these. LangGraph uses nodes, edges, and states, all of which are part of a graph. State management. LangChain's state management is somewhat limited. It can pass information back and forth through the chain, but it doesn't easily maintain a persistent state across multiple runs. Its memory components can maintain some state across interactions. LangGraph's state management is more robust because state is a core component that all nodes can access and modify, which allows for more complex, context-aware behaviors. Use cases. LangChain excels at sequential tasks, such as a process that retrieves data, processes it, and outputs a result. It can handle non-sequential tasks to some extent through its agents feature. LangGraph's wheelhouse is scenarios with much more complexity: systems requiring ongoing interaction and adaptation, such as a virtual assistant that needs to maintain context over long conversations and handle varying types of requests. ▶ Watch this part of the video (00:05:41) Which One Should You Use? The two frameworks are aimed at different shapes of problem, so the decision usually comes down to how your workflow behaves rather than which one is "better." Reach for LangChain when the work is a straightforward chain. Its focus is providing an abstraction layer for chaining LLM operations into large language model applications. The chain structure acts as a DAG — a directed acyclic graph — meaning tasks execute in a specific order and always move forward. You might start with task one, branch into tasks two and three, then converge back on task four. That is a great fit when you know the exact sequence of steps needed, such as a process that retrieves data, processes it, and outputs a result. Reach for LangGraph when the workflow is stateful, multi-agent, and nonlinear. Its primary focus is creating and managing multi-agent systems and workflows. The graph structure allows for loops and revisiting previous states — state A can move backwards and forwards with state B and state C. That matters for interactive systems where the next step depends on evolving conditions or user input. State management is the sharpest dividing line: LangChain can pass information back and forth through the chain, but it doesn't easily maintain a persistent state across multiple runs. Its memory components can hold some state across interactions. LangGraph treats state as a core component that all nodes can access and modify, which enables more complex, context-aware behaviors. On use cases, LangChain handles sequential tasks well and can stretch to non-sequential work to some extent through its agents feature. LangGraph's wheelhouse is scenarios with much more complexity: systems requiring ongoing interaction and adaptation, like a virtual assistant that has to maintain context over long conversations and handle varying types of requests. The two are complementary rather than mutually exclusive. LangGraph lives inside the LangChain ecosystem, so the choice is often about layering — use LangChain for the chaining and components, and add LangGraph when the workflow needs loops, persistent state, and multiple agents. ▶ Watch this part of the video (00:05:41) Conclusion The decision usually comes down to how your workflow behaves, not which framework is better. If you know the exact sequence of steps — retrieve, process, output — LangChain's DAG chain is a great fit and its modular components mean you can even swap models between steps. If the next step depends on evolving conditions or user input, and you need context to persist over extended interactions, reach for LangGraph. And remember you don't have to pick a side: start with LangChain, then layer LangGraph in when your workflow outgrows a straight line.

title: How to track new FDA recalls with Python and the openFDA API
summary: Every week the US Food and Drug Administration publishes its Enforcement Report: every food, drug and medical device recall it has classified. The openFDA API serves the same data as JSON, free, with no sign-up. If you work in food safety, run a pharmacy, buy from suppliers, or report on public health, a small script can tell you about the recalls that matter to you, every week, without anyone checking a website. This guide builds that script in plain Python (standard library only), and covers the parts of the API that are easy to get wrong. The three endpoints Recalls live in one endpoint per product area. All three share the same fields. Products Endpoint Food, including dietary supplements and cosmetics https://api.fda.gov/food/enforcement.json Drugs https://api.fda.gov/drug/enforcement.json Medical devices https://api.fda.gov/device/enforcement.json A first request The script below asks for Class I food recalls (the most serious kind) that FDA reported in the last 30 days. import json import urllib.error import urllib.parse import urllib.request from datetime import date , timedelta end = date . today () start = end - timedelta ( days = 30 ) params = { " search " : f ' report_date:[ { start : % Y % m % d } TO { end : % Y % m % d } ] AND classification: " Class I "' , " sort " : " report_date:desc " , " limit " : 10 , } url = " https://api.fda.gov/food/enforcement.json? " + urllib . parse . urlencode ( params ) try : with urllib . request . urlopen ( url , timeout = 60 ) as response : data = json . load ( response ) except urllib . error . HTTPError as error : if error . code != 404 : # openFDA answers 404 when nothing matches raise data = { " results " : []} total = data . get ( " meta " , {}). get ( " results " , {}). get ( " total " , 0 ) print ( f " { total } Class I food recalls reported in the last 30 days " ) for recall in data [ " results " ]: print ( recall [ " report_date " ], recall [ " recall_number " ], recall [ " recalling_firm " ]) print ( " " , recall [ " reason_for_recall " ][: 120 ]) When this was written (19 October 2026), it printed this, plus eight more recalls: 51 Class I food recalls reported in the last 30 days 20261007 H-1403-2026 Coco G's Snack Foods, Inc. Potential Salmonella contamination. 20260930 H-1396-2026 GIAS FOOD INC. Contamination with Listeria monocytogenes A few things are going on in that search string: Fields and values are written as field:value . Put values with spaces in double quotes. Date ranges use [start TO end] , and openFDA dates are YYYYMMDD without dashes. AND and OR combine clauses. urlencode turns the spaces into + , which is what openFDA expects. Which date to filter on Each recall carries several dates, and picking the wrong one is the most common mistake: recall_initiation_date : when the company started the recall. This can be weeks or months before FDA publishes anything. center_classification_date : when FDA assigned the class. report_date : when the recall appeared in the weekly Enforcement Report. If your question is "what is new since I last looked?", use report_date . A recall initiated in March can first appear in a report in May, and a filter on recall_initiation_date would never show it to a weekly job. What the classes mean Class I: a reasonable probability that the product will cause serious health problems or death. Class II: the product may cause temporary or medically reversible health problems, or the chance of serious harm is remote. Class III: the product is unlikely to cause adverse health consequences, but breaks FDA rules (a labeling error, for example). Gotchas worth knowing 404 is not an error here. When no record matches, openFDA returns HTTP 404 with "No matches found!". Treat it as an empty result, as the first script does. limit stops at 1,000 and skip at 25,000. For bigger result sets, follow the Link header. When a page is full, openFDA includes a Link: <...>; rel="next" header that pages with search_after , with no 25,000 cap. state is the company's state, not where the product went. Distribution is free text in distribution_pattern ("Nationwide", "CA, NV and AZ"). To find recalls that reached your state, search that field as text. The openfda block is often empty for food. Brand and generic names are filled in mostly for drugs. For food, the product is described in product_description . Watch for stray ¿ characters. Some text fields contain ¿ where the original had a special character: jalape¿no in a reason for recall, 30¿ for degrees in a device description. Clean them up before you show them to people. Rate limits. Without a key you get 240 requests per minute and 1,000 per day per IP address. A free key from open.fda.gov raises the daily limit to 120,000. A weekly job like the one below needs a handful of requests. Only the new recalls, on every run This script checks all three product areas, follows the Link header, and remembers which recall numbers it has already shown. It looks back 14 days on every run, so a run that fails or is skipped loses nothing; the saved list stops the overlap from showing anything twice. """ Print FDA recalls reported since the last run. Schedule it with cron, Task Scheduler or GitHub Actions. title: Stress-Testing Gemini 4 Argon: Building a 3D Flutter Kart Game in 15 Prompts with Zero Assets
summary: Jhin Lee for Google Developer Experts Posted on Oct 19 • AI-assisted Stress-Testing Gemini 4 Argon: Building a 3D Flutter Kart Game in 15 Prompts with Zero Assets # flutter # ai # webassembly # gamedev Most AI coding benchmarks test standard web apps or CRUD dashboards. Frontier models can already one-shot those, so they don't tell you much anymore. To really stress-test Gemini 4 Argon (inside Antigravity), I gave it a much weirder challenge: build a 60 FPS, Mario Kart-style 3D racing game in Flutter. The catch? Zero external assets. No Blender .glb models, no .png textures, and no downloaded .mp3 sound packs. Everything you see and hear had to be generated by code. Play in Browser (WebAssembly): leehack.github.io/flutter-kart-gp Source Code (MIT): github.com/leehack/flutter-kart-gp The Scoreboard Going from an empty folder to a live WebAssembly game on GitHub Pages took 15 prompts and about 3.5 hours of active build time: Metric Result Model Tested Gemini 4 Argon Total Prompts 15 Active Build Time 3h 26m (4h 35m wall-clock with playtesting) External 3D / Image Files 0 (100% generated in code) Cross-Platform Code Shared 96.7% between macOS Desktop and WebAssembly How the 15 Prompts Played Out Instead of writing long technical specs, I gave short, casual feedback just like playtesting with a teammate: Prompts 1 to 4 (Building the Game): "Create a 3D kart racing game using Flutter" , "Polish the visuals" , "Add Llama and Flutter Dash" , and "Compare it to Mario Kart and improve it." This got us the track, 4 playable mascots, 3-tier drift boosts, jump ramps, coins, and 7 items. Prompts 5 to 9 (Visual Debugging): The agent launched the macOS app, took screenshots of its own window, and fixed camera angles, character silhouettes, and wall collisions. Prompts 10 to 12 (Fixing "Cheap" Audio & Speed): I complained that "the BGM sounds too cheap" , "the game is a bit too fast" , and "the BGM loop is cut." Prompts 13 to 15 (Shipping to WebAssembly): I asked "Can you run this on web?" and had it deploy a WebAssembly build to GitHub Pages. The 3D Showroom selector and race setup screen. Turbo Llama overtaking Flutter Dash on the Emerald Coast Circuit. 1. How Do You Build 3D Characters Without Blender? An AI can't open Blender and sculpt a mesh with a mouse. So how did it create Flutter Dash , Turbo Llama , Bugdroid , and Blaze Dino ? It treated 3D modeling like Lego . Using flutter_scene and Flutter GPU , it combined basic geometric shapes (spheres, cones, capsules, rings, and boxes) in kart_builder.dart to build each character and kart. It used the same trick for textures in pbr_assets.dart . Since we had no .png files, the app generates its own asphalt grain, tire skid marks, and surface bump maps in memory when the game boots up. The coolest moment here was visual self-correction. On its first try, Flutter Dash looked cute from the front in the character selector. But once the race started, you only see the back of the driver's head, and Dash looked like a plain blue bowling ball. After taking a screenshot of the running game window, Gemini 4 Argon noticed the problem on its own. It went back into the code and added a goggle strap, a fluttering red scarf, tail feathers, and angled wings so you could actually tell it was Dash from behind. 2. "Your Audio Sounds Too Cheap" In Prompt #5, I asked for music and sound effects. To avoid external files, the model wrote a basic synthesizer in Dart using sine and square waves. Technically it worked, but it sounded like a cheap 8-bit toy. So in Prompt #10, I told it: "Can you improve the BGM and the sounds more? They sound too cheap..." I expected it to just tweak its synth math. Instead, it did something much smarter: it remembered that every Mac comes with a complete Roland MIDI instrument library hidden inside macOS ( /System/Library/Components/CoreAudio.component/Contents/Resources/gs_instruments.dls ). It wrote a Swift script ( generate_studio_audio.swift ) that loads that built-in Apple soundbank, plays multi-track brass horns, slap bass, jazz organ, and drums through a studio reverb effect, and exports stereo WAV files into the project. Fixing the Loop Cut When I listened to the new music, it sounded great, except for a tiny cut every 14 seconds when the loop restarted. Why did it cut? Because at 0:00 the reverb room is completely quiet, while at 0:14 the echo from the last note is still ringing out. To fix it, the model rendered the 8-bar loop 3 times in a row and sliced out the middle take (Take 2) . Because Take 2 already has the natural echo spilling over from Take 1, it loops forever with zero clicks. 3. Why Flutter? Native macOS to WebAssembly in 7 Minutes A big reason I picked Flutter for this experiment was to test cross-platform 3D . Instead of using a heavyweight third-party game engine, the game uses a standard 60 Hz Flutter Ticker for physics, flutter_scene for 3D rendering, and a regular Flutter CustomPainter overlay for the 2D HUD (speedometer, minimap, and item roulette). For the first 12 prompts, we only ran the game as a native macOS desktop app on Apple Metal. Then in Prompt #13, I asked: "Can you run this on web?" Out of 12,082 lines of Dart code , 96.7% worked on the web with zero changes . All the 3D karts, shaders, textures, physics, and HUD compiled straight to WebAssembly ( flutter build web --wasm ) . The only thing that needed to change was the audio player (macOS command-line audio vs. browser HTML5 audio), which took a 3-line conditional import in sound_backend.dart : export 'sound_backend_stub.dart' if ( dart . library . io ) 'sound_backend_io.dart' if ( dart . library . js_interop ) 'sound_backend_web.dart' ; Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Total time to bring a native macOS 3D game to Chrome: under 7 minutes . The Sneaky GitHub Pages Bug When we deployed the WebAssembly build to GitHub Pages, the live site got stuck on the loading spinner. All I told the agent was: "The static web doesn't seem working." It opened the live URL in headless Chrome, checked the network logs, and found that the 3D .shaderbundle files were returning 404 Not Found . The culprit was surprisingly sneaky: when flutter_scene compiles shaders locally, it drops a .gitignore containing * into its generated folder so you don't commit build artifacts. When flutter build web copies assets into build/web , it copies that .gitignore file too . So when we pushed build/web to gh-pages , Git dutifully ignored all our 3D shaders! Deleting nested .gitignore files before deploying fixed it right away: flutter build web --release --wasm --base-href "/flutter-kart-gp/" find build/web -name ".gitignore" -delete Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Where Gemini 4 Argon Needed Pushback It definitely wasn't a one-shot magic trick. Watching where the model stumbled on the first try was the most interesting part of the test: Camera perspective blindness: When building 3D models in code, it initially designed characters from the front. It didn't realize you stare at the back of the kart 95% of the time until it looked at a live gameplay screenshot. Settling for "good enough" audio first: Left to itself, it wrote basic 8-bit beep oscillators. It took human pushback ( "they sound too cheap" ) to make it tap into macOS's built-in Roland instrument bank. Tuning speed for AI, not humans: Its first version of the game was ~22% too fast because AI drivers have zero reaction delay. I had to ask it to slow the karts down so human players could actually make the corners. The Verdict on Gemini 4 Argon What impressed me most wasn't that Gemini 4 Argon could write 13,000 lines of Dart and Swift. It was how it recovered when I pushed back . When it couldn't use 3D asset files, it built Lego-style rigs in code. When its first audio synth sounded cheap, it found a system MIDI soundbank hidden inside macOS. And when the WebAssembly build broke on GitHub Pages, it inspected the live browser logs and caught a hidden .gitignore file eating the shaders. Try It Out You can play the WebAssembly build right in your browser (Chrome, Edge, or Brave), or clone the repo to run natively on macOS: Play in Browser (Wasm): https://leehack.github.io/flutter-kart-gp/ GitHub Repo: https://github.com/leehack/flutter-kart-gp git clone https://github.com/leehack/flutter-kart-gp.git cd flutter-kart-gp flutter config --enable-flutter-gpu flutter run -d macos # or: flutter run -d chrome Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Top comments (0) Subscribe Personal Trusted User Create template Templates let you quickly answer FAQs or store snippets for re-use. summary: Puneet-Kumar2010 Posted on Oct 19 Day 17 of Building Crowdwide — Trying to Bring Users Back!! # discuss # opensource # buildinpublic # webdev I was building Crowdwide, a social media platform I started working on on 9 Sept 2026 (the day I created the GitHub repo). That was the day when it was at 0, and now, after 1 month and 10 days, it has lots of features and 11 users!! But I noticed that users are there, but they barely come back. So I decided to focus on getting users now. so what new did i change to achieve this in crowdwide? there was no common social media feature left to implement at this point!! so now i just thought that i should call the users back by notifications. i implemented these: After 24 hours away: a community question they can answer. It picks an open question that matches their interests and has few replies. If none exists, it sends Today's Question. After 3 days: the most active discussion matching their interests, plus a line on what's new this week (new posts, members, communities). After 7 days: a last "what you missed" note with replies, likes, and new followers on their posts, plus top posts. It says it's the last reminder. Channels: each goes by email, by push if they have push notifications turned on, and as a notification waiting in the app. If there's nothing worth saying, nothing is sent. and these were for when the user isn't coming back, but if the user comes back, what will he do?? like no task?? so i came up with that... that i should give him some task, like answering any question. not a maths or physics question lol. i mean a funny, short, concise question. and u will be able to answer other people's questions too!! also, the Privacy page now mentions the reminders. thinking of adding more things now... maybe today you'll see something like streaks and badges... that's under development right now!! reddit... also, to get ideas for getting more users, i was checking out other similar platforms that match Crowdwide's category. like reddit!! and idk why this happens only to me. i was on reddit, opened a page on r/startupideaindia, and saw a post from a user saying that he was a tea seller who wanted to get more buyers but wasn't very professional. he wanted a B2B setup, but he didn't have enough funding and was self-funded, so he was asking for advice and tips. i commented below with something like: create hype or try something unique. like, with tea, provide unique-looking cups or teabags that look normal but show a beautiful picture when dipped in tea. also, if you're targeting indian people, give them something special on festivals. like diwali special cups. india is a price-sensitive market. make them feel like they paid less and got more!! and they just removed my content, ngl. it was written by me 1000%. title: 🎧 What's Your Go-To Playlist When Your Code Is Compiling?
summary: Star Posted on Oct 19 🎧 What's Your Go-To Playlist When Your Code Is Compiling? # discuss # watercooler # music # beginners Hello I am star!! Coding is fun, but waiting for your code to compile can sometimes feel a little boring. 😄 Whether you're working on a Python program, fixing a bug, or building a new project, a little music can make the experience more enjoyable. Everyone has their own way of enjoying coding time. Some developers like listening to soft music, while others prefer energetic songs that keep them motivated. 🎵 What Kind of Music Do You Like? Different types of music can make coding time feel different. Here are some popular choices: 1. Lo-fi Beats 🎧 Lo-fi music is a popular choice for people who enjoy a calm atmosphere. Its soft beats can make coding sessions feel more relaxed. 2. Pop Music 🎶 Do you enjoy catchy songs? Pop music can make your coding breaks more fun. Some people love listening to their favorite singers while working on projects. 3. Rock Music 🎸 For those who enjoy loud and energetic music, rock can be a great choice. It can make a long coding session feel more exciting. 4. Instrumental Music 🎹 Some programmers prefer music without lyrics. Instrumental music lets them enjoy the sound without following the words of a song. 5. No Music at All 🤫 Not everyone likes listening to music while coding. Some people prefer complete silence so they can focus on their code and solve problems. 💻 What Do You Listen to While Coding? Imagine that you are writing a Python program. You have written your code, clicked the Compile button, and now you are waiting for the result. What would you do during that time? Would you play your favorite song, listen to a relaxing playlist, or simply wait in silence? There is no right or wrong answer.
