title: 10 Prompting Techniques My Deep Learning Exam Taught Me (That I Actually Use Now)
summary: Dhruv Jani Posted on Oct 17 • Edited on Oct 19 • AI-assisted 10 Prompting Techniques My Deep Learning Exam Taught Me (That I Actually Use Now) # promptengineering # ai # discuss # beginners Academic AI theory turned into practical dev tips You already use prompting every day. You just don't know the names of what you're doing. Every time you type "fix this error" into ChatGPT or "refactor this function" into Cursor — that's a prompting technique. You're already doing it. You just haven't been told there are ten distinct ways to do it, and most of them are better than what you're doing right now. I had to study all of this for my Deep Learning exam. Two 50-page PDFs full of academic examples like "Recommend science-fiction books" and "Convert 0°C to Fahrenheit." Technically correct. Practically useless. Nobody is opening ChatGPT to convert Celsius. So here's the version I wish those PDFs had been — every technique from my syllabus, explained with examples you'll actually use as a developer. Table of Contents 1. Zero-Shot Prompting 2. Few-Shot Prompting 3. Chain-of-Thought Prompting 4. Tree-of-Thought Prompting 5. Role-Playing Prompts 6. Generated Knowledge Prompting 7. Maieutic Prompting 8. Least-to-Most Prompting 9. Format-Specific Prompting 10. Multi-Turn Prompting The Cheat Sheet 🧪 The Real Trick: Combine Them 1. Zero-Shot Prompting What it is: You ask the AI something directly. No examples. No context. No hand-holding. Just the question. The textbook example: "Can you recommend science-fiction books?" The developer example: "What does the useEffect cleanup function do in React?" Or: "Explain the difference between git rebase and git merge in 3 sentences." You're already doing this. Every time you paste an error into ChatGPT with zero context and pray — that's zero-shot prompting. It works great for questions the model has seen a million times. It falls apart the moment your problem is even slightly niche. When to use it: Quick lookups, syntax questions, "what does X do" queries. Anything where the AI's pre-trained knowledge is enough. When it fails: The moment your question involves YOUR codebase, YOUR architecture, or anything the model hasn't been trained on. That's when you need the next one. 2. Few-Shot Prompting What it is: You show the AI 2-5 examples of what you want, then let it figure out the pattern and apply it to a new input. The textbook example: Convert Celsius to Fahrenheit: 0°C → 32°F 25°C → 77°F 100°C → ? The developer example: Say you're writing commit messages for your team and you want a consistent style: Here are my commit messages so far: feat: add user authentication with JWT fix: resolve null pointer in payment service refactor: extract validation logic into middleware Now write a commit message for: I added rate limiting to the API endpoints. Output: feat: add rate limiting to API endpoints The model picks up your prefix convention ( feat: , fix: , refactor: ), your sentence casing, your level of detail — without you having to explain any of it. Another real use: You're converting an old API response format to a new one. Show 3 examples of old → new, paste the 4th old response, and let the model transform it. Saves you from writing a throwaway script. When to use it: Consistent formatting, style matching, repetitive transformations. Anytime you're thinking "I need to do this same thing 40 more times." 3. Chain-of-Thought Prompting What it is: You ask the AI to work through a problem systematically — step by step — instead of jumping straight to a conclusion. The textbook example: What is 23 × 47? Show your work. The developer example: This function is supposed to return the total price after discount, but it's returning NaN for some inputs. Walk me through what's happening step by step: function getTotal ( price , discount ) { const total = price - ( price * discount / 100 ); return total . toFixed ( 2 ); } Without "step by step," the AI might just say "the function looks fine." With it, the AI will trace through edge cases: "If discount is passed as a string like '10%', the multiplication produces NaN, which propagates through the calculation..." Asking for a step-by-step breakdown doesn't necessarily reveal the model's actual internal reasoning — but it does force a more inspectable answer: stated assumptions, intermediate checks, edge cases considered, and only then a conclusion. That structure is what makes the mistakes easier to catch. This is exactly how I tracked down a clients.matchAll() race condition in one of my project's service workers. Copilot's first answer was confident and completely wrong. Asking it to walk through the event lifecycle step by step — not "fix this," but "trace what happens between these two events" — is what actually surfaced the timing bug. When to use it: Debugging, code reviews, any question where the reasoning matters more than the answer. If you've ever gotten a confident but completely wrong answer from an AI — this is probably what was missing. 4. Tree-of-Thought Prompting What it is: Instead of following one reasoning path, the AI explores multiple paths in parallel. Chain-of-thought is a straight line. Tree-of-thought is a decision tree. The textbook example: List the environmental and social effects of climate change separately. The developer example: I need to add real-time notifications to my app. Explore three different approaches — WebSockets, Server-Sent Events, and polling — and for each one, explain the trade-offs in terms of complexity, scalability, and browser support. Then recommend which one fits a small team with a Node backend. Instead of the AI just picking one and defending it (which is what zero-shot would do), this prompt makes the comparison explicit instead of letting the AI jump straight to one recommendation. Another real use: Architecture decisions. "We need to store user sessions. Compare Redis, database sessions, and JWT tokens. For each: list pros, cons, and failure modes. Then recommend one for a team of two building an MVP." When to use it: Any decision with multiple valid options where you need the AI to compare, not just pick. Tech stack choices, architecture decisions, debugging when you're not sure which subsystem is the problem. 5. Role-Playing Prompts What it is: You tell the AI to act as a specific expert. This isn't a gimmick — it genuinely changes the depth and angle of the response. The textbook example: "Imagine you are a seasoned venture capitalist. Review this startup pitch." The developer example: You are a senior backend engineer conducting a code review. Review this Express.js route handler and flag any security vulnerabilities, performance issues, or architectural concerns. Be specific — cite the line and explain why it's a problem. Without the role, the AI gives you a polite, generic review. With the role, it starts acting like that one senior dev who actually catches things — "Line 14: you're interpolating user input directly into the SQL query. This is a textbook SQL injection vector." I've also used this the other way around during placement season: "You are a strict technical interviewer at a product-based company. Ask me follow-up questions on this project until you find a gap in my understanding." It's uncomfortable. It's also the closest free rehearsal you'll get before the real thing. Other roles that actually help: "You are a tech recruiter. What's weak about this resume?" "You are a QA engineer. Find edge cases in this function." "You are a DevOps engineer. What's wrong with this Dockerfile?" When to use it: Code reviews, resume feedback, interview prep, getting a second opinion from a perspective you don't have on your team. The role narrows the AI's focus to what that specific expert would care about. 6. Generated Knowledge Prompting What it is: Before asking the AI to do the actual task, you first ask it to list everything it knows about the topic. Research first, write second. The textbook example: "Write an essay on deforestation. First, list key facts." The developer example: I need to write documentation for our authentication flow. Before you write anything: List every step that happens from when a user clicks "Login" to when they land on the dashboard — including token generation, cookie handling, and redirect logic. Now write the developer documentation based on that list. The magic here is Step 1. By forcing the AI to generate a knowledge base first, you get a factual foundation that the writing stays grounded in. Without it, the AI often drifts into generic documentation that misses your specific flow. When to use it: Writing documentation, README files, technical blog posts (ironic, right?), or any task where factual accuracy matters more than creativity. The "list what you know first" step acts as a self-fact-check. 7. Maieutic Prompting What it is: Named after the Socratic method — you ask a question, then ask the AI to explain its own answer deeper, then deeper again. Recursive questioning until you actually understand. The textbook example: "Explain why the sky is blue. Then explain why blue light scatters more." The developer example: Why is my React component re-rendering on every state change even though I'm using useMemo ? Now explain why the dependency array matters for useMemo specifically. Now explain what "referential equality" means in the context of JavaScript objects and why it breaks memoization. Each follow-up forces the AI to go one layer deeper. By the third question, you've gone from "it's re-rendering" to understanding how JavaScript's object comparison model fundamentally interacts with React's reconciliation algorithm. When to use it: Learning new concepts. When the first answer makes sense but you can feel there's something underneath you don't fully get. It's the "but why?" technique. 8. Least-to-Most Prompting What it is: You tell the AI to break a big problem into subproblems first, then solve each one in order. Decompose, then execute. The textbook example: "List the subproblems to solve 3x + 5 = 20, then solve each." The developer example: I need to add Google OAuth to my Next.js app. Break this down into every subproblem I need to solve, in order. Then walk me through each one with code. Output would look something like: Set up Google Cloud Console project and get credentials Install and configure NextAuth.js Create the auth API route Add the Google provider configuration Protect routes with session checks Handle the callback and store user data Then the AI solves each one sequentially, and each step builds on the last. This is basically how I survived every hackathon deadline — breaking "build a working demo in 24 hours" into an actual ordered sequence instead of staring at the whole scope and panicking. When to use it: Implementing features you've never built before. Instead of asking "how do I add auth" (which gets you a vague overview), you force the AI to give you a buildable sequence. 9. Format-Specific Prompting What it is: You explicitly tell the AI what format you want the output in. Bullet points, table, JSON, markdown, CSV — specify it and the AI follows. The textbook example: "List the top 5 movies in bullet points." The developer example: Compare these three state management libraries for React. Output as a markdown table with columns: Library, Bundle Size, Learning Curve, Best For, and Drawback. Or: Convert this error log into a JSON array where each object has timestamp , level , message , and source fields. This is one of the most underrated techniques. Most devs don't specify format and then spend 5 minutes reformatting the AI's response. Just tell it upfront. When to use it: Literally every time you want the output in a specific shape. Tables, JSON, code blocks, bullet points, numbered steps. If you're going to reformat the output anyway, you're wasting time. 10. Multi-Turn Prompting What it is: Building context across multiple messages in a conversation. Each prompt builds on the last response. This is how you turn AI from a search engine into a collaborator. The textbook example: Turn 1: "Summarize this article." Turn 2: "Now rewrite it for a 10-year-old." Turn 3: "Add three quiz questions." The developer example: Turn 1: "Here's my Express app's folder structure. [paste tree output]. Explain the architecture." Turn 2: "Now I want to add a notifications service. Where should it live in this structure, and what should it import?" Turn 3: "Write the boilerplate for that service following the same patterns as the existing services." Turn 4: "Now write the tests for it, matching the testing style in __tests__/user.service.test.js ." By Turn 4, the AI knows your folder structure, your architectural patterns, your naming conventions, and your testing style. A single-shot prompt could never produce output this tailored. When to use it: Any substantial coding task. Building features, refactoring, writing tests. If you're copy-pasting the same context into every new prompt, you should be using multi-turn instead. The Cheat Sheet Technique In one sentence Use when... Zero-Shot Just ask Quick lookups, simple questions Few-Shot Show examples first You need consistent formatting or style Chain-of-Thought "Think step by step" Debugging, complex reasoning Tree-of-Thought Explore multiple paths Comparing options, architecture decisions Role-Playing "You are a senior dev..." Code reviews, interview prep, expert perspectives Generated Knowledge "List facts first, then write" Documentation, technical writing Maieutic "Now explain WHY" Learning new concepts deeply Least-to-Most "Break it into subproblems" Implementing features you've never built Format-Specific "Output as a table/JSON/list" Every time you want structured output Multi-Turn Build context over messages Any substantial coding task 🧪 The Real Trick: Combine Them Here's the thing nobody in those textbooks told me: you don't pick one technique and stick with it. The best prompts combine two or three. Chain-of-thought + role-playing: "You are a senior engineer. Debug this function step by step." Few-shot + format-specific: "Here are three examples of my commit messages. Write the next five in the same style, as a bullet list." Generated knowledge + least-to-most: "List everything involved in deploying a Next.js app to AWS. Then break it into subproblems and walk me through each one." The techniques are ingredients. The skill is knowing which ones to combine. I learned all of this from two academic PDFs full of Celsius conversions and science-fiction book recommendations. Now you've learned it from examples you'll actually open a terminal and use tomorrow. If this saved you from reading 50 pages of textbook formatting — you're welcome. title: How Much Context Fits Beside a 12B on an 8 GB GPU? Gemma 4 12B's Context Cache on an RTX 3050
summary: xbill for Google Developer Experts Posted on Oct 19 How Much Context Fits Beside a 12B on an 8 GB GPU? Gemma 4 12B's Context Cache on an RTX 3050 # gemma # llamacpp # cuda # benchmarking This article provides a step by step guide to choosing the context cache, context size and drafter settings for Gemma 4 12B, Google's quantization-aware trained (QAT) build, on an 8 GB NVIDIA RTX 3050 with llama.cpp. The target workload is one long agentic session, a coding assistant whose conversation grows turn by turn, so the measure is how much context fits, how fast the model generates with that context held, and whether the answers change. A suite of Python MCP tools is built to simplify management of the llama.cpp hosted deployment. This is the fourth part of a short series. Part 1, Gemma 4's MTP Drafter, Explained , covers how the drafter works. Part 2, Do Drafters Work on Small Models? , measures E2B and E4B on this card. Part 3, Can a QAT 12B Fit an 8 GB GPU? , fits the 12B and its drafter on the card with a 16-bit cache. This part makes room for a long conversation. https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev How much context fits beside the 12B and its drafter? 81,920 tokens, with a 4-bit context cache , and the answers stay the same: RTX 3050 OEM, 8 GB, 12B + drafter 16-bit cache 4-bit cache Most context that loads 24,576 tokens 81,920 tokens Generation, nothing held 57.5 tok/s 55.1 tok/s Generation, 16,384 tokens held 49.8 tok/s 42.4 tok/s Generation, 65,536 tokens held does not fit 30.8 tok/s GSM8K / BFCL simple 0.960 / 0.950 0.961 / 0.950 The 4-bit cache holds 3.3x the tokens for 4% of the generation speed with nothing held and 15% at 16,384 tokens. Without the drafter the same cache holds the model's full 131,072 tokens at about half the speed. What Is Being Measured? Gemma 4 12B's weights take 6,390 MiB of the card's 8,192 MiB in the exact Q4_0 rebuild from Part 3. Everything else shares what is left: the context cache (the keys and values of every token already read), the drafter (Google's 12B multi-token prediction assistant, 227 MiB of weights), and working buffers. The context cache is the part that grows with the conversation. llama.cpp stores it at 16 bits by default and can store it at 8 bits ( q8_0 ) or 4 bits ( q4_0 ), which halves and quarters what each token costs. The questions are what a smaller cache costs in speed and in answers, and whether the drafter is still worth its memory once the context is long. Every setting is measured on one llama.cpp build, 7182ef71e , with the same model and drafter files and one request at a time ( --parallel 1 ), because the workload is one conversation. Step 1 — Serve the Rig The rig is local-llamacpp-3050oem-12b-q4_0 . Its tpu.env holds every serving setting, and make serve starts llama-server from it: git clone https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev cd gemma4-dev/local-llamacpp-3050oem-12b-q4_0 make download draft make serve Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode The setting this article arrives at: llama-server -m gemma-4-12B-it-q4_0-exact.gguf -ngl 99 -c 81920 -ctk q4_0 -ctv q4_0 -fa 1 \ -t 6 -tb 12 --parallel 1 --reasoning off --metrics \ -md gemma-4-12B-it-qat-assistant-q4_0-exact.gguf --spec-type draft-mtp -ngld all --spec-draft-n-max 2 Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Step 2 — Find the Most Context That Fits kv_sweep.py starts llama-server with each cache type, with and without the drafter, at falling context sizes, and keeps the largest that loads: python3 kv_sweep.py ../../.. . Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode RTX 3050, 8,192 MiB with the drafter without 16-bit cache 24,576 tokens 40,960 tokens 8-bit cache 49,152 tokens 65,536 tokens 4-bit cache 81,920 tokens , 7,853 MiB 131,072 tokens With the drafter, 86,016 tokens fail to load. 131,072 is the model's own limit, so without the drafter the 4-bit cache holds all of it. Step 3 — Measure Speed With a Long Conversation Held The same script puts 0 to 98,304 tokens of a long document (the NVIDIA driver README) ahead of three questions (a story, a Python function, a summary) and measures 256 greedy tokens of generation, with the prompt cache on as a conversation would use it: tokens already in context 0 16,384 32,768 65,536 98,304 16-bit cache, drafter 57.5 tok/s 49.8 — — — 8-bit cache, drafter 55.1 43.3 39.3 — — 4-bit cache, drafter 55.1 42.4 37.8 30.8 — 16-bit cache, no drafter 28.1 25.7 24.8 — — 4-bit cache, no drafter 27.5 24.1 22.2 19.2 16.8 Each figure is the geometric mean of the three questions. Reading new text is level across cache types: about 840 tok/s for 8,192 tokens, 720 at 16,384, 600 at 32,768 and 408 at 65,536. The drafter keeps paying with a long conversation held : with the 4-bit cache it is 2.00x faster with nothing held, 1.70x at 32,768 tokens and 1.60x at 65,536. It keeps 61% to 71% of drafted tokens at every depth and cache type. 🔎 Tip: A Smaller Cache Costs the Drafter More Without the drafter, the 4-bit cache generates at 0.94x the 16-bit cache with 16,384 tokens held. With the drafter, 0.85x. The drafter checks two drafted tokens in one pass over the whole cache, so a cache that is slower to read costs it more. The drafter still wins at every depth: the slowest drafter setting at 16,384 tokens (42.4 tok/s) is 1.65x the fastest setting without one (25.7, arithmetic). Step 4 — Check the Answers gen_eval.py runs GSM8K (1,319 grade-school math questions, up to 2,048 tokens per reply) and BFCL simple (400 single function calls), one request at a time, with each cache at its largest context: JEV_GEN_MAX_TOKENS = 2048 python3 gen_eval.py run http://127.0.0.1:8080 google/gemma-4-12B-it gsm8k gsm8k-q4x.jsonl --concurrency 1 Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode one request at a time GSM8K BFCL simple 16-bit cache, drafter 0.960 0.950 16-bit cache, no drafter 0.963 0.948 8-bit cache, drafter 0.960 0.948 8-bit cache, no drafter 0.959 0.948 4-bit cache, drafter 0.961 0.950 4-bit cache, no drafter 0.962 0.950 The cache type changes no score. compare.py pairs each run question by question against the 16-bit cache with the same drafter setting. For the 4-bit cache with the drafter the difference is +0.15 points on GSM8K (95% range −0.45 to +0.76) and zero on BFCL (−1.0 to +1.0), and every other range also includes zero. The time a run takes is set by the drafter: GSM8K took 1 h 57 min with the drafter and 4 h 20 min without, on the 4-bit cache. Step 5 — Check Recall From a Long Document GSM8K and BFCL questions are short. recall.py tests the long context itself: it plants eight lines of the form "The access code for project Heron is 601531." through the document, asks for every code as JSON, and scores the codes returned, ten trials per depth with the same codes for every setting: codes right, of 80 16,384 32,768 64,000 98,304 126,976 16-bit cache, no drafter 69 55 — — — 8-bit cache, no drafter 68 58 57 — — 4-bit cache, no drafter 67 58 59 48 56 4-bit cache, drafter — 58 57 — — The cache type and the drafter leave recall level at every depth they share. Recall falls with depth on every cache, from about 85% of codes at 16,384 tokens to about 70% from 32,768 on. Step 6 — Tune the Drafter and Prompt Batch tune.py tries the remaining settings on the 4-bit cache at 81,920 tokens: 4-bit cache, drafter 0 tokens held 32,768 65,536 drafted tokens kept 1 drafted token 42.9 tok/s 30.9 27.3 0.72–0.77 2 drafted tokens 55.1 37.8 30.8 0.64–0.71 3 drafted tokens 56.0 39.3 32.1 0.55–0.59 3 drafted tokens ran within 4% of 2, inside this card's spread from one server start to the next: two starts of the same setting read a 32,768-token prompt at 589 and 673 tok/s. 2 stays. A larger prompt batch ( -ub 1024 or 2048 ) does not load beside the drafter, even at 65,536 tokens. 🔎 Tip: Keep the Conversation in the Prompt Cache Reading 65,536 tokens from scratch at about 406 tok/s takes about 160 seconds (arithmetic). In one conversation llama.cpp's prompt cache keeps what it has already read, so each turn reads only the new text. One request at a time ( --parallel 1 ) keeps the whole 81,920 tokens for that one conversation, because llama.cpp splits the context across parallel slots. Compare and Contrast RTX 3050 OEM, 8 GB, Gemma 4 12B 16-bit cache + drafter 🥇 4-bit cache + drafter 4-bit cache, no drafter Most context 24,576 tokens 81,920 tokens 131,072 tokens Generation, nothing held 57.5 tok/s 55.1 tok/s 27.5 tok/s Generation, 16,384 held 49.8 tok/s 42.4 tok/s 24.1 tok/s Generation, 65,536 held — 30.8 tok/s 19.2 tok/s GSM8K 0.960 0.961 0.962 BFCL simple 0.950 0.950 0.950 Codes recalled at 32,768 — 58 of 80 58 of 80 So, Which One? For one long conversation, the 4-bit cache with the drafter at 81,920 tokens. It holds 3.3x the 16-bit cache's context with the same answers, and generates at 55 tok/s with nothing held and 31 tok/s at 65,536 tokens. For a conversation that must go past 81,920 tokens, drop the drafter: the 4-bit cache then holds the full 131,072 tokens at about half the speed. For short conversations only, the 16-bit cache with the drafter is the fastest setting, up to 24,576 tokens. What Comes Next The answer tests here use short questions, and the recall test is the only one with a long context held. The next measurements are function calling with 32,768 to 81,920 tokens of conversation ahead of each call, a replayed multi-turn coding session that measures each turn's speed and how much of the prompt cache it reuses, and repeated server starts to resolve the 2-against-3 drafted-token gap. Summary The goal of this article was to find the context cache, context size and drafter settings that serve Gemma 4 12B best for one long conversation on an 8 GB RTX 3050. The key to the solution was measuring speed with a long conversation already held and checking answers question by question for each cache type. The results were: 🟢 A 4-bit context cache holds 81,920 tokens beside the 12B and its drafter, 3.3x the 16-bit cache's 24,576 🟢 GSM8K, BFCL and long-document recall are level across the 16-bit, 8-bit and 4-bit caches, with and without the drafter 🟢 The drafter is still 1.60x faster with 65,536 tokens held ⚠️ With the drafter, the 4-bit cache generates at 0.85x the 16-bit cache once 16,384 tokens are held ⚠️ The full 131,072-token context fits only without the drafter, at about half the speed ❌ Recall of eight facts planted in a long document falls from about 85% at 16,384 tokens to about 70% from 32,768 on, on every cache Scope: Gemma 4 12B-it QAT only, exact Q4_0 rebuild and exact Q4_0 12B drafter, text only, one RTX 3050 OEM (8 GB) in an i7-5820K desktop, llama.cpp 7182ef71e , 16-bit, 8-bit and 4-bit context caches, 0 to 98,304 tokens of one document held for speed and up to 126,976 for recall, greedy decoding, thinking off, GSM8K and BFCL simple with short prompts, one request at a time throughout. The strategy for using MCP for local accelerator comparison was validated with an incremental step by step approach. References Part 1, Gemma 4's MTP Drafter, Explained: https://dev.to/gde/gemma-4s-mtp-drafter-explained-speculative-decoding-and-a-4-bit-drafter-at-60-of-the-size-1oc0 Part 2, Do Drafters Work on Small Models?: https://dev.to/gde/do-drafters-work-on-small-models-gemma-4-e2b-and-e4b-on-two-small-gpus-1b4g Part 3, Can a QAT 12B Fit an 8 GB GPU?: https://dev.to/gde/can-a-qat-12b-fit-an-8-gb-gpu-gemma-4-12b-on-an-rtx-3050-1267 Repository: https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev 12B rig: https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev/tree/main/local-llamacpp-3050oem-12b-q4_0 The chosen settings, trade-offs and open questions: https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev/blob/main/local-llamacpp-3050oem-12b-q4_0/SERVING-CONFIG.md Context cache run: https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev/blob/main/local-llamacpp-3050oem-12b-q4_0/benchmarks/runs/2026-10-17-kvcache-12b-3050oem/REPORT.md 16-bit cache answers: https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev/blob/main/local-llamacpp-3050oem-12b-q4_0/benchmarks/runs/2026-10-16-accuracy-12b-3050oem/REPORT.md 12B GGUF: https://huggingface.co/xbill9/gemma-4-12B-it-qat-q4_0-exact-gguf 12B drafter: https://huggingface.co/xbill9/gemma-4-12B-it-qat-assistant-q4_0-exact-gguf llama.cpp: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp Top comments (0) Subscribe Personal Trusted User Create template Templates let you quickly answer FAQs or store snippets for re-use. title: Can a 26B MoE Run on an 8 GB GPU? Gemma 4 26B A4B on an RTX 3050
summary: xbill for Google Developer Experts Posted on Oct 19 Can a 26B MoE Run on an 8 GB GPU? Gemma 4 26B A4B on an RTX 3050 # gemma # llamacpp # cuda # benchmarking This article provides a step by step guide to serving Gemma 4 26B A4B, Google's quantization-aware trained (QAT) mixture-of-experts model, on an 8 GB NVIDIA RTX 3050 with llama.cpp. The model file is 14.4 GB, so it cannot fit on the card. llama.cpp can keep the experts in system RAM and run them on the CPU, while the rest of the model runs on the GPU. The measures are how fast it generates, how much context fits, what the drafter adds, and whether the answers match the 12B that fits the card whole. A suite of Python MCP tools is built to simplify management of the llama.cpp hosted deployment. This is the fifth part of a short series. Part 1, Gemma 4's MTP Drafter, Explained , covers how the drafter works. Part 2, Do Drafters Work on Small Models? , measures E2B and E4B on this card. Part 3, Can a QAT 12B Fit an 8 GB GPU? , fits the 12B and its drafter on the card. Part 4, How Much Context Fits Beside a 12B on an 8 GB GPU? , gives the 12B a 4-bit context cache for long conversations. This part runs a model twice the card's size. https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev Can a 26B run on an 8 GB card? Yes, with 21 of its 30 expert layers in system RAM , and its answers match the 12B's: RTX 3050 OEM, 8 GB, 4-bit cache, drafter Gemma 4 12B Gemma 4 26B A4B Model file 6.7 GB, all on the card 14.4 GB, experts mostly in RAM Most context that loads 81,920 tokens 131,072 tokens Generation, nothing held 55.1 tok/s 33.7 tok/s Generation, 65,536 tokens held 30.8 tok/s 22.8 tok/s GSM8K / BFCL simple 0.961 / 0.950 0.965 / 0.945 GSM8K run, 1,319 questions 1 h 57 min 3 h 26 min The 26B holds 1.6x the 12B's context and scores the same, at 0.61x to 0.74x the 12B's generation speed. What Is Being Measured? Gemma 4 26B A4B is a mixture-of-experts model. Each of its 30 layers holds 128 experts, small feed-forward networks, and a router picks 8 of them for each token. The file is 14.4 GB: 12,251 MiB of expert weights (408 MiB per layer) and 1,505 MiB of everything else (attention, norms, routers and the token embedding). So 89% of the file is experts, and each token reads only a sixteenth of them. llama.cpp's -ncmoe N keeps the experts of the first N layers in system RAM, where the CPU runs them, and puts everything else on the GPU. Every token still crosses the CPU, so the CPU and its memory are part of the serving path, unlike on the 12B. The host is an i7-5820K desktop (6 cores, 12 threads, quad-channel DDR4, 46 GiB) with the RTX 3050 OEM. Every setting is measured on one llama.cpp build, 7182ef71e , with Google's google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-q4_0-gguf unmodified, and one request at a time ( --parallel 1 ). Step 1 — Serve the Rig The rig is local-llamacpp-3050oem-26b-q4_0 . Its tpu.env holds every serving setting, and make serve starts llama-server from it: git clone https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev cd gemma4-dev/local-llamacpp-3050oem-26b-q4_0 make download draft make serve Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode The setting this article arrives at: llama-server -m gemma-4-26B_q4_0-it.gguf -ngl 99 -ncmoe 21 -c 131072 -ctk q4_0 -ctv q4_0 -fa 1 \ -t 8 -tb 12 --parallel 1 --reasoning off --metrics \ -md gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-assistant-q4_0-exact.gguf --spec-type draft-mtp -ngld all --spec-draft-n-max 2 Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode -ngl 99 puts every layer on the GPU; -ncmoe 21 then takes the experts of the first 21 layers back to system RAM. Step 2 — Find How Many Expert Layers the Card Can Hold llama-bench measures generation (128 tokens) and prompt reading (512 tokens) with the experts of 30 down to 16 layers in RAM: experts in RAM, of 30 layers 30 (all) 24 20 18 17 16 Generation, tok/s 24.35 27.66 30.65 32.27 33.31 does not load Prompt reading, tok/s 264 313 365 394 408 Each expert layer moved to the card adds about half a token per second. With every expert in RAM the 26B already generates at 24 tok/s; 17 layers in RAM is the fastest setting that loads, 1.37x faster. At 16 the working buffer no longer fits. 🔎 Tip: Threads Matter Here Here the CPU runs most of the experts, so the thread count sets part of the speed. At 17 layers in RAM, 4 threads generate at 28.49 tok/s, 6 at 33.03 and 8 at 33.97, with 12 level with 8 inside the run's spread. The rig serves -t 8 , and anything else busy on the CPU or the memory bus slows the model. Step 3 — Trade Expert Layers for Context Every expert layer on the card costs about 410 MiB that the context cache could use. Each row below is the most context that loads with that many layers in RAM, one request at a time: experts in RAM 16-bit cache 8-bit cache 4-bit cache 4-bit cache + drafter 18 does not load 98,304 19 32,768 65,536 131,072 65,536 20 32,768 65,536 131,072 98,304 21 32,768 131,072 131,072 131,072 , 7,836 MiB 22 131,072 262,144 , 7,874 MiB 131,072 Blank cells were not tried. The 26B holds more context than the 12B on the same card : 131,072 tokens beside the drafter against the 12B's 81,920. Its weights mostly live in RAM, so the card's memory goes to the cache. Without the drafter, 22 layers in RAM hold the model's full 262,144 tokens. The rig serves 21 with the drafter, the most context that fits with it. Step 4 — Measure the Drafter Google ships a QAT drafter for the 26B, a small model that proposes the next tokens for the 26B to check. It is stored as exact 4-bit (Q4_0) on its trained grid, 252 MB against 462 MB for the converter's 8-bit file, and published as xbill9/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-assistant-q4_0-exact-gguf . spec_ab.py runs six prompts, greedy three times and sampled once, 256 tokens each, with 20 expert layers in RAM: drafter setting greedy tok/s x no drafter drafted tokens kept sampled x no drafter none 29.6 1.00x — 1.00x exact Q4_0, 1 token 37.0 1.25x 0.76 1.25x exact Q4_0, 2 tokens 36.8 1.24x 0.65 1.22x exact Q4_0, 3 tokens 30.1 1.01x 0.58 0.61x 8-bit, 2 tokens 35.6 1.20x 0.66 1.17x The drafter gives 1.24x here against 2.01x on the 12B. It keeps as many drafted tokens as the 12B's does, so the gain is lost in the checking: each drafted token the 26B checks routes to its own 8 experts, and the CPU reads them (inferred, not measured). By prompt it ranges from 1.51x on code to 1.12x on a story. 2 tokens are served: level with 1 overall and ahead on code. 3 tokens lose on sampled text. Step 5 — Measure Speed With a Long Conversation Held The 12B's context test at the serving setting: 0 to 98,304 tokens of a long document (the NVIDIA driver README) ahead of three questions (a story, a Python function, a summary of the document), 256 greedy tokens each, with the prompt cache on: tokens already in context 0 16,384 32,768 65,536 98,304 26B, drafter 33.7 tok/s 30.0 28.0 22.8 19.3 26B, no drafter 28.2 24.9 22.3 17.5 14.2 12B, drafter 55.1 42.4 37.8 30.8 does not fit 12B, no drafter 27.5 24.1 22.2 19.2 16.8 Each figure is the geometric mean of the questions (story and code only with nothing held). Without drafters the 26B generates as fast as the 12B up to 32,768 tokens held (1.00x to 1.03x), and falls to 0.85x at 98,304. The 12B's drafter is what puts it ahead. The 26B's drafter gains with depth , from 1.20x with nothing held to 1.36x at 98,304 tokens, while the 12B's falls from 2.00x to 1.60x at 65,536. On code alone the 26B's drafter reaches 1.67x at 98,304 tokens (23.6 against 14.1 tok/s). Reading new text falls from 302 tok/s at 8,192 tokens to 227 at 98,304; the 12B reads 828 tok/s at 8,192. Step 6 — Check the Answers gen_eval.py runs GSM8K (1,319 grade-school math questions, up to 2,048 tokens per reply) and BFCL simple (400 single function calls), one request at a time, at the serving setting: JEV_GEN_MAX_TOKENS = 2048 python3 gen_eval.py run http://127.0.0.1:8080 google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it gsm8k gsm8k-q4x.jsonl --concurrency 1 Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode one request at a time, 4-bit cache GSM8K BFCL simple 26B, drafter 0.965 0.945 26B, no drafter 0.962 0.945 12B, drafter 0.961 0.950 12B, no drafter 0.962 0.950 The 26B scores level with the 12B, and the drafter changes neither score. compare.py pairs the runs question by question. 26B against 12B with drafters: +0.38 points on GSM8K (95% range −0.45 to +1.29) and −0.50 on BFCL (−2.50 to +1.50). 26B with the drafter against without: +0.30 on GSM8K (−0.23 to +0.83), with 12 of 1,319 answers different, and zero on BFCL, with 392 of 400 replies word for word the same. The time is where the two models part. GSM8K took the 26B 3 h 26 min with the drafter and 4 h 38 min without (1.35x), against 1 h 57 min for the 12B with its drafter. 🔎 Tip: An MoE Model Keeps Its Speed With Its Experts Off the Card A dense model with two thirds of its layers on the CPU reads all of them for every token. On this card the dense 31B generates at 2.5 tok/s with 20 of 60 layers on the GPU. The 26B reads 8 of 128 experts per layer, so its CPU share per token is small, and it generates at 24 tok/s with every expert in RAM. For a model larger than the card, the active parameter count decides the speed. Compare and Contrast RTX 3050 OEM, 8 GB 🥇 12B, 4-bit cache + drafter 26B, 4-bit cache + drafter 26B, 4-bit cache, no drafter Expert layers in RAM — 21 of 30 22 of 30 Most context 81,920 tokens 131,072 tokens 262,144 tokens Generation, nothing held 55.1 tok/s 33.7 tok/s 28.2 tok/s Generation, 65,536 held 30.8 tok/s 22.8 tok/s 17.5 tok/s GSM8K 0.961 0.965 0.962 BFCL simple 0.950 0.945 0.945 GSM8K run 1 h 57 min 3 h 26 min 4 h 38 min So, Which One? For one long conversation up to 81,920 tokens, the 12B with its drafter. It gives the same GSM8K and BFCL answers as the 26B and generates 1.35x to 1.64x faster. For a conversation between 81,920 and 131,072 tokens, the 26B with its drafter at 21 expert layers in RAM. It holds the context with the drafter on, where the 12B has to drop its drafter to get there. For the model's full 262,144 tokens, the 26B without the drafter at 22 expert layers in RAM, at 28 tok/s with nothing held. What Comes Next The answer tests here use short questions. The next measurements are the dense 31B on the same card, now running GSM8K, function calling with a long conversation held, and the 26B's 4-bit cache against the 16-bit cache for answers. Summary The goal of this article was to find whether Gemma 4 26B A4B, a model twice the card's size, can serve from an 8 GB RTX 3050, and how it compares with the 12B that fits. The key to the solution was keeping the experts in system RAM with -ncmoe and spending the freed card memory on context. The results were: 🟢 The 14.4 GB 26B serves from an 8 GB card with 21 of its 30 expert layers in system RAM 🟢 It holds 131,072 tokens of context with its drafter, 1.6x the 12B, and the full 262,144 without it 🟢 GSM8K 0.965 and BFCL 0.945, level with the 12B, with or without the drafter 🟢 Without drafters it generates as fast as the 12B up to 32,768 tokens held ⚠️ Its drafter gives 1.24x against the 12B's 2.01x, so with drafters it runs at 0.61x to 0.74x the 12B ⚠️ The CPU is in the serving path: thread count and other load on the host change its speed ❌ A GSM8K run takes 1.76x the 12B's time for the same score Scope: Gemma 4 26B A4B-it QAT only, Google's Q4_0 GGUF unmodified with the exact Q4_0 26B drafter, text only, one RTX 3050 OEM (8 GB) in an i7-5820K desktop, llama.cpp 7182ef71e , 16-bit, 8-bit and 4-bit context caches, 0 to 98,304 tokens of one document held for speed, greedy decoding, thinking off, GSM8K and BFCL simple with short prompts, one request at a time throughout. The strategy for using MCP for local accelerator comparison was validated with an incremental step by step approach. References Part 1, Gemma 4's MTP Drafter, Explained: https://dev.to/gde/gemma-4s-mtp-drafter-explained-speculative-decoding-and-a-4-bit-drafter-at-60-of-the-size-1oc0 Part 2, Do Drafters Work on Small Models?: https://dev.to/gde/do-drafters-work-on-small-models-gemma-4-e2b-and-e4b-on-two-small-gpus-1b4g Part 3, Can a QAT 12B Fit an 8 GB GPU?: https://dev.to/gde/can-a-qat-12b-fit-an-8-gb-gpu-gemma-4-12b-on-an-rtx-3050-1267 Part 4, How Much Context Fits Beside a 12B on an 8 GB GPU?: https://dev.to/gde/how-much-context-fits-beside-a-12b-on-an-8-gb-gpu-gemma-4-12bs-context-cache-on-an-rtx-3050-20im Repository: https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev 26B rig: https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev/tree/main/local-llamacpp-3050oem-26b-q4_0 First light run: https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev/blob/main/local-llamacpp-3050oem-26b-q4_0/benchmarks/runs/2026-10-18-first-light-3050oem/REPORT.md Answers run: https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev/blob/main/local-llamacpp-3050oem-26b-q4_0/benchmarks/runs/2026-10-18-accuracy-26b-3050oem/REPORT.md 12B context cache run: https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev/blob/main/local-llamacpp-3050oem-12b-q4_0/benchmarks/runs/2026-10-17-kvcache-12b-3050oem/REPORT.md 31B first light run: https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev/blob/main/local-llamacpp-3050oem-31b-q4_0/benchmarks/runs/2026-10-18-first-light-3050oem/REPORT.md 26B GGUF: https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-q4_0-gguf 26B drafter: https://huggingface.co/xbill9/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-assistant-q4_0-exact-gguf llama.cpp: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp Top comments (0) Subscribe Personal Trusted User Create template Templates let you quickly answer FAQs or store snippets for re-use. title: Fine-Tuning Qwen3-8B with Tinker: From 50% to 76% Accuracy, and Burning Through My Budget
summary: Daniel Balcarek Posted on Oct 18 Fine-Tuning Qwen3-8B with Tinker: From 50% to 76% Accuracy, and Burning Through My Budget # devchallenge # hf26challenge # ai # machinelearning Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle Submission 💸 This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle Oktoberfest? YES! 🍺 Ah... this one is Hacktoberfest. Okay, still nice! 😁 I couldn't miss Hacktoberfest, and Side Hustle sounds like a pretty good challenge name. And with so many prize categories and promo codes, hmm... let's pick something that could save me some money. Thinking Machines actually sounds interesting (it reminds me of the Mortal Engines movie, which makes it even better). So, let's fine-tune a model. Since this is my introduction to fine-tuning, I wanted to pick something relatively simple, but also useful. Ideally, something that could save me or my fellow developers some money on AI API calls. It should be fast, work with an open-weight model, and actually make sense as a side hustle. And that's how I came up with Complexity Scorer . What I Built So, what exactly is Complexity Scorer? The idea is simple. Imagine you're using an expensive AI model for every request, even trivial ones like extracting a value from JSON or formatting some text. Do you really need an expensive reasoning model for that? Probably not. But your AI application doesn't necessarily know how complex an incoming prompt is, so it might send everything to the same model. That's where Complexity Scorer comes in. Before sending a prompt to an AI model, your application calls Complexity Scorer, a lightweight endpoint backed by a fine-tuned open-weight model. It estimates the prompt's complexity and returns a score between 0.00 and 1.00 . Here are the reference levels: Score Complexity Description 0.00 Trivial Almost no reasoning. Extraction, formatting, or deterministic transformations. 0.25 Easy Limited interpretation or a few straightforward steps. 0.50 Moderate Multiple steps, combining information, some domain knowledge, or several constraints. 0.75 Hard Substantial reasoning, non-obvious tradeoffs, domain expertise, or many interacting constraints. 1.00 Very hard Deep multi-step reasoning, expert-level analysis, significant uncertainty, or interactions between several complex systems. Your application can then use that score to decide which AI model should handle the actual request. Simple prompt? Use a cheaper model. Complex problem? Send it to something more capable. That's it. Of course, it's not limited to API endpoints. You could use it in AI agents, coding tools or any application that needs to choose between different models. And because it's based on an open-weight model, you could even run it locally using something like Ollama, once the fine-tuned model is exported into a compatible format. The potential customers? Developers and teams building AI-powered applications who want to reduce their API costs without blindly routing everything to cheaper models. And how would I actually make money from this? Well, the model itself would remain free for anyone to download and use. I'd charge only for the convenience of using my hosted API, probably with a small free tier and monthly subscriptions that include a certain number of requests. Of course, the pricing would have to be low enough that developers actually save money by using Complexity Scorer. Otherwise, what's the point? Demo Code Gramli / complexity-scorer-api Complexity Scorer API Complexity Scorer estimates how much reasoning a prompt needs. Your application can use that estimate to choose which AI model should answer it, such as a cheaper model for a simple task or a more capable model for a difficult one. Send a prompt to POST /api/complexity and receive a score between 0.00 and 1.00 . This endpoint evaluates the prompt; it does not answer it. Score Level Example of the work involved 0.00 Trivial Extract a value or format text 0.25 Easy Interpret a short request or follow a few simple steps 0.50 Moderate Combine information and follow several constraints 0.75 Hard Analyze tradeoffs or use substantial domain knowledge 1.00 Very hard Perform deep analysis across complex systems Scores between these reference points are allowed. They are estimates, not guarantees that a particular model can solve the task. Before you start You need: The .NET 10 … View on GitHub Gramli / complexity-scorer Complexity Scorer A Python training project that uses Tinker to fine-tune Qwen3-8B to estimate how difficult a user request is for a language model to answer correctly. The experiment compares the original model with a fine-tuned version on the same evaluation dataset. The model reads a prompt and returns only JSON, for example {"complexity": 0.50} . It scores the reasoning and understanding needed, rather than just the prompt's length: Score Meaning 0.00 Trivial: extracting a value or reformatting text 0.25 Easy: a few straightforward steps 0.50 Moderate: combining information or following several constraints 0.75 Hard: substantial reasoning, expertise, or tradeoffs 1.00 Very hard: deep reasoning across complex systems or uncertainty How the experiment works Measure the baseline: ask the original model to score 50 labeled prompts. Prepare training data: validate 2,500 examples (500 per score) and convert them into chat conversations. Duplicate prompts and overlap with evaluation prompts are rejected. … View on GitHub Gramli/complexity-scorer · Hugging Face We’re on a journey to advance and democratize artificial intelligence through open source and open science. huggingface.co How I Built It Okay, let's start with the model training process, because this was probably the most interesting part of the whole project. To use Tinker, I first needed to set up a Python environment. I'm mostly a .NET developer, and I only use Python on rare occasions, so I had to install Python, the Tinker packages, and authenticate with Tinker. Fortunately, with a little help from ChatGPT, it was pretty straightforward. I ran into some trouble with Microsoft C++ Build Tools along the way, but nothing too dramatic. With the environment ready, I moved on to what might be the most important decision of the project: choosing the model to fine-tune. Choosing the model The open-weight model is the core of Complexity Scorer. My first selection criterion was simple: training cost on Tinker . After comparing the available models, I narrowed my options down to two of the cheapest candidates that seemed suitable for this task. Model Context Type Parameters Prefill / 1M Sampling / 1M Training / 1M Qwen3-8B 32K Hybrid 8B $0.195 $0.60 $0.44 GPT-OSS-20B 32K Reasoning 21B / 3.6B active $0.18 $0.45 $0.396 Source: Tinker Models & Pricing GPT-OSS-20B is actually cheaper on paper, but there's a catch: it's a reasoning model that always generates chain-of-thought tokens before answering. That's not ideal for a classifier that's supposed to return a single number as quickly and cheaply as possible. Qwen3-8B , on the other hand, is a Hybrid model. It supports both thinking and non-thinking modes, which means we can disable reasoning for faster classification. So I picked Qwen3-8B for three reasons: Hybrid architecture: We can disable reasoning to reduce unnecessary tokens and latency. No unnecessary vision capabilities: We're classifying text prompts, not images. Task-specific fine-tuning: Tinker specifically recommends starting with Hybrid models for this type of task. And with a 32K context window, it should be more than enough for the prompts I want to classify. Now comes the interesting part: can I actually teach it to estimate prompt complexity? Smoke Tests Okay, I didn't jump straight into fine-tuning. First, I started with a simple Python script ( test_tinker.py ) just to check whether I could actually call Tinker. Once that worked, I prepared a small evaluation dataset with 50 examples ( eval.jsonl ) and a baseline.py script to evaluate the selected model against it. My first evaluation was against the original Qwen3-8B , without any fine-tuning. The result? 50% accuracy . Not bad for a starting point. Next, I prepared 50 training examples (different from the evaluation dataset), saved them in train.jsonl , and ran my train.py script. After fine-tuning finished, I evaluated the model again using the same 50 evaluation examples. And the result? 86% accuracy! That was a little shocking, but also pretty exciting. Just 50 training examples and such a big improvement? Naturally, I thought that more training data would give me even better results. So I prepared another dataset with 500 training examples and trained the model again. Well... I couldn't have been more wrong. 🤣 The accuracy actually dropped to 74% . Hmm... not exactly what I expected. I tried experimenting a little with the hyperparameters, but the accuracy stayed around 74%. And since I'm definitely not an ML engineer, I decided to stop experimenting with smoke tests and move on to the full fine-tuning run. Fine-Tuning At this point, I had everything prepared. The scripts worked, the evaluation dataset was ready, and I knew the model could learn the task. The last thing I needed was more training data. I chose 2,500 training examples as a balance between dataset diversity, generation effort, and training cost. With five complexity levels, that meant 500 examples per class, which sounded like a reasonable starting point. So I prepared a prompt and gave it to GPT-6.1 Sol with high thinking effort. And then it happened... I asked Sol to generate 2,500 training examples for my LLM. It started working, and I left it alone. Previously, generating 500 examples had taken around 30 minutes, so I expected this to take a while. But after approximately 47 minutes, things started looking suspicious. Still, I thought, well, 2,500 examples is a lot of data. Maybe it just needs more time. Meanwhile, I was browsing the web and randomly opened the billing tab on Tinker. $2.47?! WHAT?! I immediately stopped Sol and checked what it was actually doing. Instead of just generating training examples, it had started running model training in the background. There were 18 sessions involving different models, including deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3.1 , moonshotai/Kimi-K2.6 , and Qwen/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B . Oh my... I asked for training data , not for an AI training marathon.. By the time I stopped it, my remaining Tinker balance was down to $2.11 . Well, there's a nice little lesson about giving AI agents access to paid services. Maybe I should write another article about that someday. Anyway, back to the dataset. This time, I decided to be a little more careful. I switched to Luna with medium thinking effort and prepared a prompt to generate just 200 training examples at a time . Then I manually ran it ten times, each time focusing on different types of prompts to improve dataset diversity, and added another 500 examples from my previous Sol generation run. Why manually? Well, after the previous incident, I wasn't exactly eager to let another AI agent run wild with my budget. And thinking about it now, I probably should have used Luna for data generation from the beginning. Sol was a bit overkill for this task. So after that incident, I finally managed to run the fine-tune with all 2,500 training examples successfully. This time, the model achieved 76% accuracy . That's a 26-percentage-point improvement over the original Qwen3-8B, which achieved only 50% accuracy on the same evaluation dataset. What's interesting? More training data didn't meant better results on my evaluation dataset. The model trained on just 50 examples still performed best, with 86% accuracy , beating the 2,500-example model by 10 percentage points. But why? Well, there are a few possible explanations how i explain it (again i am not ML engineer) First, all my training data was AI-generated, and AI doesn't always judge complexity consistently. One example might be labeled 0.50 , while a very similar one might get 0.75 . With more generated examples, there are also more opportunities for inconsistent labels, which can confuse the model during training. And Second, my evaluation dataset contained only 50 examples. That's pretty small, and it's possible the first fine-tuned model simply happened to perform particularly well on those specific examples. A larger and more diverse evaluation dataset might tell a different story. Still, the 2,500-example model learned to recognize all five complexity levels pretty well. The final model's accuracy across the five complexity levels looked like this: Complexity score Level Correct Accuracy 0.00 Trivial 8/10 80% 0.25 Easy 6/10 60% 0.50 Moderate 7/10 70% 0.75 Hard 7/10 70% 1.00 Very hard 10/10 100% Total 38/50 76% All 12 incorrect predictions were off by just one complexity level, so even when the model was wrong, it wasn't completely wrong. And increasing the dataset from 500 to 2,500 examples only improved accuracy from 74% to 76% . That's just one additional correct prediction out of 50, which is too small a difference to draw any meaningful conclusions. So, what did I learn? More training data doesn't automatically mean a better model. The quality of the training data matters, and so does how you evaluate the results. You can see the accuracy results for all four models I tested below: Bringing It to Life So, the model was finally trained. The next step was to publish it somewhere so other developers could download and use it. I was a little worried about this step, but fortunately, Tinker supports pushing fine-tuned model adapters directly to Hugging Face. And it turned out to be surprisingly easy, just one command: tinker checkpoint push-hf "tinker://c2148695-43ab-5758-aaff-bd78ddda980d:train:0/sampler_weights/final" --repo Gramli/complexity-scorer --public Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode And that's it. My fine-tuned adapter was available on Hugging Face . Now, the last thing was to build the API. As a backend developer, this was probably the most boring part of the project. I simply created a .NET Minimal API with the usual API stuff like API key authentication, rate limiting, exception handling, etc. Then I added a service to communicate with Tinker API. Yep, Tinker has its own API endpoint: https://tinker.thinkingmachines.dev/services/tinker-prod/oai/api/v1/ Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode So you can actually call your fine-tuned model without deploying it yourself, which is great for experimenting. Of course, these inference requests still cost money. I also added a simple Svelte playground so developers can enter their own prompts and see the complexity scores directly in the browser. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Well, I could have built Complexity Scorer by simply calling some powerful closed AI model and asking it to classify prompt complexity. That would probably have been much easier. But then every request would depend on that provider's API, availability, and pricing. With an open-weight model like Qwen3-8B, I can actually fine-tune it for my specific task, experiment with different training datasets, and share the result with other developers, potentially at a fraction of the cost (or maybe not if you use Sol like I did 🤣). Sure, it cost me some time, but that's part of open innovation. And here's the biggest advantage: anyone can download my fine-tuned adapter from Hugging Face, combine it with the base model, and run it on their own hardware with a compatible runtime. No need to use my API or pay Tinker for every request. Other developers can also improve the project, train their own versions, or integrate it into their applications. Of course, running a model locally still requires hardware and electricity, but at least you're not tied to a single API provider. And that's what I like about open innovation. I'm not just building an API that other developers can call. I'm sharing what I learned while building it and giving them something they can actually build upon. Prize Categories I'm entering the Best Use of Tinker category because, as a good old backend developer, I got to tinker with the world of ML engineering, learn something new, share my journey, and actually build and deploy something useful. Not bad for my first fine-tuning experiment! 😁 Top comments (22) Subscribe Personal Trusted User Create template Templates let you quickly answer FAQs or store snippets for re-use. title: "Rails Magic" Isn't Magic. How a Request Actually Travels Through Rails.
summary:
S M Tahosin Posted on Oct 19 "Rails Magic" Isn't Magic. How a Request Actually Travels Through Rails. # rails # ruby # webdev # architecture Ask any developer who has worked with modern web frameworks what they think of Ruby on Rails, and you will almost certainly hear the same word within thirty seconds: "Magic." You run a generator, and entire database tables spring to life. You write an empty model class, and it immediately knows every column in your schema without a single property declaration. You define an instance variable inside a controller action, and it appears inside a separate view template as if object boundaries ceased to exist. You reference a class you have never required, and Ruby finds it instantly. To newcomers, it feels like witchcraft. To skeptics, it feels like a dangerous black box that cannot be reasoned about or debugged when things go wrong. Except there is no magic in Rails. Every single convention in Rails is built out of plain Ruby metaprogramming, standard object-oriented design patterns, and an elegant pipeline architecture that has quietly powered some of the largest applications on the web for over twenty years. When you peel back the syntactic sugar, Rails reveals itself not as an inscrutable black box, but as a masterpiece of systems architecture. To truly master Rails and debug it with total confidence, you have to follow an HTTP request from the moment it hits your server socket, through the middleware onion, into the router, through the model reflection engine, and out through the view renderer. Here is what is actually happening behind the curtain. The Request Onion: From Puma to ActionDispatch Before Rails ever touches your code, your request must travel through what software architects call the Request Onion . At the outer edge sits your web server (typically Puma). Puma listens on a raw TCP socket, accepts an incoming HTTP request, parses the raw headers and body, and wraps that data into a plain Ruby hash known as the Rack environment ( env ). Puma then hands this hash to Rails using the universal contract of the Ruby web world: the Rack interface . [HTTP Request] ──> Puma Web Server ──> call(env) ──> [Rack Middleware Stack] ──> [ActionDispatch Router] Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode A Rack application is disarmingly simple: it is any Ruby object that responds to call(env) and returns a three-element array containing: An integer HTTP status code (such as 200 ). A hash of HTTP response headers. An enumerable body stream. When Puma calls Rails.application.call(env) , the request does not jump straight into your controller. Instead, it cascades through a stack of more than twenty built-in Rack Middlewares . Each middleware wraps the next one like layers of an onion: ActionDispatch::HostAuthorization : Guards against DNS rebinding attacks by verifying the Host header against authorized hostnames. ActionDispatch::SSL : Enforces HTTPS redirection and sets Strict-Transport-Security headers. Rack::Sendfile : Offloads static file serving to reverse proxies like Nginx when appropriate. ActionDispatch::Cookies and CookieStore : Decrypts the signed session cookie, verifying its HMAC signature to prevent tampering, and deserializes your session payload into memory. ActionDispatch::ShowExceptions : Catches unhandled errors raised deeper in the application, translating them into friendly HTML error pages or JSON diagnostics. Only after surviving this protective gauntlet does the request arrive at ActionDispatch::Journey , the Rails routing engine. Journey parses your config/routes.rb file on boot and compiles it into a deterministic routing tree. It matches the HTTP verb ( GET ) and path ( /articles/42 ), extracts the parameters ( id: "42" ), determines that ArticlesController#show should handle the request, and dispatches the call. The Mystery of Missing Columns: ActiveRecord Schema Reflection Once inside the controller, you run your database query: class ArticlesController < ApplicationController def show @article = Article . find ( params [ :id ]) end end Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Now consider your model file, app/models/article.rb : class Article < ApplicationRecord end Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Look closely at that class definition: there are no column declarations. There is no attr_accessor :title . There is no property :body, String . There is no schema definition file inside your model directory. Yet you can write article.title , article.body , and article.published? , and Ruby executes them flawlessly. How does a pure Ruby object know the names and types of its attributes when you never declared them? The answer lies in Dynamic Schema Reflection . When your Rails application boots, or the very first time Article is referenced in code, ActiveRecord does something clever: Database Catalog Introspection: ActiveRecord connects to your database adapter and queries the database catalog (in PostgreSQL, it queries information_schema.columns ; in SQLite, it runs PRAGMA table_info(articles) ). Schema Ingestion: It retrieves the exact column names, data types, nullability constraints, and default values directly from the database engine itself. Dynamic Module Generation: Instead of defining methods directly on Article , ActiveRecord creates a hidden internal module called GeneratedAttributeMethods . Metaprogramming the Getters and Setters: For every column returned by the database catalog, ActiveRecord evaluates method definitions into this module: # Conceptual representation of what ActiveRecord generates internally: module GeneratedAttributeMethods def title _read_attribute ( 'title' ) end def title = ( value ) _write_attribute ( 'title' , value ) end def title? _query_attribute ( 'title' ) end end Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Module Inclusion: ActiveRecord includes GeneratedAttributeMethods into Article . Because the methods live inside an included module rather than the Article class itself, you can easily override def title in your own model, call super , and add custom formatting without breaking ActiveRecord's internal storage engine! The database remains the single source of truth for your data model. Rails reflects that truth dynamically into Ruby's method tables, eliminating the need to synchronize manual class declarations with database migrations. Crossing the Object Boundary: How Controller State Reaches Views Next comes one of the most baffling behaviors for programmers arriving from other languages: # app/controllers/articles_controller.rb class ArticlesController < ApplicationController def show @article = Article . find ( params [ :id ]) @comments = @article . comments end end Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode And in your view template:

<%= @article . title %>

<%= @article . body %>

Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode In standard object-oriented programming, instance variables ( @article , @comments ) are strictly private to the specific object instance that created them. An instance of ArticlesController cannot expose its private @variables to an instance of ActionView::Base . Controllers and views are entirely different classes instantiated at different points in time. How does @article cross the boundary between two completely separate objects? The bridge is a method called view_assigns . When your controller action finishes running, Rails initiates the rendering sequence: Extracting Instance State: The controller calls view_assigns . This method inspects all instance variables on the controller object, strips internal Rails variables (like @_response and @_request ), and converts the remaining user variables into a plain Ruby hash: # What view_assigns returns: { "article" => #
, "comments" => [ #, #] } Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Instantiating the View Context: Rails instantiates a fresh ActionView::Base object responsible for rendering the template. Metaprogramming the Handoff: Rails iterates through the assigns hash and injects each key and value directly into the new view instance using Ruby's reflection method: assigns . each do | key , value | view . instance_variable_set ( "@ #{ key } " , value ) end Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Compiling the ERB Template: Rails takes your ERB template, compiles the HTML and embedded Ruby tags into a pure Ruby method, and executes that method in the context of the view instance. Because the view instance now possesses identical @article and @comments instance variables, your template reads them seamlessly. What looked like boundary-defying magic was simply an automated dictionary handoff executed through instance_variable_set . Zeitwerk: Why You Never Write require In standard Ruby, before you can use a class defined in another file, you must explicitly load it: require_relative "../services/payment_processor" Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode In Rails, you simply write PaymentProcessor.charge(user) anywhere in your codebase, and it works. You almost never write require statements. For many years, Rails accomplished this using a custom mechanism hooked into Ruby's const_missing callback. But const_missing suffered from notorious edge cases: circular dependency deadlocks, thread-safety hazards, and confusing load-order bugs. Modern Rails solved this by adopting Zeitwerk , an autoloading engine written specifically for Ruby. Zeitwerk enforces a clean convention: file paths must strictly mirror constant names. Constant User maps to app/models/user.rb . Constant Users::AccountNotifier maps to app/services/users/account_notifier.rb . How does Zeitwerk handle this across different environments? In Development: Instant Reloading Without Restarts In development, booting the server loads virtually zero application files into memory. When your code first encounters an unreferenced constant like User , Zeitwerk intercepts the lookup, inflects the name into app/models/user.rb , and requires the file on demand. More importantly, Zeitwerk integrates with a file-system watcher. When you modify a file in your text editor, Zeitwerk unloads the matching constants from Ruby's memory space. On your next browser reload, Rails re-evaluates the file freshly from disk. You get instant updates without restarting Puma or waiting for a compilation step. In Production: Eager Loading and Copy-on-Write In production, on-demand autoloading is completely disabled. Instead, during application boot, Zeitwerk executes an eager load . It crawls every directory inside app/ and loads every single class, module, and template into Ruby's memory space before Puma spawns its worker processes. This delivers two vital production benefits: Zero Runtime Disk I/O: Incoming user requests never spend CPU cycles looking up or requiring files from disk. Copy-on-Write (CoW) Memory Optimization: Because all classes are allocated in the master process before Puma forks child workers, all worker processes share the exact same physical RAM pages. A Rails application with five worker processes consumes drastically less memory than five separate instances started independently. The Thread Highway: ActiveRecord Connection Pooling When your application receives dozens of concurrent requests, how does Rails ensure that multiple threads do not corrupt your database connections? Puma is a multi-threaded web server. Each Puma worker process runs a thread pool (typically 3 to 5 threads per worker). Each thread handles an independent HTTP request concurrently. If two threads attempted to write raw SQL commands simultaneously across the same TCP connection to PostgreSQL, the protocol stream would interleave and crash the socket. To manage this safely, ActiveRecord uses a Connection Pool . The connection pool acts as a thread-safe leasing office: Connection Checkout: When Thread 1 executes Article.find(42) , it asks the ConnectionPool for a database connection. Thread Affinity: The pool assigns an available connection to Thread 1 and associates that connection with the thread's local storage. Query Execution: Thread 1 executes its SQL statements safely across its dedicated connection. Connection Check-in: When the HTTP request finishes and the Rack response leaves the controller, an outer Rack middleware ( ActiveRecord::Rack::ConnectionManagement or the executor hook) checks the connection back into the pool, making it available for other waiting threads. The Pool Size Equation Understanding the connection pool prevents one of the most common production disasters in Rails: ActiveRecord::ConnectionTimeoutError . Your config/database.yml defines the pool size: production : adapter : postgresql pool : <%= ENV.fetch("RAILS_MAX_THREADS") { 5 } %> Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode If Puma is configured to run 10 threads, but your database pool size is set to 5, the sixth concurrent thread will freeze, waiting up to 5 seconds for an active connection to become free before throwing a fatal timeout error. Keeping your database pool size equal to or slightly greater than Puma's max_threads guarantees that every active worker thread can execute queries without contention. Guarding the Mass Assignment Door: Strong Parameters One of the most consequential security innovations in Rails history is Strong Parameters . In early versions of Rails, developers wrote: # ❌ The old, dangerous way: def create @user = User . create ( params [ :user ]) end Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode This created a critical vulnerability known as a Mass Assignment Attack . A malicious user could send a crafted POST request including unintended attributes: { "user" : { "name" : "Attacker" , "email" : "attacker@evil.com" , "admin" : true } } Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Because ActiveRecord mapped all hash keys directly to database columns, the attacker could elevate themselves to an administrator simply by appending "admin": true to the form payload. Modern Rails prevents this by wrapping all incoming request parameters inside ActionController::Parameters . By default, an ActionController::Parameters instance is marked with an internal flag: permitted: false . If you attempt to pass an unpermitted parameters object directly into an ActiveRecord write method like User.create(params[:user]) , ActiveRecord intercepts the call and immediately raises an ActiveModel::ForbiddenAttributesError . To persist the data, you must explicitly declare an attribute whitelist: private def user_params params . require ( :user ). permit ( :name , :email ) end Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode The pipeline operates in two stages: require(:user) : Verifies that the :user key exists in the payload, raising ActionController::ParameterMissing (which automatically renders a 400 Bad Request) if absent. permit(:name, :email) : Iterates across the keys, strips out unauthorized attributes (such as :admin or :account_balance ), and returns a new Parameters instance marked permitted: true . Only sanitized, explicitly authorized data ever reaches your database layer. The Paradigm Shift: From Magic to Mastery When developers complain about "Rails magic," they are usually reacting to the fact that Rails hides boilerplate code so effectively that the underlying mechanics become invisible. Yet none of these behaviors are mysterious: The Request Onion is a modular chain of Rack middleware wrappers following a universal Ruby interface. ActiveRecord Schema Reflection is dynamic database catalog introspection paired with runtime module inclusion. The View Handoff is automated dictionary assignment via view_assigns . Zeitwerk Autoloading is strict constant-to-path inflection optimized with production eager loading. Connection Pooling is thread-safe connection leasing tailored to Puma's concurrency model. Strong Parameters is strict parameter filtering protecting models from mass assignment exploits. When you understand the machinery powering these conventions, Rails stops feeling like an unpredictable trick. It becomes what it was always designed to be: an exceptionally well-engineered, productive framework that lets you focus on building features without getting bogged down in low-level plumbing. When you first started working with Rails, which of these "magical" behaviors felt the most puzzling? And what under-the-hood discovery made the biggest difference in how you write and debug your code? title: The Scariest Lines of Code I've Ever Written. Boooo!!!
summary: Cesar Aguirre Posted on Oct 19 • Originally published at canro91.github.io The Scariest Lines of Code I've Ever Written. Boooo!!! # discuss # beginners # sql # sqlserver I don't remember if it was rainy or sunny outside. It was more than five years ago. I was still becoming a senior coder. I've written hundreds of thousands of lines of code that I don't remember anymore. But I still remember these ones. As part of my daily tasks, I wrote this query in a stored procedure, SELECT * FROM dbo . HugeTableWithoutIndexes WHERE DATEDIFF ( DAY , ADateColumn , @ InputDate ) = 0 Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode I was working with an email system built with Amazon SES. I needed to show all email activity: delivered, opened, bounced, and so on. I wrapped a column in a function . A deadly sin! The table had millions of records and no indexes. My query forced a full scan of the table. The next thing I knew the server was on fire. Not literally, of course. LOL! Those days I refused to learn SQL, convinced ORMs and NoSQL were enough. I couldn’t have been more wrong. Relational databases and SQL still reign. Eventually I learned about indexing , scans vs seeks, and SQL Server internals. Shout out to Brent Ozar's courses . A painful lesson I will never forget. Take your vitamins, exercise, and use indexes. You can't escape from SQL. That's why I made it one of the lessons in Street-Smart Coding . It's the guide I wish I'd had on my journey to becoming a senior coder.
