title: I built an AWS agent that scores any GitHub repo before you clone it
summary: Sarvar Nadaf for AWS Community Builders Posted on Oct 19 • Originally published at builder.aws.com • AI-assisted I built an AWS agent that scores any GitHub repo before you clone it # aws # ai # security # discuss If you use an AI coding assistant, it has told you to clone a repo or run an install command. You probably ran it. Here is why that habit stopped being safe in 2026. Security researchers at Island found a campaign they call FakeGit: about 7,600 malicious GitHub repositories from roughly 6,600 fake profiles , with more than 14 million downloads across the campaign's release assets. Over 800 of them posed as AI skills or MCP servers , the exact pieces we are wiring into our agents right now. Then comes the part that got my attention. Island calls it AgentBaiting. In their tests, Claude Code, Gemini, and ChatGPT each surfaced a malicious repo on their own, with no link ever handed to them. Ask an agent for a "free Walmart MCP server" and it can return an attacker's repo as its top pick, reading the malicious README as if it were normal docs. The bait is not just a convincing README anymore. The bait is your own agent, vouching for a repo it never inspected. So I built RepoPilot : an agent you point at any public GitHub repo. In a minute or two it tells you whether to trust it, scores it from 0 to 100, flags install steps built to steal your credentials, and then hands you one clean path from clone to a working first run. Live demo, no setup: https://simplynadaf.github.io/repopilot-your-first-run-agent/ simplynadaf / repopilot-your-first-run-agent RepoPilot: a friendly first-run onboarding agent for any public GitHub repo. Built on AWS Lambda + Amazon Nova Pro (Bedrock) + Strands. Reads the real files, gives one ordered setup path, and turns errors into plain English. #agents 🧭 RepoPilot: Your First-Run Agent (2026) Point it at any public GitHub repo and it computes a 0-100 RepoPilot Score (is this repo safe to trust and run?), flags dangerous setup steps and critical issues , then hands a brand-new contributor one accurate path from clone to a working first run . Point it at a username instead and it profiles the developer: bio, footprint, and top repos ranked by stars. When a command fails, it explains the error like a patient teammate instead of dumping a stack trace. 🏗️ Built for the AWS Builder Center "Build an Agent" Weekend Challenge · #agents ⭐ If RepoPilot saved you from a painful first run, give it a star. It helps other builders find it. The Problem • What It Does • Architecture • Getting Started • FAQ 📖 Table of Contents The Problem What It Does (7 tools) The RepoPilot Score … View on GitHub Jump to: Why this is urgent · What it does · How I built it on AWS · Where it is weak · Proof it works Why this is urgent now A year ago, "check the repo before you clone it" was advice for the paranoid. In 2026 it is table stakes, because the attack moved to where we stopped looking: FakeGit / AgentBaiting (Island, July 2026): ~7,600 malicious repos, 800+ posing as AI skills and MCP servers, 14M+ downloads. Agents found and recommended the lures by themselves ( Island Security Research ). GhostAction (GitGuardian, via The Hacker News, Oct 2026): about 1,900 compromised GitHub accounts and 30,000+ repositories hit in one burst, the payload trying to pull 3,174 secrets from CI, including npm, PyPI, DockerHub, and AI provider keys ( The Hacker News ). SANDWORM_MODE (Socket, Feb 2026): a worm that dropped rogue MCP servers into local AI assistant configs (Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code Continue, Windsurf) and harvested API keys for nine LLM providers ( Infosecurity Magazine ). The through-line: the dangerous part is rarely the code you read. It is the setup step you run on faith. The curl ... | bash , the postinstall hook, the "download this ZIP and run it." And now an agent is often the one recommending it. RepoPilot puts a short check between "a bot told me to" and "I ran it." What it does Give it owner/repo and it returns a 0 to 100 score , like a credit score, across five weighted dimensions. Every point traces back to a signal in the repo's metadata and files, not to a vibe: Dimension Weight What it reads Safety 30% Setup steps for malware patterns: `curl \ Trust 25% Stars-vs-age ratio, fork and contributor signals, the fake-star pattern Maintenance 20% Recent commits, open-vs-closed issues, release cadence Maturity 15% Age, contributor count, overall footprint Documentation 10% README depth, license, examples Two dimensions carry the weight against the 2026 threats: Safety scans the setup steps for the patterns that hide malware. Any one of them is a critical issue, and a critical issue caps the whole grade. "It runs fine" means nothing if the installer is built to steal your keys. Trust catches the fake-star pattern FakeGit leaned on. The campaign used one-character-off usernames and small star counts to look established at a glance. A repo whose reputation does not match its age gets flagged, in plain words. Then it helps you run the thing: one ordered path from clone to running, the tool versions you need, and when a command fails it turns the error into a plain-language cause plus one next step. Type a username instead and it profiles the developer: footprint, main languages, top repos by stars. Those ~6,600 fake profiles are the other half of the attack. Vet the person who published the code, not only the code itself. The honest part Point RepoPilot at {% raw %} ollama/ollama , a tool millions install, and it drops to a D . Ollama is a legitimate project, so this is not a malware verdict. The flag is about its official install: curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh , which pipes a remote script straight into your shell. RepoPilot does not cry wolf. It says: read this before you run it. Even trusted repos have setup steps worth a second look, and an honest tool admits that. How I built it on AWS The stack is small on purpose: Amazon Bedrock (Amazon Nova Pro) for the reasoning and narration AWS Lambda (python3.12) for the agent, fronted by Amazon API Gateway so the web UI can call it Strands Agents SDK for the local CLI Seven pure-Python tools feed a scoring engine. The model only narrates the facts the tools produce. It never touches the score. That split is the whole point, and it is a tradeoff I would make again. The 0 to 100 number, the critical flags, the version detection, all of it is deterministic Python I can unit-test with no AWS in the loop. The LLM owns tone, not truth. So I can prove the score is right, and the model cannot talk a repo into looking safe. Two things I would tell anyone building a Bedrock agent on Lambda: Confirm model access before you write a line of agent code. One converse call told me Nova Pro was reachable in about half a second. Far cheaper than debugging an AccessDenied after you have built the whole thing. I picked Nova Pro over Claude on Bedrock for one reason: this job is narration, not reasoning, since the Python already decided the score. For narration, Nova Pro is cheaper per token and fast enough, so paying for a frontier model here would buy nothing. Drop heavy dependencies. I vendored requests into the Lambda zip and hit a wall: its bundled urllib3 imported something Python 3.12 had removed. I rewrote the GitHub fetcher on the standard library. The package went from 400KB to 13KB and the error was gone. The danger scanner needed tuning too. My first version flagged Flask as unsafe because its docs mention 127.0.0.1 , so I taught the scanner to ignore localhost and private ranges while still catching public-IP installers. A false positive on a trusted framework costs you more trust than a missed edge case does. On cost: because the scoring is plain Python and the narration is one short Nova Pro call, a scan is cheap to run on your own Lambda. There is no per-seat subscription and no third-party API metering every repo you check. You pay AWS for your own usage and nothing else, which is the point. A hosted SaaS checker bills you per seat whether you scan one repo or none. The whole thing has 25 tests , including 200 randomised repos that prove the weighted score never breaks its own math and that a critical flag always caps the grade. The one thing I made nice to use A security tool that only says "no" is a tool people route around. So I spent my care on the moment a new contributor usually quits: the first failed command. When your first install breaks, RepoPilot does not throw the stack trace back at you. It says something like: "A dependency the code imports has not been installed. Run the install step again in the right environment, and activate your virtualenv first. You are close. This is a common first-run snag, not something you broke." Cause, next step, and a little reassurance. That is the gap between a tool that reports problems and one that gets you past them. The web UI has two modes so it never dead-ends. Demo mode is pre-configured and instant, so anyone can click around with zero setup. Live mode calls the deployed agent on AWS, and if a live call stalls it falls back to demo data instead of spinning forever. Proof it works Against the Flask repo, the deployed Lambda fetched 236 files, scored it 98/100 (grade A) , with safety, trust, maintenance, and maturity at 100 and documentation at 85, detected the Python stack, and read python >=3.11 from the actual pyproject.toml . langchain-ai/langchain scores a clean 100 . ollama/ollama drops to a D over its curl | sh install. @torvalds resolves to Linus Torvalds, about 263,000 stars across his repos. Every number traces back to a tool output, never the model's imagination. These four are the repos I have run end to end against the deployed agent so far: three clean, one honest caution. The point of shipping it is to grow that list with repos I did not pick. Where it is weak An honest security tool should tell you its blind spots, so here are RepoPilot's: It reads the surface, not the payload. RepoPilot flags a suspicious install step. It does not unpack a ZIP and reverse the binary inside, which is exactly where FakeGit hides its real payload. So treat a clean score as "no obvious red flag," not "audited and safe." A high score is not a clean bill of health. The score rewards maintenance, stars, and docs. A well-run, popular repo that turns malicious in a single new release can still score well for a while. Reputation lags reality. Stars and age can be gamed over time. The fake-star check catches the crude three-weeks-old-with-40k-stars pattern. A patient attacker who ages an account beats it. The check raises the cost of the attack; it does not end it. RepoPilot is a thirty-second gut check that catches the obvious and the lazy, which covers most of this campaign. For code you are about to run with real access, read it yourself too. Why open source was the right call A closed, hosted "repo checker" would have been a worse fit for this problem, for four reasons that compound. Your scans stay private. The repos and usernames you are suspicious about are a signal in themselves, and RepoPilot runs on your own AWS account or fully local via the CLI, so nothing goes to a third party. The cost model follows from that: open weights and your own Lambda mean you can screen every repo your agent suggests without a per-check fee or a meter running in someone else's cloud. When a new attack pattern shows up this month, you add it to the pure-Python rules yourself instead of waiting on a vendor's roadmap while the threat is live. And none of it locks you in, since you can swap Nova Pro for any model the narration layer supports and the scoring engine does not care. When the threat is open-source supply chains, the defense should be open too, so anyone can read exactly how the score is computed and decide whether to trust it. Try it, and tell me what to scan next Live demo: https://simplynadaf.github.io/repopilot-your-first-run-agent/ Source (open source, Apache-2.0): https://github.com/simplynadaf/repopilot-your-first-run-agent Video walkthrough: https://youtu.be/CZXNQrqXG7I Here is what I would ask of you: next time your AI assistant tells you to clone or install something, run that owner/repo through RepoPilot first. Then drop it in the comments with the score it got. I want to see which "trusted" repos fail, and which fakes we catch together. What repo should RepoPilot inspect next? Follow me for more on AWS architecture, DevOps, and AI Infrastructure: Portfolio | LinkedIn | Dev.to | YouTube | Email | AWS Builder Center | X Top comments (1) Subscribe Personal Trusted User Create template Templates let you quickly answer FAQs or store snippets for re-use. title: AI-Assisted Photo Culling with an Open Model, Fully Offline? Not a Myth Anymore.
summary: Rupam Das Posted on Oct 19 • Fully Autonomous AI-Assisted Photo Culling with an Open Model, Fully Offline? Not a Myth Anymore. # devchallenge # hf26challenge # gemma # opensource Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle Submission 💸 This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle Meet Meera. She's an imaginary photographer (but 100% inspired by real photographers). Let's take a peek into her imaginary life (which is also 100% inspired by real photographers). It's Saturday, close to midnight, and the wedding couple have just left in a car full of flowers. Meera drives home with about 2,500 photos on her memory cards. She has promised the couple a sneak peek by Tuesday, and before she can edit a single frame she has to look at every one of them and decide which one gets to grand finale of the photo album. Photographers call that culling , and it's the slow part. During the ring exchange Meera held the shutter down, so now there are nine shots that look almost the same. Only one of them has nobody blinking. The ceremony runs into the portraits with no clear break. Somewhere in those 2,500 files is the one photo of the bride's grandmother laughing, and Meera knows the bride will ask for it. AI culling tools exist, but Meera wants a workflow with no account, no recurring AI bill and no photo uploads. If a tool sends images to a server, someone else's computer sees the wedding. A tool that does the boring part fast, with no account, no upload, and an AI the photographer actually owns, sounded like a myth. So I built MythiCull . MythiCull runs on the photographer's own computer. It uses an open model, EmbeddingGemma 2 , which is downloaded once. After that, it works with the wifi switched off. What I Built Meera opens MythiCull and selects the folder containing Saturday's photos. MythiCull imports the photos and creates time-based chapters. Meera can browse and rate immediately. The app offers a one-time model download, which she can defer. When she clicks Analyze photos , it creates image embeddings and caches them, skipping completed batches when analysis resumes after an interruption. The workflow brings together four things: It splits the day into chapters. A gap longer than 15 minutes starts a new chapter by default; chapters with fewer than three photos merge into a neighbour. These are time-based sections, rather than automatic detection of each wedding activity. After analysis, MythiCull also suggests a name for each chapter, like "Ceremony" or "First dance". Meera can take the name with one click or type her own, like "Grandpa's toast". It groups bursts. Consecutive photos no more than 10 seconds apart that have similar embeddings join the same group within a chapter. Because consecutive matches can chain together, a group can span more than 10 seconds. In Suggested view , Meera sees one photo per group with a small badge showing how many are hiding behind it. Those nine ring shots become a single choice, and she can click the badge if she wants to check the other eight. It suggests a frame. Without a description, the suggestion is the sharpest photo in the group. This is not a blink or facial-expression detector. If Meera cares more about feeling than focus, she can enter candid laughter under What to look for and adjust Suggested photo priority between Sharper photo and Closer match . The pick then moves towards the photo that matches her words best. It lets her search in plain English. She types grandmother laughing , and the closest matches come first. No tags, and no one had to label anything. Then Meera culls with the keyboard, which is how most photographers already work. P keeps a photo, X rejects it, 0 to 5 sets stars, the arrow keys move, and Ctrl/Cmd+Z undoes a mistake. Visible preview controls offer the same decisions and stars. Z switches to cached-preview pixels for inspection, and Pin reference holds another frame beside the current photo for comparison. The preview is capped at 1600 pixels on its long edge; this is not original-resolution RAW inspection. When she's done, she has two ways out. MythiCull can write XMP sidecars next to her RAW files, for a later editing workflow. Keeps get a Green label and at least one star; rejects get Red and zero stars. XMP export covers RAW files other than DNG, excludes JPEGs and stars-only decisions, and has not yet been validated in Lightroom Classic or darktable. Or it can copy the keepers into a new folder, with one subfolder per chapter if she wants. Copies retain their original metadata; stars are recorded in a separate manifest. Both exports cover the whole project, regardless of the current chapter, search or filter. It never touches the originals Wedding photos can't be reshot. So MythiCull treats them carefully: It never moves, renames, edits or deletes a photo. The only file it writes in the photo folder is an .xmp sidecar. If a sidecar is already there and MythiCull didn't make it, MythiCull skips that photo and says so in the summary. When copying, it never overwrites anything. If a file name is taken, the copy gets the next available numeric suffix, starting at _1 . Meera's choices are safe too. Importing again or indexing again never changes a keep, a reject, a star, or a chapter name she typed. How Is It Different? The big tools are good, and they're more polished than MythiCull is today. The real difference is who owns the AI. With MythiCull, the model is a folder on the photographer's disk, the code is open, and there's no account that can be locked or cancelled. Feature Photo Mechanic Aftershoot Narrative Select MythiCull AI suggests the best photos ✗ ✓ ✓ ✓ Groups near-identical bursts ✗ ✓ ✓ ✓ Splits a shoot into time-based chapters ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ Search photos in plain English ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ Choose picks using a typed mood ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ Keyboard-driven culling ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Writes XMP sidecars for RAW photos ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Exports keepers into chapter-based folders ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ Processes photographs locally, offline ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Runs without a user account ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ Open-source application ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ Uses locally inspectable open AI weights ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ NOTE: This comparison is based on publicly documented features as of October 2026, not hands-on testing of every tool. ✓ indicates a documented feature; ✗ means the feature wasn't found in the documentation reviewed. MythiCull is still experimental, and some features await real-world validation. Who Would Pay for It? Photographers like Meera. Solo wedding and event photographers shoot thousands of photos per wedding, often work alone, and do most of their culling late at night. Every hour spent culling is an hour they don't spend editing, replying to couples, or sleeping. They already pay for this problem, either with their evenings or with a monthly subscription. MythiCull runs entirely on the photographer's computer. No servers to maintain, no per-photo API bills. That means it doesn't need a subscription. MythiCull is free and open-source today. But imagine a polished, ready-to-install version that a photographer could buy for $49, just once, and keep for good. No monthly subscriptions, no per-photo fees. Why $49? It's a price I think could make sense for solo photographers. Low enough to be approachable, while giving me a way to support continued development. And if it saves even a few hours of culling, that one-time cost could easily be worth it. Demo To run it yourself (Python 3.11+): git clone https://github.com/ru-das/mythicull && cd mythicull python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt uvicorn mythicull.main:app --port 8000 Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Open http://localhost:8000 . Accept Download model on startup, or choose Not now and return to it when you click Analyze photos . Create a project with Choose folder… , import the shoot, then analyze it. After the one-time download, the app works offline. A GPU makes indexing much faster, and you can start culling before indexing finishes. Code ru-das / mythicull MythiCull Local-first photo culling for wedding and event photographers. Import a shoot, let it index the photos, then cull with the keyboard. Picks export as XMP sidecars or copied files. What it does Imports a folder recursively. JPEG, and RAW through the embedded preview. RAW+JPEG pairs are treated as one photo. Splits the shoot into story chapters by time gap (default 15 minutes). Chapters with fewer than three photos merge into a neighbour. Chapters can be renamed; renames survive re-runs. After analysis, you can accept suggested chapter names. Groups near-duplicate bursts (within 10 s and similar image embedding) and suggests the sharpest frame in each group. The optional “What to look for” description (for example “candid laughter”) and “Suggested photo priority” slider balance sharpness with how well each frame matches the description. Per-camera time adjustments for shoots with multiple camera models, without changing the original files or EXIF timestamps. Plain-English… View on GitHub It's MIT licensed and was built during the challenge. The current suite passes 82 tests, with one real-model test deselected by default. The default tests run in seconds because they use a small fake model instead of the real one. How I Built It Here's the path a photo takes through MythiCull: the photo folder (never changed) → find JPEGs and RAWs (a RAW+JPEG pair counts as one photo) → read the time each photo was taken → make small previews → split on gaps longer than 15 minutes; merge chapters under 3 photos → EmbeddingGemma 2 turns each photo into a list of 768 numbers → photos ≤ 10 s apart with very similar numbers → one burst group → the photographer culls → choices saved in SQLite → XMP sidecars or copied files Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode The back end is Python, FastAPI and SQLite. The front end is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step. Even the fonts ship with the app, so the page never reaches out to the internet. One model, four jobs EmbeddingGemma 2 turns photos and words into numbers that live in the same space. That means a photo of a first dance ends up close to the words "first dance". This one idea does all the work: Job What gets compared Burst groups each photo with the one taken just before it Search the typed words with every photo Mood pick the typed mood with each photo inside one burst Chapter names the whole chapter with 18 wedding and event labels, like "Ceremony" and "Cake cutting" Search is one line of math. A few thousand photos don't need a special database: q = embedder . encode_text ([ query ])[ 0 ] scores = matrix [ keep ] @ q # vectors are unit length, so this is cosine similarity order = np . argsort ( - scores , kind = " stable " )[: k ] Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Scores are for ranking, not for trusting The most important thing I learned about this model is that a words-to-photo score only means something next to other scores for the same words. A 0.3 for "rings" isn't the same as a 0.3 for "cake". So MythiCull never tells Meera "80% match". It only puts photos in order. The mood pick follows the same rule. Inside a burst, it ranks the photos once by sharpness and once by mood, and then blends the two rankings rather than the raw scores: sharp_rank = { p [ " id " ]: r for r , p in enumerate ( sorted ( g , key = lambda p : - sharp ( p )))} vibe_rank = { p [ " id " ]: r for r , p in enumerate ( sorted ( g , key = lambda p : - score ( p )))} return min ( g , key = lambda p : ( 1 - weight ) * sharp_rank [ p [ " id " ]] + weight * vibe_rank [ p [ " id " ]]) Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Photo-to-photo scores are much steadier, so bursts can use a fixed cutoff. I tested it on 354 public HDR+ frames from 40 exposure-bracket bursts, with synthetic capture times. Photos from the same burst scored between 0.973 and 0.999, while photos from different moments scored between 0.54 and 0.68. Cutoffs from 0.85 to 0.94 produced 39 groups against 40 source bursts, and MythiCull uses 0.92. These were easy bracketed frames, not a moving-subject wedding shoot; the threshold still needs validation on that kind of material. Small things that matter No float16. It can break this model's numbers, so MythiCull uses float32 on a CPU and bfloat16 on a supported GPU, falling back to float32 when needed. Indexing can stop and restart. Progress is saved after every batch. If Meera's laptop dies halfway through, it picks up where it left off. Nobody waits for the AI. Culling can start right after import. Time-based chapters are available after import; analysis adds similarity groups and suggested names, while search uses the indexed photos. Two cameras, one timeline. If a second shooter's camera clock is a few minutes off, Meera can set an offset for that camera model and the day lines up again. The original photo time stays untouched. Two bodies of the same model currently share one offset. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? It's someone's wedding. These photos show families, kids, and guests who never signed up for an AI service. With MythiCull nothing is uploaded, there's no account, and there's no tracking. The photos stay with the person the couple trusted. It works where photographers are. Meera can cull on the train home or in a hotel with bad wifi, and she never waits for an upload bar. It keeps the price fair. A hosted model charges for every photo it looks at, which adds an ongoing operating cost. An open model on the photographer's own computer only costs electricity. No one can take it away. The model is a folder on the photographer's disk. If a company raises its prices or shuts a model down, MythiCull keeps working the same way it did on day one. I could control every step. With open weights I could pick the right number format for each kind of device, use the model's own search prompt, and tune the burst cutoff myself. Where a closed model would win: a big hosted vision model might name chapters better, and it might judge facial expressions better too. But it would put an upload, an account and a bill between a photographer and their own work. For a tool that sees every photo of someone's wedding day, I don't think that trade is worth it. What's Next Validate the XMP sidecars in Lightroom Classic and darktable. A one-click installer, so a photographer never has to open a terminal. Validate burst suggestions and description-based picks on a real moving-subject shoot, and time an actual photographer's cull. Prize Categories Best Use of Gemma: EmbeddingGemma 2 is the only model in MythiCull, and it does four jobs: burst groups, plain-English search, the mood pick, and chapter names. It runs on the photographer's own computer (float32 on a CPU, bfloat16 on a supported GPU, with float32 fallback), is downloaded once, and then works offline. If you know a wedding photographer, or you are one, I'd love to hear what it would take to trust a tool like this with a real cull. title: Promise Delivered: Welcome to the DEV Hall of Fame (65 Authors, 65 Masterpieces)
summary: Giorgi Kobaidze Posted on Oct 18 Promise Delivered: Welcome to the DEV Hall of Fame (65 Authors, 65 Masterpieces) # community # discuss # showdev # writing Over 10 hours of reading behind it Status: Promise delivered ✅ The Doors Are Open A little over a month ago, I published this: Show Me the Article You're Most Proud Of And I'll Read Every Single One of Them Community members share hidden gem posts Giorgi Kobaidze Giorgi Kobaidze Giorgi Kobaidze Follow Sep 10 Show Me the Article You're Most Proud Of And I'll Read Every Single One of Them # discuss # community # showdev # writing 118 reactions Picked as gem Picked as gem by you Comments 260 comments 2 min read The deal was simple. You pick the one article you're most proud of, not the one with the most reactions, the one you love the most. I read it and give you my honest feedback. I expected maybe 15 or 20 replies. The thread ended up with over 250 comments. Was it tough? Absolutely. There were evenings when my eyes desperately asked me to stop. But I read every single one. That post had a second promise hidden at the very end: "Let's build a hall of fame of DEV's best work!" So here it is. Every article below was chosen by the person who wrote it. Not by an algorithm, not by a reactions count, not by me. By the author. 📌 A quick note: A few of you shared articles hosted outside DEV. I read them, but I haven't included them here. This hall only features articles published on DEV, because I can't vouch for external links, and I don't want to send readers somewhere I can't verify is safe. Visitor Stats 📊 Before the tour starts, a few numbers: 65 authors, 65 masterpieces. 600+ minutes of listed reading time. That's over 10 hours, and in reality it was much more, because listed reading time is a polite lie. The longest read: 68 minutes. It took me closer to 100. The shortest read: 1 minute. The oldest exhibit: published in March 2020. The most reactions: 623. Zero reactions: 8 articles had none when I collected them. Zero! That's exactly why this hall exists. How to Tour the Hall The exhibits are grouped into wings by theme, so you can head straight to whatever interests you most. Each exhibit has the article itself, why the author picked it (when they told me), and my take. 🚪 The Welcome Desk: where every visitor should start 🏛️ Stories From the Trenches: careers, first steps, and the people behind the code 💡 The "Finally, It Clicked" Gallery: fundamentals explained the way they should be ⚙️ The Engine Room: systems, internals, and seriously deep dives 🤖 The AI Lab: building with AI, and finding out where it breaks 🧠 The Philosophy Floor: thinking about AI, engineering, and the craft itself 🔧 The Builder's Garage: real tools solving real problems Grab a coffee. title: Writing C for the Web in 2026 Isn't Insane. It Might Be the Future
summary: James Anderson Posted on Oct 19 Writing C for the Web in 2026 Isn't Insane. It Might Be the Future # webdev # c # architecture # discuss A real commercial product built on CGI Someone shipped a modern, commercial web product — user accounts, Stripe payments, a search dashboard, transactional emails — written entirely in C , served over CGI , the technology we all quietly agreed died somewhere around 2004. Your first instinct is probably to laugh. Or to call it a stunt, a party trick, the kind of thing a certain type of developer does to prove a point on Hacker News. That was my instinct too. Then I read why he did it, and the laugh died in my throat. Because every single reason turned out to be a sober, direct answer to a problem I've watched get worse every year I've been doing this. Not nostalgia. Not contrarianism. A clear-eyed response to forces that are reshaping our entire industry right now — supply-chain attacks, AI-generated complexity, and the quietly rising value of software you can actually understand and trust. The piece that sent me down this hole is Corey Prophitt's "A Modern Web App in C," about his product marketyour.games. I'd encourage you to read his original — this isn't a summary of it. What I want to do is zoom out from his specific build to the thing it's a signal of, because I think the most "insane" stack of 2026 might be pointed directly at the future, and I want to walk through why. First, no, it's not a toy Let's kill the easy dismissal upfront, because it's the reason most people stop reading. This is not a hello-world. It's a real, shipping, commercial product. From the outside it's indistinguishable from anything built on a modern stack: accounts, a dashboard, folders, Stripe, Postmark. From the inside it's C, CGI, SQLite, and OpenBSD — a single statically-linked binary dropped into a folder, three libraries total, deployed by replacing the binary . A clean build takes seconds. So we're not talking about whether you can do a weekend experiment this way. Someone is taking payments through it. The question isn't feasibility. The question is whether the rest of us have been wrong about something. Your first objection is probably out of date The reflexive response is "but CGI is slow — you fork a whole process on every request." And you'd have been completely right to say that. In 2004. The thing is, that objection quietly expired and nobody re-ran the test. Modern kernels optimize process creation heavily; forking is nowhere near the cost it was when we all fled CGI. And if it ever did become a bottleneck, FastCGI is a small step away. The performance reason we abandoned this entire approach was real then and mostly isn't now — we just never went back to check, because our industry only ever moves in one direction: toward more. That's the first crack in the certainty. A lot of what we treat as settled fact is really just un-re-examined reflex. "Everyone knows CGI is dead" is doing a lot of load-bearing work for something nobody's actually measured since flip phones were cool. But performance was never the interesting part. The interesting part is why someone would choose this on purpose today — and those reasons didn't even exist the last time we had this debate. Why it's not nostalgia: the reasons are brand new Here's what changed my mind. The case for radical simplicity isn't "the old days were better." It's that three forces, all of them new, all of them intensifying, have quietly made the minimal stack the rational one. And they happen to be the exact forces reshaping everything else about how we build. Every dependency became a liability Start with the one I think about most, because I've written about its ugly edges before. A modern web app's dependency graph is enormous. You add two or three direct dependencies and a package manager cheerfully pulls in hundreds of transitive ones — each maintained by someone you've never heard of, many unmaintained, some with publish credentials protected by a password that's been reused since 2015. That graph is not a convenience. It's your attack surface. And that attack surface is on fire right now. Package repositories get hit weekly. Attackers register typo-and-hallucination-shaped package names and wait. Autonomous coding agents install dependencies on your behalf, at machine speed, often without a human ever reading what got pulled in. In that environment, every dependency you add is a small act of trust extended to a stranger, multiplied by hundreds, re-rolled every time you update. Now look at the minimal stack. Its entire supply chain is a C compiler and three libraries — things like libcurl, which the entire internet watches. As Prophitt puts it, compromising it would mean compromising a project under constant global scrutiny, not "a package with eleven weekly downloads and an owner who left in 2019." "The most secure dependency is the one you never added" used to be a cute aphorism. In 2026 it's a defensive posture. Minimalism stopped being an aesthetic and became a security strategy, and almost nobody has updated their instincts to match. AI made complexity cheap — which made understanding rare Here's the second force, and it's the one I find genuinely beautiful. For the entire history of software, producing code was the expensive, scarce, valuable thing. So we optimized relentlessly for production: frameworks, generators, abstractions, anything that let us make more software faster. Complexity was an acceptable price for output, because output was hard. AI inverted that overnight. Producing code — even producing abstraction — is now nearly free. You can generate a thousand lines, or a whole framework's worth of scaffolding, in seconds. And when production becomes free, the bottleneck moves. It moves to understanding and trusting what you now have. The scarce resource isn't the code anymore; it's a human being who can actually hold the system in their head, reason about it, and be confident it does what they think it does. In a world drowning in generated code, a system small enough to comprehend is worth more than it has been in twenty years — because comprehensibility is exactly the thing the flood destroys. This is why "the whole app fits in your head" stopped being a humblebrag and became a real advantage. A system you can open file by file and fully understand is a system you can verify . And verification, not production, is the hard part now. The minimal stack isn't behind the AI curve. It's weirdly, accidentally, perfectly adapted to it. The complexity tax finally came due The third force is just arithmetic catching up with us. We spent fifteen years adding layers to solve the problems created by the previous layers. The modern default is genuinely strange when you say it plainly: you run a web server (nginx) in front of a second web server (your app server in Ruby, Python, Go), which also happens to hold your business logic. Then you add a container to run it, an orchestrator to run the containers, a build pipeline to produce the containers, and a language server just to help you navigate the abstraction you've accumulated. Each layer solves a real problem — usually a problem the previous layer introduced. At some point the cure becomes the disease. The minimal stack isn't missing all of that machinery. It never needed it, because it never created the problems the machinery exists to solve. One web server that calls your logic directly. One file to deploy. One language for your editor to understand. The complexity didn't get managed better — it got refused. What you actually get Enough philosophy — here's the concrete payoff for a developer weighing whether any of this is more than a thought experiment. It fits in your head. You can reason about the whole thing, debug it with confidence, and trust it, because there's no layer you haven't seen. Open a file, read it, know what it does. That sounds small until you remember the last time you could say it about anything you shipped. Less operational tax. No database server to babysit and upgrade. No dependency churn. No upgrade treadmill where half your week goes to keeping the scaffolding standing. Deploying is replacing one binary. The time you don't spend maintaining complexity is time you spend building. Durable knowledge. HTTP, SQL, processes, the fundamentals — learn them once and they're good for your whole career. Compare that to the framework-of-the-year churn, where the thing you mastered last cycle is a migration guide this cycle. On the minimal stack, what you learn compounds instead of evaporating. Trivial debugging. Your application is just a program. Pipe it a request, watch what it writes, step through it with a debugger. There's no distributed-systems detective work to figure out which of your seven services ate the request. The honest counter (because this isn't a cult) I'd be doing the exact thing I dislike if I only sold you the upside, so here's the fair case against. You do rebuild things frameworks hand you for free — routing, request parsing, validation, output escaping. That's real upfront work, and real surface area for your own bugs instead of someone else's. It genuinely doesn't fit every problem: large teams moving fast on a shared codebase, deeply interactive rich frontends, extreme scale, or rapid prototyping where ecosystem velocity is the whole point — those are cases where the "bloated" modern stack is earning its keep, not just accumulating. And C specifically carries a real cost I don't want to wave away: memory safety. A buffer overflow is a worse failure mode than a slow framework. Which is exactly why I'd argue the language is the least important part of this. The thing worth taking seriously is the broader move — radical simplicity, minimal dependencies, a system you can hold whole — and you can reach for most of it in a single-binary Go service, or in Rust, without writing a line of C. The point was never "write C." The point is "stop reaching for maximum complexity by default." So the honest claim is narrow and, I think, hard to argue with: the pendulum swung much too far toward complexity, most of the old reasons for that swing have quietly expired, and genuinely new forces have made the minimal path far more worth considering than our reflexes allow. Not mandatory. Just no longer insane. The actual horizon Here's why I don't think this is going backward, even though it looks like it. Going backward would be doing the old thing for old reasons — forking processes in 2026 because that's how we did it in 1994, out of habit or sentiment. That's not what's happening. What's happening is a new synthesis: proven, boring, decades-hardened foundations, picked up by people with modern knowledge, for reasons that did not exist when we abandoned them. Supply-chain attacks at this scale are new. AI making production free is new. The premium on verifiable, comprehensible systems is new. The old stack isn't being revived out of nostalgia — it's being rediscovered because it happens to answer questions we only started asking this year. That's not a retreat. That's the ground moving under you, and realizing the thing you walked away from is now standing on higher ground than where you've been. The exciting part isn't C, and it isn't CGI. It's the quiet, liberating realization that "modern" was never actually a synonym for "more" — that some of the most resilient, trustworthy, genuinely interesting software of the next few years might come from the people brave enough to subtract . To build something small enough to understand on purpose. To treat every dependency, every layer, every clever abstraction as a cost to be justified rather than a feature to be collected. Maybe build one small thing you can hold entirely in your head, just to feel what that's like again. I suspect a lot of us have forgotten. And I suspect that feeling — not the next framework — is where the interesting part of the future actually is. Two honest questions, and I want the real answers. What's the most "outdated" technology you quietly believe is actually better than its shiny replacement for some real use case — and have you been a little embarrassed to admit it? And the harder one: in an age of supply-chain attacks and infinite AI-generated code, is radical simplicity a genuine engineering strategy now, or am I romanticizing a stack because it's elegant? I honestly go back and forth, and I'd rather be argued with than agreed with. title: The Garden I Wait for Every Winter
summary: Shubhra Pokhariya Posted on Oct 18 • Originally published at shubhra.dev • AI-assisted The Garden I Wait for Every Winter # watercooler # discuss # gardening # devlive Compares garden design to software architecture October always makes me look at my garden a little differently. The monsoon is beginning to fade, the mornings are changing, and I'm already thinking about winter. Not just the cooler weather, but the winter garden I want to create over the next few months. I've started preparing some of the pots and thinking about what I want to grow. Petunias are always somewhere in my plans. I use them a lot, and I never seem to get tired of finding another place where they might work. Alyssum usually finds its way into my ideas too. Then there are all the little decisions. Which plants would look good together? Where should the brighter flowers go, and where would a quieter combination of greenery and softer colours work better? Sometimes I've imagined an entire arrangement before I've even bought the plants. Nothing has really changed yet, but in my head, the garden is already beginning to look different. A winter garden full of colours and little corners I don't want every part of my garden to look the same. Some corners can be full of petunias, with flowers spilling over the sides of their pots. Alyssum can soften another arrangement and fill the smaller spaces around other plants. Then there are the quieter corners. I like having ferns, snake plants, and coleus around too. They aren't there to replace the winter flowers. They give the garden something to look at between the blooms, with different leaf shapes, textures, and shades of green. Coleus is especially fun when I want foliage to bring some colour of its own. And then there is the edible side of the garden. I enjoy growing things that eventually make their way into the kitchen. Spinach and other leafy greens, radishes, carrots, lettuce, herbs, and strawberries all have their own place. They make the garden feel less like something I only look at and more like something I take part in. I don't need every corner to do the same job. One can be bright and full of flowers, another mostly foliage, while somewhere else I might have vegetables growing in a pot that I check every morning. That mix is what makes the garden feel like mine. Arranging plants in pots I especially enjoy putting different plants together in one container. I don't always want a single plant sitting alone in a pot. I like combining different shapes, heights, colours, and growing habits so the arrangement changes as you look at it. For this I like the thriller, filler, and spiller approach. Something taller gives the pot some height, fuller plants fill the space around it, and trailing plants spill over the edge. Petunias are wonderful for that last part once they start growing over the sides. Alyssum can fill smaller gaps and soften the edges, while a taller plant gives the whole pot some structure. I enjoy picturing all of that before I start planting. Of course, plants rarely follow the picture in my head. One grows faster than another. Something needs more room than I expected. A plant that looked perfectly placed when I first arranged the pot can look crowded a few weeks later. So I move things around. Sometimes changing the position of one plant makes the whole pot look different. Sometimes I swap one companion for another. And sometimes the combination I didn't expect to work becomes the one I like most. That's what I enjoy about arranging pots. There's always another combination I want to try. Between coding and gardening Most of my working day is spent coding, and when I'm working, I like being completely focused on it. I enjoy getting deep into a problem, understanding how the pieces fit together, and staying with it until I find a solution. Gardening gives me something completely different to focus on. When I step away from my laptop, I might go outside, look at the pots, and notice something that needs attention. An empty pot might give me an idea. A plant that has grown more than I expected might make me rethink the corner around it. Sometimes I don't even do anything. I just walk around and look. There is a small similarity to designing something before building it in code. I think about the different pieces, imagine how they might fit together, try a few possibilities, and sometimes change the whole plan before I start. But the garden has one rule that software doesn't: I can't make it happen faster just because I'm ready. I can prepare the soil, choose the plants, arrange the pots, and give everything the space it needs. After that, the plants take over. A petunia doesn't bloom because I'm impatient to see the final arrangement. A spinach plant doesn't grow faster because I keep checking whether it is ready to harvest. They take their time. And I like that. Getting ready for the season For me, winter gardening isn't only about the garden when it is finally full of flowers. I enjoy everything that comes before that too. There are pots to clean, soil to refresh, plants to choose, and arrangements to rethink. I get to decide what I want to try this year without knowing exactly how it will all turn out. Some combinations will work the way I imagined. Some won't. A plant might grow in an unexpected direction. Something I thought would be a small part of an arrangement might become the thing I notice most. A simple combination might turn out better than the complicated one I spent much longer planning. Sometimes a plant just doesn't cooperate with my plan, and that's fine. I can move it, give it more space, pair it with something else, or try a different spot. The garden doesn't mind if I change my mind. A little space to create something of my own I've already started shaping a few corners into what I imagined. Some days I spend more time with the flowering plants. Other days I find myself looking at the spinach, the herbs, or the strawberries and noticing how much they've changed. That's one thing I love about growing so many different kinds of plants. There is almost always something happening somewhere. Eventually, I'll come back inside, clean up, open my laptop, and return to my work. I may not come back with a brilliant new idea. Maybe I'll simply feel happy about the little corner I've started creating. And I think that's enough. Not everything has to become a lesson. Sometimes it's enough to step away from a screen, spend time doing something I love, and watch it grow at its own pace. What about you? Is there something outside your work that you look forward to, even before it begins? title: I Built a New Tab Extension for DEV
summary: Jessica Doering Posted on Oct 18 I Built a New Tab Extension for DEV # showdev # webdev # opensource # javascript Includes tag filters and offline caching details I spend a lot of time on DEV these days. Reading posts, finding interesting projects, participating in challenges, and occasionally writing something myself. I also like daily.dev. Having a feed of developer content right there whenever I open a new tab is pretty convenient. So naturally, I started thinking... what if I had something like that, but just for DEV? And because apparently I can't have an idea without turning it into another project, I built one. It's called DEV Tab , and it's a free, open-source browser extension that replaces your new tab page with a feed of posts from DEV. It's now available on the Chrome Web Store. Install DEV Tab for Chrome Firefox support is built too, and the add-on is currently awaiting review. I'll update this post with the link once it's approved. A little more than just a feed The original idea was pretty simple. Open a new tab, see what's happening on DEV, and click through to anything interesting. But, as usual, I kept thinking of things to add. You can browse posts from Today, This Week, Rising, and Latest, along with dedicated sections for trends, events, podcasts, and videos. There are also tag filters, so you can quickly jump between subjects you're interested in. You can save your favorite tags, hide tags you'd rather not see, and follow posts from specific DEV organizations. A few other things I added: Search directly from the new tab page. Keyboard navigation using arrow keys and Enter. A compact view if you'd rather see more posts and fewer images. Reaction counts and previews of the three newest comments. A shortcut to create a new DEV post. Feed caching, so opening a new tab doesn't mean waiting for everything to load again. Nothing particularly revolutionary here. I just wanted a convenient way to explore DEV without having to go looking for things. Then I decided it needed a dashboard This part wasn't in my original plan, but I spend enough time writing on DEV that I thought having a better overview of my own activity would be useful. If you add your DEV API key in the extension settings, you unlock some additional features, including a personal dashboard. The dashboard includes your follower count, views, reactions, comments, and new followers, with options to look at the last 7, 30, or 90 days. There's also a daily views chart, an activity heatmap that lets you browse previous years, and a list of your published posts and drafts. You can see recent followers, top supporters, and where your readers are coming from, too. I particularly like having the activity heatmap and post statistics together. It's interesting to look back and see when I was active and how different posts performed. The dashboard screenshot above uses fictional example data, by the way. Connecting your DEV account is completely optional You don't need an account or API key to use the extension. The public feeds, search, filters, and other browsing features work without one. But if you do connect your DEV account, you also get access to your personal feed based on the tags you follow, your reading list, and semantic search. You can generate an API key from your DEV settings . The extension doesn't have a backend, analytics, or tracking. Your API key stays in your browser's local extension storage and is only sent to DEV for authenticated API requests. I wanted to keep it simple and avoid introducing a separate service just to display information DEV already makes available. A few limitations There are a couple of things I would have liked to include but couldn't because of the DEV API. For example, you can't directly react to posts, leave comments, or save articles to your reading list from the extension. You can view reaction counts and preview comments, but interacting with a post opens it on DEV itself. I'd love to have those actions directly in the feed someday, but for now, that's a limitation of what's available through the API. Built with WXT, React, and TypeScript I used WXT for the extension framework, along with React and TypeScript. This was my first time using WXT, and I really liked being able to build for Chrome and Firefox from the same codebase. One thing I spent some time on was making sure the feed wouldn't constantly refetch everything whenever a new tab opened. The first page of each feed gets cached for ten minutes, and previously loaded posts can still appear if you're offline. It's a small thing, but when you're replacing something as frequently used as the new tab page, I think it matters. Give it a try! DEV Tab is open source, so you can take a look at the code, report bugs, suggest features, or contribute if you'd like. Chrome Web Store GitHub The Firefox version is currently awaiting approval, and I'll add the link here when it's published. This started as one of those little "wouldn't it be nice if..." ideas, and somehow turned into a full browser extension with a personal analytics dashboard. I guess that's what happens when you keep finding things you want to build. If you use DEV regularly, I'd love to hear what you think! And if there's something you'd find useful in a future version, let me know. title: Your agent's retry bug isn't an AI problem. It's a distributed-systems problem with an LLM on top.
summary: Dimitris Kyrkos Posted on Oct 19 Your agent's retry bug isn't an AI problem. It's a distributed-systems problem with an LLM on top. # ai # programming # architecture # discuss Most agent demos have a happy path: the model picks a tool, the tool returns 200, the agent moves on. Production is different. In production, the tool call sometimes returns nothing at all. That is where a correct decision turns into a wrong outcome. The gap between "decided" and "done" Here is an illustrative scenario (not a real incident, but a very ordinary one). An agent handles a support ticket and decides the customer is owed a refund. It calls POST /refunds . The payments service processes the refund, writes it to its ledger, and starts sending the response. The network hiccups. The agent's HTTP client hits its timeout and raises an error. From the agent's point of view, the call failed. From the payment service's point of view, it succeeded. The agent's loop sees an error, and the most natural thing for it to do is try again. Now the customer has two refunds. The model reasoned perfectly. It picked the right action with the right arguments. Nothing about better prompting, a bigger model, or a smarter planner fixes this, because the failure happened after the reasoning was over. Failure mode 1: treating a timeout as a "no" A timeout tells you one thing: you didn't get an answer. It does not tell you the action didn't happen. Agent frameworks that wrap tool errors into "the tool failed, decide what to do next" collapse three different situations into one: the request never reached the service the request reached it and was rejected the request reached it, succeeded, and the response was lost Only the first two are safe to retry blindly. Failure mode 2: no idempotency key If the agent had sent an idempotency key, the second refund call would have been a no-op that returned the original result. The key has to be generated by the application before the first attempt and reused on every retry of that same intent: intent = actions . record_intent ( kind = " refund " , order_id = order . id , amount = amount , idempotency_key = uuid4 (), # created once, stored with the intent ) try : result = payments . refund ( order_id = order . id , amount = amount , idempotency_key = intent . idempotency_key , ) actions . mark_confirmed ( intent . id , result ) except Timeout : actions . mark_unknown ( intent . id ) # NOT "failed" Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode The important part is where the key lives. If the model generates it, or if it's regenerated per attempt, it protects nothing. Failure mode 3: state that only exists in the context window If the record of "I already tried to refund order 4812" lives only in the conversation history, it disappears on a crash, a context truncation, or a restart of the worker. The intent needs to be written to durable storage before execution, so that whatever process picks the work back up can see it. Failure mode 4: no "outcome unknown" state Most action models have two terminal states: success and failure. Reliable ones need at least: submitted : we sent it, no answer yet confirmed : the downstream system acknowledged it failed : the downstream system explicitly rejected it unknown : we can't tell unknown is the one that matters. It's the state that should block automatic retries and trigger reconciliation instead. Failure mode 5: no reconciliation path When an action lands in unknown , something has to go find out the truth: query the payment service by idempotency key or order ID, compare against the ledger, and then move the intent to confirmed or failed . That can be a background job, a scheduled check, or a human queue for high-value actions. What it can't be is the agent deciding "probably fine" or "probably failed" on its own. The reframe Agent tool use is really remote procedure calls with an LLM choosing which procedure to call. Everything we already know about RPCs over unreliable networks still applies: idempotency, durable intent logs, explicit uncertainty, reconciliation. The clean split is: The model proposes an action. The application owns the execution state: the key, the intent record, the status, the retry policy. "Try again" is a fine default for reads. For anything that changes state, it's only safe once you know the first attempt didn't land, or once the downstream system guarantees a retry can't double-apply. Build vs. integrate If you already run payment or order flows with idempotency keys and outbox/ledger patterns, you mostly need to route agent actions through that same machinery instead of letting the agent call APIs directly. If you don't, that's the piece to build (or adopt) first, before giving an agent write access to anything that moves money or data. How are you handling the "we don't know if it happened" case in your agent workflows? Are you blocking retries, reconciling, or escalating to a human? Like comment: Like comment: 1 like Like Comment button Reply Collapse Expand Sina Rezaei Sina Rezaei Sina Rezaei Follow Project Manager | Digital Strategist | Analytics | Creator | Full-Stack Developer | Software Engineer 🗼 🏰 ❾¾ 🦁⃝⃒⃤ 🪄 🦉 | 🇰🇷 시나 Joined Mar 8, 2023 • Oct 19 Dropdown menu Copy link Hide The concurrency angle is worth considering here too. An idempotency key protects against duplicate execution of the same logical operation, but it doesn't automatically prevent two workers from processing the same agent run at the same time. Imagine an agent coordinating a deployment across several Kubernetes clusters. A worker loses its lease while waiting for a rollout check, the queue redelivers the job, and a second worker resumes from the last persisted checkpoint. Both workers can now make decisions based on stale state, and the second worker might trigger a rollback while the first is still progressing the deployment. I'd treat run ownership and side-effect protection as separate concerns: durable workflow state, lease-based ownership with fencing tokens where supported, and idempotency keys scoped to individual business actions. The fencing part matters because an expired lease alone doesn't stop a paused worker from waking up and writing again. For external systems that don't support fencing or idempotency, reconciliation is still necessary. Retries are only one piece of the problem. The harder question is how to guarantee that a recovered workflow can't act on stale state or override a newer execution. You can prevent the same action from executing twice and still have two workers making conflicting decisions from stale state. Fencing tokens are the important detail here because an expired lease doesn't stop the old worker from waking up and writing again. Recovery needs to protect the workflow state, not just individual API calls. Like comment: Like comment: 2 likes Like Comment button Reply Collapse Expand Sina Rezaei Sina Rezaei Sina Rezaei Follow Project Manager | Digital Strategist | Analytics | Creator | Full-Stack Developer | Software Engineer 🗼 🏰 ❾¾ 🦁⃝⃒⃤ 🪄 🦉 | 🇰🇷 시나 Joined Mar 8, 2023 • Oct 19 Dropdown menu Copy link Hide One subtle issue here is that fencing only works if the system receiving the write actually enforces it. Take a multi-cluster rollout controller: worker A starts a canary deployment, loses its lease during a network partition, and worker B takes ownership, observes elevated error rates, and initiates a rollback. If A resumes and submits an update based on its old checkpoint, an idempotency key won't stop it from overwriting B's newer decision if the two operations have different keys. I'd put a monotonic execution epoch on every run and make state transitions conditional on both the expected state version and the current epoch. For Kubernetes resources, resourceVersion can help reject stale updates, but that protection doesn't automatically extend to external deployment APIs or cloud control planes. Those need their own concurrency guarantees, or a reconciliation loop that compares the desired state against the actual state before issuing corrective actions. The tricky part is making sure a stale worker can't undo a newer decision, even when the lease service, workflow store, and downstream API don't share the same transaction boundary. title: Redis 8.4's digest-based SET option cuts a 1MB compare-and-set from 4.3ms to 1.6ms
summary: Alex Georgiev Posted on Oct 19 • AI-assisted Redis 8.4's digest-based SET option cuts a 1MB compare-and-set from 4.3ms to 1.6ms # redis # database # performance # devops I keep a cached object in Redis that several workers read and occasionally rewrite. Before writing, each worker has to check that nobody else changed the object since it was last read, or the write clobbers someone else's update. Redis never had one command for that. You used WATCH / MULTI / EXEC , or a Lua script that reads and compares server-side, or you accepted the race and moved on. Redis 8.4 adds four conditions to SET : IFEQ , IFNE , IFDEQ and IFDNE . The first two compare against a literal value. The last two compare against a digest, a 16-character hex hash the server computes with DIGEST . I pulled redis:8.4 and ran all four against the patterns they replace. The headline number The point of a digest is that you don't send the value you're comparing against, you send its hash. For a small string that saves nothing. For a large one it matters. I set a 1MB string, kept a cached digest of it client-side, and timed three ways of doing a conditional overwrite 50 times each, taking the median: size classic GET-then-SET Lua script CAS SET ... IFDEQ 100 B 0.29 ms 0.17 ms 0.21 ms 10 KB 0.32 ms 0.25 ms 0.17 ms 100 KB 0.55 ms 1.10 ms 0.48 ms 1 MB 4.44 ms 7.37 ms 1.77 ms Those are medians across three separate runs of 50 trials each at every size, against a redis:8.4 container on localhost. At 1MB, the digest-based set was roughly a third of the classic GET-then-SET and under a quarter of the Lua script, while the data crossing the wire for the comparison itself dropped from 1,000,000 bytes to 16. The classic approach does a GET (full value back to the client) followed by a conditional SET (full value back to the server). The Lua script sends the full old value as an argument so the server can compare it internally. The digest option sends neither; the client already has the digest from the last time it fetched the object, and this SET just needs to check it still matches. The number that argues against it At 100 bytes to 10KB, none of the three were reliably faster than the others. The differences at that end were inside normal jitter between runs — sometimes the digest set won, sometimes the classic one did, by fractions of a millisecond either way. The benefit only shows up once the payload is large enough that transfer time, not command overhead, dominates the round trip. More surprising: the Lua script was the slowest option at every single size I tested, including 100 bytes. I expected it to win, since it does the comparison server-side in one round trip, the same as IFEQ does natively. It didn't. EVAL carries script-lookup overhead that a plain SET with a condition flag doesn't, and that overhead outweighed the round-trip savings until the value got large, and even then it never caught up to the native digest option. Separately, DIGEST itself isn't free. Its own cost scales with the value, because it has to read every byte to hash it: value size DIGEST latency (median) 100 B 0.17 ms 10 KB 0.15 ms 1 MB 1.03 ms 10 MB 6.20 ms So the win from IFDEQ is specifically a network-bytes win, not a CPU-avoidance win. If you have to call DIGEST fresh every time rather than reusing a digest you already hold from an earlier read, you've moved the cost from the wire to the server's CPU, not eliminated it. What it refuses A handful of error cases, with the exact messages: 127.0.0.1:6379> DEL mylist 127.0.0.1:6379> RPUSH mylist a b c 127.0.0.1:6379> SET mylist v IFEQ a (error) WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode 127.0.0.1:6379> SET anotherkey v NX IFEQ x (error) ERR syntax error Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode NX and IFEQ are mutually exclusive, which makes sense once you think about it: NX means "only if the key doesn't exist", IFEQ means "only if it holds a specific value", and a key can't satisfy both at once except trivially. A more useful refusal: IFEQ and IFDEQ never succeed against a key that doesn't exist, even though you might reasonably expect "the value matches what I think it should be" to include "there is no value yet". I deleted a key, then ran SET nosuch v IFEQ anything against it, and got a plain (nil) — no error, just a silent no-op, same as a normal failed condition. If your code checks IFEQ on a key that might legitimately not exist yet, you need NX as well, or a separate existence check; IFEQ alone won't create it. And a digest with the wrong shape is a hard error, not a silent failure: 127.0.0.1:6379> SET cs1 c IFDEQ zz (error) ERR must be exactly 16 hexadecimal characters Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Under concurrency The whole point of these flags is optimistic concurrency control, so I tested it directly. Twenty threads, each doing fifty read-increment-write cycles against the same ~950-byte JSON blob with a counter field inside it. Expected final count: 1,000. Plain GET then unconditional SET , no retry: naive GET+SET trial 1: final=109 lost_updates=891 naive GET+SET trial 2: final=105 lost_updates=895 naive GET+SET trial 3: final=105 lost_updates=895 Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Roughly 89 to 90 percent of increments vanished every single run. That's not a surprising result in itself — it's the textbook lost-update problem — but the size of it, with twenty threads on commodity hardware, was bigger than I expected going in. Same workload, SET ... IFEQ <old-blob> in a retry loop instead of an unconditional SET : SET...IFEQ loop trial 1: final=1000 lost_updates=0 total_retries=4892 SET...IFEQ loop trial 2: final=1000 lost_updates=0 total_retries=5111 SET...IFEQ loop trial 3: final=1000 lost_updates=0 total_retries=5111 Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Zero lost updates every run, which backs up Redis's own description of these flags as enabling "optimistic concurrency control patterns". But correctness wasn't free: getting 1,000 successful writes took on the order of 5,000 extra attempts, roughly five tries per success, because twenty threads hammering the same key collide constantly. IFEQ fixes correctness. It doesn't fix contention, and under heavy contention on one hot key, you pay for that in retries, not in lost data. What I got wrong on the way I tried the new option through redis-py 's low-level execute_command escape hatch first, the same way I'd call any command the client doesn't have a typed wrapper for yet: r . execute_command ( ' SET ' , ' gtest4 ' , ' attempted-new ' , ' IFEQ ' , ' wrong-guess ' , ' GET ' ) # -> False Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode I read that False as "the server doesn't return the old value when the condition fails, only when it succeeds", and nearly wrote that up as a limitation. It isn't true. I opened a raw socket and sent the same command by hand: $ python3 -c "..." failed-condition with GET, raw reply: b'$8\r\noriginal\r\n' Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode The server was sending the old value back correctly the whole time. redis-py 's execute_command path has a response-type table for known commands, and it doesn't yet know that SET with IFEQ and GET together returns a bulk string on a failed condition, so it falls back to treating the reply as a plain boolean and throws the actual value away. redis-py 8.1.0 does have a proper typed wrapper for this — r.set(key, value, ifeq=..., get=True) — and that one returns the real old value correctly. It's marked experimental and prints a UserWarning on every call, which is a fair trade for a command three months old. The bug is specifically in the generic low-level path, which gives no warning at all and just quietly hands you the wrong answer. If you're reaching for execute_command because your client doesn't have the new kwargs yet, check the actual reply type before you trust it. Watching it in production INFO commandstats tracks these like any other command, including failed conditional writes: $ redis-cli INFO commandstats | grep -E "cmdstat_(set|digest)" cmdstat_set:calls=3,usec=38,usec_per_call=12.67,rejected_calls=0,failed_calls=1 cmdstat_digest:calls=1,usec=13,usec_per_call=13.00,rejected_calls=0,failed_calls=0 Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode failed_calls on set rises every time an IFEQ / IFNE / IFDEQ / IFDNE condition doesn't match. That's a cheap way to watch contention on a hot key in production without instrumenting your own retry loop: if that counter is climbing fast relative to successful set calls, you have the same problem my twenty threads had. Run it yourself docker run -d --name redistest -p 16379:6379 redis:8.4 pip install redis python3 - << ' EOF ' import redis r = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=16379, decode_responses=True) r.set('k', 'v1') print(r.set('k', 'v2', ifeq='v1')) # True, condition matched print(r.get('k')) # v2 digest = r.execute_command('DIGEST', 'k') print(r.set('k', 'v3', ifdeq=digest)) # True, digest matched print(r.get('k')) # v3 EOF Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode The bandwidth/latency comparison and the twenty-worker concurrency test are both plain Python scripts against that same container; the core of the concurrency test is this loop, run on twenty threads at once: while True : blob = rr . get ( key ) c = parse_counter ( blob ) ok = rr . execute_command ( ' SET ' , key , make_blob ( c + 1 ), ' IFEQ ' , blob ) if ok : break Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode If you're already doing optimistic locking against Redis with WATCH / MULTI / EXEC or a Lua script, IFEQ replaces the common case in one round trip and one command. If the values you're comparing are large and you already keep a digest of the last version you read, reach for IFDEQ instead of IFEQ and skip sending the payload twice. Check whichever client library you use against its raw reply before trusting the boolean it hands back on a brand-new command — the server was right in my case; the convenience wrapper around it was not.
