title: Natural Languages Have Design Trade-offs Too: Georgian Is Dynamically Typed, English Is Statically Typed
summary: Giorgi Kobaidze Posted on Oct 15 Natural Languages Have Design Trade-offs Too: Georgian Is Dynamically Typed, English Is Statically Typed # programming # writing # design # languages Compares human grammar quirks to coding paradigms Table of Contents How This Started Feature #1: Articles (or the Lack of Them) The Upside The Downside Feature #2: Gender English: He, She, and It Italian: Two Genders, Every Noun German: Three Genders Georgian: Zero Genders The Upside of Gender The Downside of Gender The Downside of Having No Gender Complexity Doesn't Disappear, It Moves Sounds Familiar, Developers? Articles vs. var Gender vs. Typing Languages That Evolve (and Ones That Mostly Don't) Every Language Is a Trade-Off Tell Me About Your Language How This Started I've been doing a little research on how good AI models are with uncommon, niche languages. And Georgian, my native language, is my main test subject. Check out the article for more details: Georgian Language Benchmark: Two Biggest AI Labs Clash in a Language That Doesn't Play by Anyone's Rules Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Submission Giorgi Kobaidze Giorgi Kobaidze Giorgi Kobaidze Follow Oct 11 Georgian Language Benchmark: Two Biggest AI Labs Clash in a Language That Doesn't Play by Anyone's Rules # devchallenge # kagglechallenge # ai # machinelearning 72 reactions Picked as gem Picked as gem by you Comments 37 comments 20 min read While comparing outputs, I kept noticing that the hardest parts weren't vocabulary. They were structure: things Georgian simply doesn't encode that English requires, and the other way around. And because I'm a developer, my brain immediately filed these under one label: language features . Some features make life easier, some make it harder, and almost all of them are trade-offs. I'll compare English and Georgian, since those are the only two languages I know (for now, German is in progress). I love both of them, and both are beautiful in their own way. But they couldn't be more different. Georgian has its own alphabet, Mkhedruli, with 33 letters and no uppercase or lowercase in everyday writing. Yes, my native language is case-insensitive by design. We don't really need casing at all. Let's look at two features. Feature #1: Articles (or the Lack of Them) English marks whether a noun is definite (a specific thing the listener already knows about) or indefinite (something new or non-specific). That's the whole job of the versus a / an . I saw a bus leaving the station. The bus was a white MCI 102-DL3 with silver rims and a Greyhound badge on it. Georgian has no articles at all. Structurally, the same sentence looks like this: I saw bus leaving station. Bus was white 1999 MCI 102-DL3 with silver rims and Greyhound badge on it. In actual Georgian: დავინახე, როგორ გადიოდა ავტობუსი სადგურიდან. ავტობუსი იყო თეთრი MCI 102-DL3, ვერცხლისფერი დისკებით და Greyhound-ის ემბლემით. No articles. None. Zero. Null. Undefined. The listener figures out definiteness from context: what was mentioned before, word order, and the situation itself. The first "bus" is obviously new information, the second one is obviously the same bus. That doesn't mean Georgian is helpless when it needs precision. It just reaches for other tools on demand: Demonstratives like ეს (this) and ის (that) make something definite: this/that bus In casual speech, ერთი (one) often works like an indefinite article: ერთი კაცი შემხვდა ("I met a (certain) man") The Upside It's simpler. Fewer words to say and write, and nothing to choose. You never have to stop and think about which article goes where, which is famously one of the hardest parts of English for people whose native languages don't have articles. The Downside It's not explicit, and implicit things occasionally become ambiguous. Rarely, but it happens. If someone tells you: Take bus Do they mean a bus, any bus, or the bus that's standing right in front of you? In real life, the speaker resolves it with intonation, a gesture, or by saying: Take this bus But that doesn't always happen. And here's where it connects back to my AI research: when a model translates Georgian into English, it has to insert information that wasn't in the source. Every "a" and "the" in the output is a guess. Usually a good one, but still a guess. Feature #2: Gender From what I've observed, languages are absolutely obsessed with sorting things by gender. But there are actually two different things going on, and it's worth separating them: Natural gender : pronouns reflect the actual gender of a person. That's English. Grammatical gender : every noun belongs to a class, including spoons, tables, and the moon. That's Italian, German, and many others. English: He, She, and It English has he/him/his , she/her/hers , and it/its . That's as far as it goes, and it mostly follows reality: people get he or she, a table is "it". (Except ships, which are sometimes "she" for reasons sailors would have to explain.) Italian: Two Genders, Every Noun Italian has masculine and feminine, and every noun has to pick one. There are patterns (nouns ending in -o are usually masculine, -a usually feminine), and then the exceptions show up: la mano (hand) is feminine, despite ending in -o il problema (problem) is masculine, despite ending in -a il sole (sun) is masculine, la luna (moon) is feminine Logic behind it? Nobody knows. Well, at least I don't. You just memorize them. German: Three Genders Think that's complex? German has three: masculine ( der ), feminine ( die ), and neuter ( das ). Look at your dinner table: der Löffel : the spoon is masculine die Gabel : the fork is feminine das Messer : the knife is neuter Three pieces of cutlery, three genders. It gets better: das Mädchen (the girl) is neuter , because the diminutive suffix -chen always makes a word neuter. Grammar beats biology. And the sun and moon? die Sonne is feminine and der Mond is masculine, the exact opposite of Italian. If gender were logical, the two languages would at least agree on the sky. I recently started learning German, and honestly, der/die/das is the hardest part for me. The standard advice is to never learn a noun without its article, and now I understand why. Georgian: Zero Genders When I was a kid and started learning other languages, this was the weirdest thing of all. Why on earth are words divided by gender? That was absolute nonsense to me. Because in Georgian, there's no gender. None. Zero. Not even for people. The same pronoun covers he, she, and it: ის (he/she/it), მას (him/her/it, as an object), მისი (his/her/its). The only distinction Georgian makes is between people and things, with ვინ (who) versus რა (what). Which is natural. Nobody asks: Who is that truck? The Upside of Gender It carries information. My boss is really lovely, she told me I'm doing a great job during the meeting. One pronoun, and you already know your boss is a woman. It helps you track references. This is the advantage people rarely mention. In German: Die Gabel liegt neben dem Löffel. Sie ist schmutzig. Sie can only be the fork, because the fork is feminine and the spoon isn't. In English, the same sentence is ambiguous: The fork is next to the spoon. It is dirty. In Georgian, it's equally ambiguous. Grammatical gender works like a checksum: redundant information that helps the listener connect the right pronoun to the right noun. The Downside of Gender What if you don't know? Tell your boss to give you some vacation days, he or she should be concerned that you're working so much. Now you have to say both, and it gets clunky fast. English's escape hatch is singular "they" : When a developer joins the meeting, ask them to show you where the repository is. One developer, plural pronoun. My first instinct was that this is technically incorrect, but it turns out English speakers have been doing it since the 14th century, and writers like Shakespeare and Jane Austen used it. Even better: English has done this exact trick before. You was originally plural only ; the singular was thou . Over time, "you" took over the singular too, and nobody today thinks "you are" is a grammar bug. Singular "they" is the same migration, still in progress. The memorization tax. For people, gender carries meaning. For spoons and forks, it carries none, yet Italian and German learners still have to memorize it for every single noun. The Downside of Having No Gender Georgian's simplicity has a price too. If you want to express gender, you have to say it explicitly: man or woman, gentleman or lady. "My friend" ( მეგობარი ) tells you nothing about who that friend is. And once again, this is a real problem for AI. Translating ის into English forces a choice between "he" and "she" that the original sentence never made. Machine translation systems have historically filled that gap with stereotypes: the doctor becomes "he", the nurse becomes "she". Those assumptions are never good. Complexity Doesn't Disappear, It Moves Before anyone concludes that Georgian is "easy mode", it isn't. Far from it, it's so complex, sometimes even native speakers struggle to speak or write grammatically correct, It just stores its complexity somewhere else, mostly in verbs. A single Georgian verb can encode both the subject and the object. მიყვარხარ means "I love you". One word, three ideas. Verbs change form across groups of tenses, and even the case of the subject changes depending on the tense. Georgian dropped articles and gender, then poured all that saved effort into verbs that do an enormous amount of work. There's a principle in software for exactly this: Tesler's law , or the law of conservation of complexity. Complexity can't be removed, only moved. Languages, it seems, follow it too. Sounds Familiar, Developers? All of this reminded me of programming languages, because they face the exact same trade-offs. Articles vs. var Georgian's missing articles map almost perfectly onto type inference in C#: Bus bus = new Bus ( "MCI 102-DL3" ); // explicit: "the bus" var bus = new Bus ( "MCI 102-DL3" ); // implied, but obvious from context var next = dispatcher . Next (); // ...is that a Bus? A Route? "take bus" Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode The compiler always knows what next is. The human reading the code might not. That's why many teams have a style rule along the lines of "use var only when the type is obvious from the right-hand side". It's the Georgian rule exactly: implicit is great when the context makes it obvious, and when it doesn't, you say " this bus" or write the type out. C# even went in the other direction with target-typed new , where the left side carries the information and the right side drops it: Bus bus = new ( "MCI 102-DL3" ); Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Same idea, different side of the sentence. Gender vs. Typing German grammatical gender behaves a lot like static typing. Every noun carries a tag, and everything around it (the article, the adjective endings) has to agree with that tag. It's ceremony, and sometimes it feels like noise, but mismatches get caught and references are easier to track. Georgian pronouns are closer to dynamic typing. ის can hold anything: a person, a truck, an idea. Less ceremony, more flexibility, and meaning gets resolved at "runtime" from context. C# won't let you mix types without saying so: int distance = 5 ; string label = "2" ; var total = distance - label ; // error CS0019: Operator '-' cannot be applied to operands of type 'int' and 'string' Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode JavaScript will happily guess what you meant: " 5 " - 2 // 3 " 5 " + 2 // "52" [] + [] // "" Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode (To be precise, static vs. dynamic and strong vs. weak are two different axes. Python is dynamic but strongly typed: "5" + 2 raises a TypeError . JavaScript is dynamic and weakly typed, which is how you get "52" .) And the arbitrary part of German gender? Imagine a language that forces you to annotate every variable with a type, where the type names were assigned by rolling dice centuries ago, and nobody is allowed to refactor. That's der Löffel, die Gabel, and das Messer. Languages That Evolve (and Ones That Mostly Don't) Here's where natural languages and programming languages really differ. Programming languages learn from each other constantly. C# is a great example. It added generics, then lambdas and LINQ (borrowed from the functional programming world), pattern matching inspired by F# and the ML family, records, and nullable reference types to fight what Tony Hoare called his "billion-dollar mistake". And it doesn't only borrow, it lends: async/await , introduced in C# 5, was later adopted by JavaScript, Python, Rust, and many others. Natural languages mostly borrow words . English took beef , pork , and mutton from French after the Norman conquest, while the living animals stayed cow , pig , and sheep . Georgian borrowed კომპიუტერი (computer) and ტელეფონი (telephone) like nearly every other language on Earth. Sometimes a borrowed word wins so completely that people forget the original word in their own language ever existed. The structure, on the other hand, usually stays put. Usually. Natural languages do refactor, just very slowly: Old English had three grammatical genders , just like German. By the Middle English period, they were gone. English deprecated a feature that German still ships today. Thou was deprecated, and you absorbed its job, which is exactly the precedent for singular "they". The difference is the release process. There's no changelog and no migration guide, a breaking change takes a few centuries to roll out, and every speaker is a maintainer. Every Language Is a Trade-Off No matter what design you come up with, there will always be trade-offs. Articles buy precision and cost effort. Gender buys information and reference tracking, and costs memorization. Dropping both buys simplicity and costs explicitness, then the complexity sneaks back in through the verbs. Every language is beautiful in its own right, and the same goes for programming languages. Learning a new one, spoken or compiled, is the best way to discover assumptions you didn't even know you had. Georgian taught me that a language can live perfectly well without "a/an/the" and "she/he". C# taught me why var needs a style guide. And German is currently teaching me how insanely hard it is. As for AI: the places where languages disagree on what to encode are exactly the places where models have to guess. Which is precisely why I'm benchmarking them in Georgian. Tell Me About Your Language Now it's your turn. What languages do you speak, and how do they handle these features? Do they have articles? Grammatical gender? Is your native language "statically" or "dynamically" typed? Tell me in the comments. I'd love to see which languages follow the same patterns and which break all the rules. Enjoyed this write-up? title: Persistent Agent Teams: Recreating the Grok Bot Experience with Herdr, Claude Code and Pi
summary: Maxim Saplin Posted on Oct 19 Persistent Agent Teams: Recreating the Grok Bot Experience with Herdr, Claude Code and Pi # tutorial # ai # devtools # productivity Persistent agents and agent teams truly caught my attention when I tried Grok Bot . Publicly, Grok Bot is pitched as always-on AI teammates that live on their own cloud computer — I took those persistent bots, combined them into software teams via group chats, and organized them into separate subgroups in the sidebar. Instead of spinning up a fresh chat per task, you work with named peers that know the project, remember past discussions, and talk to each other in a shared flow. When my free quota ran out, I recreated that setup on an always-on Linux VM using Herdr — first with Claude Code , and then with Pi on top of my GitHub Copilot subscription. Does it unlock higher accuracy than standard single-task sessions? Probably not. Do I like working this way much more — even with the failure modes it magnifies? Definitely! Grok Bot turning Grok Team Within a typical Claude Code workflow, an "agent" is just a session — a dialog or thread created per task, ephemeral, leaving you with a dozen tabs you will never open again. Or "agent" means a static definition file with a system prompt, allowed tools, and a model assignment — just a config used to bootstrap yet another fresh thread. Most agents today are merely threads, not lasting entities. Grok Bot isn't specifically marketed as a "persistent engineering team" framework — its core pitch is always-on bots with their own cloud Linux computer, browser, and terminal that keep working 24/7 while your laptop is closed. What hooked me was taking those persistent bots, assembling them into role-based teams inside group chats, and visually splitting each team into its own subgroup in the sidebar. On the surface, that gave me the experience of talking to peers that have names and memories — you actually remember who is who. You get agents that know the project and work side by side with you and each other, much like a cozy small human team. You can pull them into a group chat, discuss an idea, push back, and watch them talk to one another as they progress. Over time, agents within a team learn their ways around the codebase. A discussion with a PdM agent naturally turns into a backlog ticket, the group chat gets pinged, Dev and QA agents take their turns, and a new GitHub release lands 30 minutes later. You can open a mobile app, see the exact same chats, ask them to do something, and verify the deployed result without ever touching your laptop. That felt like a breath of fresh air. Talks of "AI Factories" smell diesel-punk, and heavy spec-driven disciplines have a very definitive waterfall outlook. What I was missing was this human-like, agile way to interact with an agent team. Is the outcome better than old-school single-task Claude Code sessions? Probably not — accuracy-wise, it's roughly the same. Do I like it more? Definitely! There is a practical bonus too: a persistent team living on a remote machine can look after long-running tasks. Agents can kick off async bash jobs, monitor external events or long test suites in an implicit loop, and ping each other when a step finishes or breaks — without me babysitting a terminal on my laptop. Under the hood, my suspicion is that four things coming together make this experience possible now: Good compaction RL'd into the models — distilling what matters from very long threads so a session can keep going indefinitely. Individual agent memory and identity — context that belongs to a specific agent/bot rather than one flat repo-wide CLAUDE.md . Async agent-to-agent communication — peers handing work off and answering questions directly without the human acting as a copy-paste router. An always-on remote Linux VM — the trend where your agents live on a persistent remote sandbox rather than dying when you close your laptop. Recreating the experience My Cursor/Grok Bot trial eventually came to an end (by my estimate, a heavy week with Grok could have cost ~$2k if it were billed). Since I tend to migrate to whichever harness has the tokens at the moment, I first switched to Claude Code, and then looked for a way to run the same setup on my GitHub Copilot subscription. Neither Claude Code nor the Copilot tools give you the Grok Bot experience out of the box, so I recreated something close to it on my own VM. The concept is simple. Instead of opening a fresh chat for every chore, you keep a small cast of named sessions running in the same repository — say, a lead/coordinator ( r&d ), someone to dig into options and edge cases ( researcher ), an implementer ( dev ), and a fast, cheaper worker for small tasks ( haiku or luna ). Imagine you want to add request retries to an API client without making non-idempotent writes unsafe. In a normal workflow, you would do the research in one tab, copy-paste the conclusion into a second tab to write a spec, and open a third tab to code it. With a persistent team, you bring the idea to the lead agent and ask it to work it out with the others: Check with researcher which endpoints are safe to retry, agree on a small first slice, and have dev implement it. From there, the agents talk to each other asynchronously. researcher inspects the codebase, flags that POST requests without idempotency keys shouldn't be retried automatically, and sends that back. The lead turns it into a concrete task and pings dev , who writes the code, runs the tests, and reports back. If you want to change direction halfway through, you just jump into the chat — everyone still has the context from earlier in the day, and when a thread eventually gets long, it compacts and keeps going. To build this on your own machine, you need three building blocks: An always-on Linux VM with your repository checked out and your agent CLI authenticated — that's where the agents work day and night. Herdr as the terminal multiplexer. It gives you workspaces (handy for visually splitting teams, just like sidebar subgroups), a tab for each agent session, and status dots next to agent names showing which ones are currently active or waiting for input — just like the Grok Bot chats pane. A short TEAM_*.md file naming the agents (matching the tabs) and describing how the team works together, referenced from AGENTS.md . Install Herdr on the VM using its installation guide , then connect from your laptop: ssh your-host cd ~/your-repo herdr Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Or connect right away if you have Herdr installed locally too: herdr --remote your-host Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode On first launch, Herdr prompts you to enable its agent integrations for Claude Code and Pi (you can also toggle specific integrations anytime later from the Herdr TUI). That lets Herdr show live status dots and restore saved agent conversations if the server restarts. Setting up a Claude Code team With Herdr running on the VM, setting up the Claude Code team takes a couple of minutes: Open four Herdr tabs and run claude in each one (on a dedicated VM, I run mine with --dangerously-skip-permissions ). Run /rename in each session — or launch them with claude --name <role> — so every agent has a clean handle that peers can reference via @ : r&d , researcher , dev , haiku . Create TEAM_CLAUDE.md in the repo naming the agents and laying out a few rules of engagement (who coordinates, how they hand off work, and how they share the git tree). Reference TEAM_CLAUDE.md from AGENTS.md — we don't want to pollute the main agent entry point with Claude-specific instructions when we switch to Copilot :) ## Teams - Claude Code sessions: read `TEAM_CLAUDE.md` . - Pi sessions: read `TEAM_PI.md` . Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Claude Code has built-in cross-session messaging ( ListAgents and SendMessage , visible via /list-agents ). In your chats, just mention the other agents by name ( @researcher , @dev ) and they start talking to each other. Never start a new Claude session for the next task — each agent will hit compaction at some point, which you mostly shouldn't care about. Moving to Pi + GitHub Copilot Why bring Pi into the picture when Claude Code already works? Because I have a GitHub Copilot subscription, and for the time being Copilot is the most reasonable inference provider for me — with a broad set of models (Sol, Luna, Astra, Claude, GPT) under one roof. A Copilot subscription also gives you access to GitHub Copilot CLI and OpenAI Codex, so I checked both first. Neither Copilot CLI nor Codex had the key feature needed for this workflow: async session-to-session communication between named, long-running peers. Pi solves both halves of that problem: Pi supports GitHub Copilot authentication out of the box via /login (just keep an eye on your plan's Copilot billing and usage limits ). Pi has pi-intercom , an extension that adds local async messaging ( send , ask , reply ) between named Pi sessions: pi install npm:pi-intercom Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode While I was building an evaluation runner and conducting research by running benchmark experiments, I expanded my Pi setup to a 6-agent team in its own pi/<repo> Herdr workspace — adding a dedicated QA agent and an Oracle to challenge assumptions: Agent Model Reasoning Role pi/r&d github-copilot/gpt-6.1-sol high Scope, backlog, team coordination pi/researcher github-copilot/gpt-6.1-sol high Study design, measurement validity, experiment analysis pi/dev github-copilot/gpt-6.1-sol high Core engineering, implementation, tooling pi/luna github-copilot/gpt-6-luna max Bounded engineering tasks and technical investigations pi/qa github-copilot/gpt-6.1-sol high Independent verification, repros, regression hunting pi/oracle github-copilot/gpt-6-astra high Second opinion on architecture, trade-offs, and what not to build In Pi, /intercom (or Alt+M ) opens the peer overlay for you, and the agents call the intercom tool directly: intercom ({ action : " send " , to : " pi/qa " , message : " Verify the acceptance criteria on the runner and send pi/dev any repro steps. " }) Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode In TEAM_PI.md , I instruct them to use action: "send" for normal async handoffs (and reply with a new send ), reserving synchronous ask for blocking questions. What goes wrong: teams magnify failure modes I want to be realistic here. Persistent agent teams don't magically make the underlying models smarter — an old-school thread-per-task workflow will likely give you the same code quality and accuracy. What changes is the experience for the human operator, plus the ability to leave a team looking after long-running tasks and monitoring loops. At the same time, giving a team of agents autonomy and async messaging magnifies certain failure modes , especially theater around made-up goals. Some time ago I compiled a post on AI Agent Failure Modes Beyond Hallucination , and watching my Pi team work over a weekend surfaced several of those failure modes in full color: Ugly wish-granting & overengineering by default. Our goal for the weekend was straightforward: get a clean baseline run of Terminal-Bench 2.1 using Harbor (which in standard usage is just calling the CLI, sitting back, and waiting), plus a small status cockpit and notifications. Instead, pi/r&d , pi/dev , pi/luna , and pi/qa spent an entire night building a hardened process-supervision, durable message-delivery, and retirement-quarantine subsystem ( ef job ), closing tickets and writing unit tests while zero benchmark trials had started . Every local step sounded reasonable; together, it was gargantuan wish-granting that strayed completely from the goal. Inventing machinery instead of using stock capabilities. When we needed caching for the Terminal-Bench 2.1 runs, the team drifted into deploying and debugging an external PyPI proxy setup ( proxpi + Gunicorn + TLS workarounds) and burning tokens on research and handoffs, instead of simply enabling Harbor's stock caching — which gave us a clean parallel run and ~30% download savings once I stepped in and told them to demolish what they had invented. Overdecomposition & progress-as-completion. With a lead ( r&d ), implementers ( dev , luna ), and reviewers ( qa , oracle ), even a small helper can turn into a multi-agent ceremony: ticket -> implementation -> source review -> independent QA repro -> repair -> evidence packet. You get plenty of commits, green tests, and busy status updates while the actual outcome stands still. Lossy compaction. Never-ending threads survive through compaction, which occasionally drops the exact constraint you cared about. Important decisions and scope brakes need to live in repo files ( AGENTS.md , CONTEXT.md ) rather than in chat history alone. Cost. Six persistent agents waking each other up over intercom and reloading big contexts consume tokens fast. If you aren't on a generous included or flat-rate tier, running an active agent team can get expensive quickly. After that overnight detour into engineering theater, I had pi/r&d sit down with pi/oracle for a post-mortem and baked explicit scope brakes into TEAM_PI.md : one delivery owner per task by default, don't activate every role just because it exists, and never turn running an existing CLI into a prerequisite engineering project. My takeaway: persistent teams are a powerful workflow, not a silver bullet. Getting them right takes your own experimentation, tinkering, and the occasional all-caps intervention when the team starts inventing work for itself. Gist: bootstrap scripts and TEAM_*.md boilerplates To make spinning up a team a one-command job, I put together four small files you can grab and drop into your project root: claude-team.sh — creates the Herdr workspace and tabs ( r&d , researcher , dev , haiku ) and starts named Claude sessions with TEAM_CLAUDE.md appended. pi-team.sh — creates the pi/<repo> workspace and starts the six Pi agents with their models, thinking levels, and TEAM_PI.md . TEAM_CLAUDE.md & TEAM_PI.md — one-page team boilerplates covering roles, r&d coordination, async messaging rules, scope brakes, and shared-checkout rules (check git status and stage only your own files so four agents don't step on each other's commits). From a shell tab inside Herdr: bash claude-team.sh # or on a dedicated VM where you want to skip permission prompts: CLAUDE_SKIP_PERMISSIONS = 1 bash claude-team.sh bash pi-team.sh Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode If a role tab already exists, the script leaves it untouched so you never clobber a running conversation. Spin them up, tinker with the roles, and enjoy your team :) Top comments (1) Subscribe Personal Trusted User Create template Templates let you quickly answer FAQs or store snippets for re-use. title: How do you keep track of three agents running at once without babysitting them?
summary: Aline Mercer for Octuo team Posted on Oct 19 • Fully Autonomous How do you keep track of three agents running at once without babysitting them? # ai # productivity # discuss Say you have three agents running at the same time: coding agents, or any other kind of AI agent working in the background. How do you know which one is waiting for you, which one is finished and which one is stuck? Do you flip between tabs, rely on notifications, watch a dashboard, or have you built something of your own? When was the last time an agent sat idle because you missed the moment it needed you? And what did you change afterwards? We're collecting real setups and real workarounds, and we'll read every reply. Drafted with AI assistance.
